signals.summary: A State Council General Office guideline made public on 5 August 2025 waives care-and-education fees for children in their final pre-primary kindergarten year (the 'big class') at public kindergartens from the autumn 2025 semester, with private kindergartens required to reduce fees to match local public exemption levels. Officials said the measure benefits about 12 million children this autumn, with lost kindergarten income reimbursed jointly by central and local government (the centre covering 80%/60%/50% in western/central/eastern regions). It is China's first step toward phased free preschool education and complements the separate national childcare subsidy for under-threes.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a distinct child-investment governance move — universalising the last year of early education — for a country whose child-rights coverage here has been minimal relative to its scale. Early childhood education is the highest-return intergenerational transfer, and centralising its financing signals a shift from fragmented local pilots to a national entitlement that lowers costs at the life stage when families' earning capacity is lowest. The child × fiscal framing is explicit: Beijing is redirecting public capital toward the youngest cohort as a demographic and human-capital hedge against rapid ageing.

signals.title: Ethiopia's Pledged 2025 Deadline to End Child Marriage and FGM Arrives With Elimination Still Far Off
signals.source_name: Ministry of Women, Children and Youth (Ethiopia) / UNICEF Ethiopia
signals.summary: Ethiopia's National Costed Roadmap to End Child Marriage and FGM/C (launched by the Ministry of Women, Children and Youth with UNICEF, UNFPA and UN Women, covering 2020–2024) set a national target — reaffirmed by the government since its 2014 Girl Summit pledge — to eliminate child marriage and female genital cutting by 2025. As that 2025 deadline arrives, Ethiopia remains among the five countries with the highest child-marriage burden globally, and analyses indicate progress would have needed to be six to ten times faster to meet the goal, shifting the effective horizon toward the SDG 5.3 target of 2030.
signals.why_it_matters: Ethiopia previously had zero child-tagged signals despite one of the world's heaviest child-marriage burdens, so this fills a critical geographic gap and doubles as a foresight/accountability marker: a flagship 2025 elimination pledge lapsing tests whether costed national roadmaps translate into results or slip quietly to 2030. The intergenerational stakes are direct — each cohort of girls married early loses schooling and health, transmitting deprivation forward — and the missed milestone is a live signal for how child-rights governance in the Horn of Africa is (or is not) being funded and enforced.

signals.title: Nigeria Reaches Near-Complete State Domestication of the Child Rights Act as Federal Review Begins
signals.source_name: Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation (Nigeria)
signals.summary: Nigeria's federal government reports that all 36 states have now adopted the Child Rights Act (CRA 2003), which domesticates the Convention on the Rights of the Child, with the last northern holdouts assenting by early 2026 — a milestone in a federal system where each state legislature must separately enact the law. Alongside domestication, the government has committed to strengthen the CRA and VAPP Acts, expand child-protection services to reach 2 million children by 2030, and is conducting a legislative review of the 2003 Act to modernise it, even as implementation remains uneven due to conflicting laws (e.g. the Young Persons Act), weak enforcement capacity and low awareness.
signals.why_it_matters: Africa's most populous country was near-zero in this database, and completing CRA domestication is a structural child-rights governance event: it extends a uniform under-18 rights and protection standard across jurisdictions that previously relied on customary or religious norms permitting early marriage and other harms. The gap between formal adoption and real enforcement is itself the strategic story — a classic test of whether ratified child-rights frameworks change children's lived outcomes, with obvious intergenerational consequences for a country where children are a majority of the population.

signals.title: Kenya Advances 2025 Children Policy and Regulations to Operationalise the Children Act 2022
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Kenya's National Council for Children's Services (NCCS) has published a suite of draft regulations for public participation to operationalise the Children Act 2022 — covering care and protection, adoption, foster-care placement, kafaalah, charitable children's institutions, welfare programmes and the NCCS itself — while the Supreme Court has finalised court rules for implementing the Act. In parallel, the Kenya Children Policy (2025) updates the 2010 national policy to align with the 2010 Constitution (Article 53) and address emerging issues such as digital safety and modern exploitation, and officials have called for a dedicated Ministry of Children and child-protection units in every police station.
signals.why_it_matters: Kenya had only a single child-tagged signal despite an active reform agenda, so this documents the machinery that turns a landmark statute into enforceable protection. Operationalising regulations and a refreshed national policy embed the best-interests and child-participation principles (CRC Article 12) into everyday administrative practice — placements, adoption, institutional oversight — rather than leaving them as statutory aspiration. It is a governance-capacity signal with intergenerational reach: how well Kenya builds this implementation layer will shape child welfare and rights across East Africa's largest child cohort.

signals.title: Colombia Enacts Law 2447 of 2025 Banning Child Marriage and Early Unions Under 18 Without Exception
signals.summary: President Gustavo Petro sanctioned Law 2447 of 2025 (promulgated 13 February 2025), which eliminates all forms of early union where one or both parties are under 18, amending Civil Code Article 116 and Law 54 of 1990 to set an absolute minimum marriage age of 18 with no parental-consent exception. Congress had approved the bill unanimously in November 2024 after 17 years and eight failed attempts, and the Constitutional Court (Ruling C-039 of 2025) had days earlier confirmed the age-18 standard as constitutional, citing CEDAW and the CRC. The law also creates a National Programme of 'Life Projects for Children and Adolescents' focused on prevention in high-risk regions.
signals.why_it_matters: Colombia sets a Latin American precedent by closing the parental-consent loophole entirely, and the country was near-zero in this database's child coverage. The child-rights framing is explicit and reinforced by both legislature and Constitutional Court — treating early union as a violation of girls' rights rather than a family matter — while the accompanying prevention programme tackles the poverty and conflict drivers. Its intergenerational logic is clear: preventing early unions keeps girls in school and out of early motherhood, interrupting a cycle that transmits deprivation to the next generation.

signals.title: Peru Creates National School Feeding Programme Prioritising Indigenous Children as Child Anaemia Persists at 34.9%
signals.source_name: Agencia Andina / Ministerio de Desarrollo e Inclusión Social (DS 008-2025-MIDIS)
signals.summary: By Supreme Decree 008-2025-MIDIS, Peru's executive created the National School Feeding Programme (Programa de Alimentación Escolar, PAE) under the Ministry of Development and Social Inclusion, replacing the extinguished Wasi Mikuna programme and mandating safe, nutritious and culturally appropriate meals for public-school pupils from age three, with explicit priority for Amazonian Indigenous children (per the Culture Ministry's official database) and an initial 10-year horizon. The move comes as INEI's ENDES 2025 reported anaemia affecting 34.9% of children aged 6–35 months (43.2% rural; 56.1% in Puno) and chronic malnutrition affecting 12.1% of under-fives, alongside the 2024–2030 Multisectoral Plan to Reduce Maternal-Infant Anaemia led across 15 ministries.
signals.why_it_matters: Peru's child coverage here was minimal, and this pairs a concrete governance instrument (a new decree-created programme with a decade-long mandate) with fresh national child-health data, sharpening a child × Indigenous-equity lens the database lacked. Targeting Indigenous Amazonian children directly confronts the sharpest geographic and ethnic disparities in early-childhood nutrition, and framing anaemia and stunting as human-capital threats makes the intergenerational stakes explicit: iron deficiency and chronic malnutrition in the first years permanently constrain cognition, schooling and lifetime productivity.

signals.title: UNICEF Argentina Reports Child Poverty Fell to 42.3% in 2025 but Warns of a 2026 Rebound
signals.summary: A UNICEF Argentina report released on 9 June 2026, based on official data, found that child poverty fell to 42.3% in the second half of 2025 — its lowest level since 2018 — meaning about 5.1 million under-18s in poor households (down from 6.3 million a year earlier), with child extreme poverty at 9.4% (1.1 million children). The agency stressed the recovery is fragile and projected a rebound to about 44.4% in the first half of 2026, noted that children remain far poorer than the general population (42.3% vs 28.2%), and that 42.8% of children face at least one non-monetary deprivation in housing, sanitation, water or education, with cash transfers doing much of the heavy lifting.
signals.why_it_matters: Argentina's under-18s bear poverty at roughly 1.5 times the national rate, making children the front line of the country's fiscal-adjustment story — a child × intergenerational-equity dynamic the database under-tracks. UNICEF's warning that gains could reverse in 2026 frames child poverty as a policy choice contingent on the design and durability of social transfers, not an accident, and quantifies the human-capital exposure: sustained early-childhood deprivation depresses schooling, health and lifetime earnings, locking today's fiscal decisions into tomorrow's generational outcomes.

signals.title: UN Child Rights Committee Advances General Comment 27 on Children's Access to Justice After Consultation With 7,200+ Children
signals.source_name: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (OHCHR)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child is finalising General Comment No. 27 (CRC/C/GC/27) on children's right to access to justice and to an effective remedy, the authoritative interpretation States parties use to implement the Convention. The Committee adopted the concept note at its 95th session (January 2024), issued the draft for public consultation, and closed submissions on 30 June 2025 after receiving 315 written submissions and the outcomes of over 141 consultations, of which more than 82 directly involved at least 7,215 children. The draft affirms that access to justice and effective, timely remedy are integral primary obligations of States parties and that all CRC rights must ultimately be justiciable for children.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a CHILD x CRC INSTITUTIONAL standard-setting event: a treaty body converting the abstract right 'to be heard' into a binding interpretive framework specifically for under-18s, distinct from generic access-to-justice or youth-council mechanisms. By grounding the drafting in structured consultation with thousands of children, the Committee is operationalising CRC Article 12 inside its own norm-production, setting the multilateral benchmark against which national children's-rights remedies, complaints systems and child-friendly courts will be assessed for years.

signals.title: UNICEF Innocenti Report Card 19 Finds Child Well-Being in Rich Nations Stalled or Reversed Post-Pandemic
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In May 2025 UNICEF's Global Office of Research and Foresight (Innocenti) published Report Card 19, 'Child Well-Being in an Unpredictable World', the flagship league table ranking 43 OECD/EU countries on children's mental well-being, physical health and skills. Updating Report Card 16 (2020) to 2022 data, it finds that after 25 years of gains, life satisfaction is deteriorating, obesity is rising and academic skills are falling in most countries, driven by the 'three Cs' (COVID-19, conflict, climate) and 'two Ds' (digital technology, demographic change). The Netherlands, Denmark and France rank highest; Mexico, Turkiye and Chile lowest.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the principal multilateral CHILD monitoring instrument for wealthy states, and its verdict reframes child well-being as a fragile public good vulnerable to macro shocks rather than a steadily improving baseline. For intergenerational equity it supplies comparative, government-facing evidence that today's children in rich democracies are losing ground on happiness and learning even amid national wealth – a direct challenge to the assumption that each generation inherits a better childhood, and a data anchor for child-budgeting and CRC accountability.

signals.title: UN Child Rights Committee's Seventh OPIC Follow-Up Report Grades State Compliance With Individual Child Complaints
signals.source_name: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (OHCHR)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 5 March 2025 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child issued its Seventh Follow-Up Progress Report on individual communications under the Optional Protocol on a communications procedure (OPIC / the third optional protocol to the CRC), the quasi-judicial mechanism through which children or their representatives complain of rights violations after exhausting domestic remedies. The report reviewed follow-up to 11 Views adopted between May 2020 and September 2023, closing seven cases and keeping four open. Cases against Belgium, Georgia and Spain were rated 'A' (largely satisfactory compliance) while three involving Switzerland and one further Spanish case received a 'B' (partial compliance), with the Committee flagging inconsistent treatment of compensation as a remedy.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the accountability spine of the CHILD x CRC INSTITUTIONAL system: the only global mechanism where individual children can hold States legally answerable, and the follow-up report is where enforcement is actually scored. Its findings – partial compliance and uneven redress – expose the gap between children's formal standing before a treaty body and real remedy, informing why states such as South Africa and Australia still refuse to ratify OPIC and why access-to-justice reform (General Comment 27) is being prioritised in parallel.

signals.title: African Children's Rights Committee Sets New Normative Agenda on Disability, Digital Space and Climate at 47th Session
signals.source_name: African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child
signals.summary: At its 47th Ordinary Session in Maseru, Lesotho (17–25 April 2026), the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) considered the inception report for a new General Comment on Article 13 of the African Children's Charter (rights of children with disabilities) and resolved to develop further normative guidance, including a General Comment on Article 4 (best interests). It decided to hold future Days of General Discussion on 'Violence against children and harmful practices: Navigating the Digital Frontier' and on children's rights in the digital space, and tasked its Working Group on Climate Change and Children's Rights with drafting guidelines for member states on integrating children's rights into their NDCs and National Adaptation Plans. The Committee scheduled its 48th session for 14–24 October 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a regional CHILD x CRC INSTITUTIONAL body building a forward agenda that mirrors and localises the UN system: interpreting the African Charter for disabled children, digital-era harms and climate obligations rather than importing Euro-centric standards. The NDC/NAP guidance is especially significant for intergenerational equity – it institutionalises child-rights impact inside Africa's climate-finance and adaptation planning, positioning African children as recognised stakeholders in the continent's long-term environmental commitments.

signals.title: Council of Europe Lanzarote and Cybercrime Committees Issue Joint Standard on AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material
signals.source_name: Council of Europe (Lanzarote Committee & Cybercrime Convention Committee)
signals.summary: In 2026 the Council of Europe's Committee of the Parties to the Lanzarote Convention (protection of children against sexual exploitation and sexual abuse) and its Cybercrime Convention Committee (T-CY) adopted a joint statement on AI-generated or AI-altered child sexual exploitation and abuse material. The statement calls on the two conventions' 90-plus states parties to criminalise such material, broaden protection to victims whose likeness is used in synthetic abuse imagery, and strengthen cross-treaty cooperation. It follows the July 2025 Valletta ministerial declaration marking 15 years of the Lanzarote Convention, which mandated the Committee to keep the treaty a 'living and forward-looking instrument' amid accelerating digital transformation.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a CHILD x CRC INSTITUTIONAL move by Europe's leading regional child-protection treaty body to close a fast-emerging governance gap before it entrenches: generative AI is manufacturing abuse material at scale, and existing law often fails to cover synthetic imagery with no direct physical victim. By coordinating two conventions, the Council of Europe sets an anticipatory multilateral standard that national online-safety and criminal codes are likely to follow, protecting future cohorts of children from a harm that regulators have historically addressed only after the fact.

signals.title: Hawaii Enacts 13% Millionaire Income Tax Bracket and Progressive Restructuring via SB 3125, Preserving Cuts for Working Families
signals.summary: On 21 May 2026, Hawaii Governor Josh Green signed SB 3125 (Act 24), a comprehensive income tax reform that creates a new 13% income tax bracket for households earning over $1 million (joint filers) or $500,000 (single filers) — the highest marginal rate in the US — while preserving the historic income tax cuts passed in 2024 for lower and middle-income earners. The law pauses future rate reductions for the top four income levels (individuals over $175,000, joint filers over $350,000) and phases out several tax credits including the Renewable Energy Technologies Income Tax Credit (by 2031) and the Capital Goods Tax Credit (by 2028). The reform was driven by a projected $400 million budget shortfall by 2032 due to federal funding cuts and the cost of the 2024 tax cuts. The standard deduction will increase nearly six-fold by 2031. The law also caps the RETITC at $40 million annually starting 2027, prompting Governor Green to issue Executive Order 26-02 preserving the 2026 credit for taxpayers who made investment decisions before the law's passage.
signals.why_it_matters: SB 3125 is a direct intergenerational fiscal mechanism: it shifts the tax burden from lower and middle-income households (disproportionately younger workers and families) toward high-income earners and millionaires, while preserving the expanded standard deduction that benefits younger taxpayers with lower incomes. The mechanism — a progressive income tax restructuring with a millionaire bracket — creates dedicated fiscal capacity for climate resilience spending (the Green Fee), housing programs (Act 121 leasehold), and social services (SNAP, Medicaid) that protect younger and future generations from federal funding cuts. The simultaneous phaseout of the solar tax credit (RETITC) creates a countervailing intergenerational cost: slower renewable energy deployment means higher long-term electricity costs for younger ratepayers. The reform illustrates the live tension in intergenerational fiscal policy between near-term tax relief for working families and long-term clean energy investment. Relationship memory: connects to the Green Fee's dedicated climate revenue, the Act 121 leasehold program, and the broader pattern of US states using progressive tax design to manage intergenerational fiscal trade-offs amid federal policy uncertainty.

signals.title: Hawaii Climate Literacy Certificate Bill HB 1925 Dies in Senate Committee, Marking Third Failed Attempt
signals.summary: Hawaii House Bill 1925, which would have authorized the state Department of Education to establish a climate literacy certificate program, died in Senate committee on 27 March 2026 when the deadline for bills to pass out of committee expired. The bill had passed the House on 6 March 2026 with 18 co-sponsors. A companion measure, Senate Bill 2473, was introduced but never heard. Four identical resolutions (SCR 82, SCR 83, SCR 84, SCR 85) proposing a Climate Literacy Seal of Excellence program also died when the legislature adjourned on 8 May 2026. The bill's failure follows similar unsuccessful attempts in prior sessions, despite growing youth advocacy and the Hawaii State Youth Commission hosting climate literacy webinars in April 2026 featuring legislators and community organizations.
signals.why_it_matters: The failure of HB 1925 represents a missed opportunity to institutionalize climate literacy in Hawaii's public education system — a core intergenerational capacity-building mechanism. Climate literacy equips younger generations with the knowledge to understand and act on the environmental and civic systems shaping their futures, yet the bill's death in committee (despite passing the House) shows the structural difficulty of embedding future-generations education in annual legislative cycles. The mechanism — a legislatively authorized certificate program — would have created a durable, state-recognized climate education pathway independent of individual school or teacher discretion. The failure is particularly notable given Hawaii's status as a climate-vulnerable state with ambitious decarbonization targets (net-negative by 2045) and a landmark youth climate settlement (Navahine) that created a Youth Transportation Council but did not extend to climate literacy. Relationship memory: connects to the Navahine settlement's youth governance mechanisms, the Green Fee's resilience funding, and the broader pattern of climate education legislation facing structural barriers in US state legislatures.

signals.title: Scotland's Children's Parliament Final Report Shows 8-12-Year-Olds' AI Calls to Action Shaped National AI Strategy
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In 2026 Children's Parliament (Scotland) published the Stage 3 final report of its three-year 'Exploring Children's Rights and A.I.' project, delivered with the Scottish A.I. Alliance and The Alan Turing Institute. 140 children aged 8-12 (Primary 4-7) from schools in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Stirling, Shetland and Dundee investigated AI's impact on their rights and produced 12 collective Calls to Action across Fairness and Bias, Safety and Security, AI in Education, and Learning about AI. The report's 'Impact on policy and practice' section states the children's Calls to Action have already influenced AI policy and guidance across Scotland, connect to the government's commitment to adopt UNICEF's AI-for-children policy guidance under Scotland's 2021 AI Strategy (with the UNCRC now incorporated into Scots law via the UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024), and were showcased internationally, including via the Beneficial A.I. for Children Coalition at the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare documented CHILD x PARTICIPATION case where primary-school-age children (8-12, not youth councils of 16-30) collectively shaped national AI governance rather than being consulted symbolically. The mechanism is a structured children's-rights participation process (space, voice, audience, influence) feeding a government AI strategy backed by Scotland's UNCRC incorporation. The report is candid that durable, institutionally-owned pathways for child influence remain missing, which is itself a foresight signal on the gap between stated participation commitments and embedded power in AI governance. Relationship memory: complements round-1's Finland pre-election inclusion pilot and the CRC's forthcoming General Comment 27 on access to justice, and extends child voice into digital/AI governance distinct from adult-led AI policy signals already in the database.

signals.title: Ireland's First Lundy-Model Participation Report Logs 4,000+ Children Feeding 60 Government Decision-Making Actions
signals.source_name: Department of Children, Disability and Equality (Ireland)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In November 2025 Ireland's Minister for Children, Disability and Equality, Norma Foley, published the first implementation report of the Participation of Children and Young People in Decision-making: Action Plan 2024-2028, coordinated by Hub na nOg within the department. The report states that in the plan's first year well over 4,000 children and young people contributed directly to national policy development across education, climate, transport, rural development, food systems and health, and it documents progress on each of the 60 actions. The Action Plan and its National Participation Framework are built on the Lundy model (space, voice, audience, influence) operationalising CRC Article 12, focus on children under 18 (extending to age 24), and carry a specific remit for seldom-heard children.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the clearest live example of a Lundy-model national participation framework - the mission's target mechanism - moving from doctrine to audited delivery, making CHILD x PARTICIPATION a whole-of-government duty with an implementation report as the accountability instrument, distinct from one-off youth councils. The Lundy model (developed at Queen's University Belfast and adopted by the EU, Council of Europe, UN and multiple governments) here shows a measurable state-level uptake metric of 4,000+ children across 60 tracked actions. Relationship memory: gives the platform a 'participation with purpose' benchmark against which round-1's Finland inclusion pilot, Mexico City children's parliament legislative pathway and the forthcoming CRC General Comment 27 can be compared.

signals.title: Scotland Publishes Children's Version and Statutory Rights Assessment After Consulting Children on 2026-2040 Climate Plan
signals.summary: Alongside the final Scotland Climate Change Plan 2026-2040 (published March 2026), the Scottish Government published an updated Children's version of the plan and a full Child Rights and Wellbeing Impact Assessment (CRWIA) undertaken against the UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024. During the consultation on the draft plan (laid in Parliament on 6 November 2025), the government ran engagement events with children and organisations representing children, including sessions in schools, and states the CRWIA and Children's version were updated using the views children shared - for example on being able to participate in planning local sustainable infrastructure such as walking, wheeling and cycling routes and in developing Local Place Plans.
signals.why_it_matters: CHILD x PARTICIPATION here means children acting as statutory consultees in national climate and spatial planning, not generic youth engagement - a duty now anchored in Scotland's UNCRC incorporation. The mechanism is a legally-mandated Child Rights and Wellbeing Impact Assessment plus a child-friendly plan version, creating an audit trail from children's consultation input to a national long-term plan. This is also an intergenerational-equity structure: the cohort that will live longest under a 2040 climate pathway is given a formal voice and a rights assessment on it. Relationship memory: complements round-1's Finland pre-election inclusion pilot and the Scotland Children's Parliament AI work, and is distinct from the adult climate-assembly and future-generations-commissioner signals already in the database.

signals.title: England's DfE and Children's Commissioner Establish Under-18 Advisory Board to Shape AI-in-Education Policy
signals.summary: In 2026 the Children's Commissioner for England, partnering with the Department for Education, established a new advisory board of up to 16 children aged 16-18 from across England to give under-18s a direct say in the government's work on AI in education. Recruitment closed on 21 June 2026, with an introductory in-person meeting in London in July 2026 and six-weekly meetings (four in person) running to December 2027. Members are tasked with helping the Department understand young people's real experiences of AI and shaping its policy advice, with the Commissioner stating the board is about 'making sure that decisions which affect children are informed by children's own views and experiences' and empowering the young people themselves to shape the agenda.
signals.why_it_matters: CHILD x PARTICIPATION: this institutionalises a child advisory board inside a government department's policy process - under-18s (16-18), not a 16-30 youth council - giving children standing on AI-in-education governance. The mechanism is a children's-commissioner-brokered, multi-year advisory body with a mandate to help set its own agenda, a step beyond one-off consultation toward embedded influence. Relationship memory: pairs with the database's existing Children's Commissioner (England) signals on AI chatbots and online-world regulation and with Scotland's Children's Parliament AI project, forming a UK cluster of child-voice mechanisms specifically targeting AI governance. Confidence Medium because the board is newly established, so documented policy influence is still prospective.

signals.title: Los Angeles School District Student Advisory Councils Shape Board Resolutions on Wellness and School Climate
signals.summary: A 2026 EdSource report documents how student advisory councils in the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD), the second-largest US school district, influence district leadership and school-board decisions. Council members survey students across board districts before making recommendations, review and feed back on draft board resolutions (including LAUSD's Domestic Violence resolution) before final votes, and the Student Advisory Council makes presentations to the school board that officials say have informed decisions and conversations on student wellness, school climate and instructional supports. District officials describe the council as 'a direct line between students and District leadership,' a structured space to elevate issues and offer feedback on district initiatives and policies.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a school/district-level student council with documented influence on board policy - the mission's 'school councils with documented policy influence' target - with under-18 protagonists rather than university-age youth advocates. The mechanism is structured student advisory councils embedded in district governance, surveying peers and shaping resolutions before adoption, which operationalises CRC Article 12 inside US public-education decision-making. Relationship memory: provides a US comparison to round-1's Mexico City children's parliament legislative pathway and the Northern Ireland school-uniform child campaigners, and addresses the platform's thin school-council participation coverage. Confidence Medium because it is sourced to high-trust education media (EdSource) citing concrete district mechanisms rather than a primary district document.

signals.title: South Africa Lifts Child Support Grant to R560 and Expands ECD Subsidy in 2025 Budget, Cushioning ~13 Million Children Against a VAT Rise
signals.summary: In the 2025 National Budget (the twice-revised 'Budget 3.0'), Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana raised South Africa's Child Support Grant from R530 to R560 per month per child from 1 April 2025 — a 5.6% increase, ahead of the ~3.2% inflation rate — for the country's largest social grant, which reaches roughly 13 million children under 18 through SASSA. The budget also lifted the Early Childhood Development (ECD) subsidy paid to registered centres from R17 to R24 per day per child and funded ECD places for an additional 700,000 under-fours, with an R8.2 billion increase to the social-grants budget over the medium term explicitly framed to cushion low-income households against a phased VAT increase.
signals.why_it_matters: The Child Support Grant is the backbone of South Africa's child anti-poverty architecture and one of the largest unconditional cash transfers to children in the Global South, so an above-inflation uprating paired with a sharp ECD-subsidy rise represents a deliberate shift of fiscal resources toward the youngest, poorest cohort. Yet at R560 the grant still sits below the food-poverty line, exposing the gap between broad reach and adequacy — the core intergenerational-equity tension in a high-inequality state where child deprivation compounds into lifelong disadvantage. It is a concrete, replicable model of child-weighted social protection for other developing economies.

signals.title: India Raises PM POSHAN School-Meal 'Material Cost' by 9.5%, Adding â‚¹954 Crore for Hot Meals to 11.2 Crore Children
signals.source_name: Press Information Bureau, Government of India (Ministry of Education)
signals.summary: On 10 April 2025 India's Ministry of Education announced a 9.5% increase in the 'material cost' (ingredient) component of the Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN, formerly the Mid-Day Meal) scheme, effective 1 May 2025, raising the per-child per-school-day rate from â‚¹6.19 to â‚¹6.78 for Bal Vatika and primary classes and from â‚¹9.29 to â‚¹10.17 for upper primary. The revision is indexed to the Labour Bureau's Consumer Price Index for Rural Labourers, adds approximately â‚¹954 crore in central spending in FY2025-26, and applies across all states and union territories to the roughly 11.2 crore (112 million) children who receive one hot cooked meal each school day.
signals.why_it_matters: PM POSHAN is the world's largest school-feeding programme and India's principal instrument against child hunger and undernutrition, so inflation-indexed uprating of the ingredient rate is a governance mechanism that protects the real nutritional value of children's meals rather than letting price rises erode it. Child food security in schools is directly tied to attendance, learning and lifetime opportunity, making this a clear child-poverty-and-deprivation lever; at the same time a â‚¹6.78 per-child-per-day allocation surfaces the adequacy question at the heart of intergenerational investment. It anchors the Global South school-meals model against which programmes like Indonesia's MBG are benchmarked.

signals.title: Brazil's Bolsa Família Early-Childhood Top-Up Pays R$150 per Child Under Six to 8.4 Million Young Children
signals.source_name: Secretaria de Comunicação Social, Governo Federal do Brasil
signals.summary: Under the Novo Bolsa Família relaunched in March 2023, Brazil pays a Benefício Primeira Infância (BPI) of R$150 per month for every child aged 0–6 in a beneficiary family, layered on top of the R$600 family minimum, the R$142-per-person floor, and R$50 add-ons for children and adolescents aged 7–18, pregnant women and nursing mothers. Official figures for June 2026 show the programme reaching 19.3 million families, with 8.44 million children aged 0–6 receiving the BPI (an investment of R$1.19 billion that month) and 14.35 million children and adolescents aged 7–18 receiving the R$50 variable benefit. Government-commissioned research (MDS with the Fundação Maria Cecília Souto Vidigal) estimates Bolsa Família reduces the share of young children living in poverty or extreme poverty by 91.7%.
signals.why_it_matters: The early-childhood top-up is a deliberate intergenerational-equity design choice: it front-loads cash toward the first years of life, when material deprivation inflicts the most lasting damage to health, cognition and future earnings. As the world's flagship conditional-cash-transfer programme, Bolsa Família's child-weighted architecture is a global reference for how fiscal transfers can be structured to reach children directly rather than incidentally, and the near-elimination of extreme poverty among covered under-sixes is measurable evidence of the mechanism working. It gives the Global South a concrete counter-model to means-tested credits that exclude the poorest children.

signals.title: Scotland Publishes Statutory 2026–2031 Child Poverty Delivery Plan, Uprating the Scottish Child Payment to £28.20 With a £40 Under-One Premium
signals.summary: In March 2026 the Scottish Government published 'Bringing Hope, Building Futures,' its second statutory Tackling Child Poverty Delivery Plan (2026–2031) under the Child Poverty (Scotland) Act 2017, which sets legally binding targets including relative child poverty below 10% by 2030-31. The plan uprates the five Family Payments in line with inflation — raising the Scottish Child Payment to £28.20 per week, backed by £524 million in 2026-27 and forecast to reach over 330,000 children and keep an estimated 50,000 out of poverty — and commits to a Scottish Child Payment premium lifting payments to £40 per week for children under one from 2027-28 (about 12,000 children), alongside over £27 million for income-maximisation and debt advice. It welcomes the UK Government's abolition of the two-child limit while pressing for removal of the benefit cap.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare legally binding, time-bound national child poverty strategy: statutory targets under the 2017 Act force ministers to treat child poverty reduction as a duty rather than an aspiration, and a dedicated child cash transfer is the core delivery instrument. Age-weighting the payment toward children under one embeds an explicit intergenerational-investment logic — concentrating support in the period of deepest poverty and highest developmental return. As one of the clearest OECD examples of enforceable child-poverty governance, it is distinct from the First Minister's May 2026 programme speech already tracked, being the formal statutory plan that operationalises those commitments.

signals.title: Australia's Rent Assistance, Reaching ~3 Million Children, Up ~45% Since 2022 as 2025 Reviews Weigh Its Effect on Child Housing Poverty
signals.summary: Following statutory maximum-rate increases to Commonwealth Rent Assistance (CRA) of 15% in September 2023 and 10% in September 2024 — on top of twice-yearly CPI indexation, together the largest real increase in about 30 years and roughly 45% since March 2022 — CRA now pays up to about $291.48 per fortnight to lower-income private and community-housing renters, with around three in ten recipient households (close to 3 million children) having dependent children and receiving CRA alongside Family Tax Benefit Part A. In 2025 the Government's Economic Inclusion Advisory Committee (report released 11 March 2025) and AHURI Research Report No. 446 assessed CRA's effectiveness for low-income renting parents and children, finding the increases materially reduced rental stress but that further rises are needed because many families still spend more than 30% of income on rent.
signals.why_it_matters: Housing costs are a primary driver of after-housing-cost child poverty, and CRA is the main federal lever reaching renting families with children, so the recent real increases plus 2025 evaluations put child housing deprivation squarely on the fiscal agenda. It is a test of whether housing-benefit design keeps pace with rents fast enough to protect the living standards of the next generation, rather than letting rental stress erode the incomes of households raising children. The evidence base linking rent-assistance adequacy to child outcomes gives advocates a governance case for indexing and further uprating housing support as an intergenerational-equity measure.

signals.title: Brazil Enacts Law 15.413/2026 Guaranteeing Children and Adolescents a Right to Mental Health Care in the Public Health System
signals.source_name: Presidencia da Republica do Brasil (Planalto) - Lei No 15.413/2026
signals.summary: On 21 May 2026 Brazil enacted Law No. 15.413/2026, amending the Statute of the Child and Adolescent (Law 8.069/1990) to add Article 11-A, which guarantees every child and adolescent access to mental health programmes promoted by the Unified Health System (SUS) for the prevention and treatment of mental-health conditions. The law requires that these programmes provide basic and specialised psychosocial care, urgent/emergency care and hospital care; that professionals working with under-18s receive specific, permanent training to detect risk signals and provide follow-up; and that vulnerable children and adolescents in treatment receive all therapeutic resources free of charge or subsidised along care pathways tailored to their needs.
signals.why_it_matters: This converts child and adolescent mental health from a discretionary service into a statutory entitlement inside a universal public-health system - a concrete child x health governance mechanism rather than a strategy document. By writing under-18 mental-health access into the country's foundational child-rights statute, Brazil creates a justiciable duty and a workforce-training mandate that shape the health architecture the youngest cohort will rely on for decades, and gives the platform a Global South counterpoint to the youth-mental-health signals (WHO Atlas, New Zealand indicators) that currently dominate this cluster.

signals.title: England Adds Chickenpox to the Routine Childhood Immunisation Schedule via Combined MMRV Vaccine From January 2026
signals.summary: From 1 January 2026, all children in England are offered the combined MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella) vaccine at 12 and 18 months of age, adding routine protection against chickenpox to the existing MMR programme, following the JCVI's 2023 recommendation for a universal 2-dose varicella programme. The change is accompanied by a selective catch-up programme (November 2026 to March 2028) for older children without a history of chickenpox, and NHS England confirmed that the 2026/27 national GP catch-up campaign will focus on MMR/MMRV after recent measles outbreaks and the loss of England's measles-elimination status. Guidance was published by UKHSA on 28 November 2025 and updated in February 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: Immunisation governance for under-18s is being actively rewritten in real time: England is expanding the mandatory-schedule offer for young children even as several US states move the other way by broadening exemptions and shrinking the childhood schedule. The MMRV change and measles catch-up show the state using the routine childhood schedule as the primary instrument for protecting the health of the next generation, and give GYC a concrete data point on divergent trajectories in child-vaccination governance across high-income democracies - directly relevant to intergenerational risk when herd immunity erodes.

signals.title: India Launches Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram, a Risk-Stratified Birth-to-Three Child Health and Nutrition Programme
signals.source_name: The New Indian Express (citing Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare)
signals.summary: On 29 June 2026, Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda launched the Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) at the 16th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare, a unified national programme providing a continuum of home- and community-based care for every child from birth to 36 months. Built around the vision 'Pehle Teen Saal Sampoorna Dekhbhal', it merges the existing Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC) schemes and, for the first time, introduces a risk-stratified approach: 'at-risk' newborns receive up to nine home visits in the first 42 days and 'at-risk' children up to eight visits to age 36 months, with growth monitoring, nutrition and early-childhood-development support, post-partum maternal mental-health screening, and digital tracking integrated with the POSHAN Tracker, U-WIN and RBSK 2.0 portals via ABHA/Baal-ABHA IDs.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a large-scale child x health governance instrument that operationalises nutrition and undernutrition surveillance for the highest-risk cohort - the first 1,000 days - where stunting and wasting are decided. By tying risk-stratified home visits and growth monitoring to India's digital nutrition backbone (the POSHAN Tracker) and to Mission Poshan 2.0, SSBSK treats early-childhood health and nutrition as a governed, data-driven entitlement rather than a campaign, and gives the platform a rare Global South example of child-nutrition programme design at population scale - a dimension the gap report flags as thinly covered outside Anglo/Euro cases.

signals.title: US Reauthorizes Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Vouchers and Strengthens Pediatric Drug Rules via the Give Kids a Chance Act
signals.source_name: US Congress (H.R. 1262, enacted within Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
signals.summary: The Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act (H.R. 1262) was enacted on 3 February 2026 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, reauthorizing the FDA's Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Voucher (PRV) programme - which had lapsed at the end of 2024 - through fiscal year 2029. The law also gives the FDA authority to require pediatric trials of new combinations of cancer therapies, authorizes enforcement against companies that fail to meet pediatric study requirements under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA), and requires the FDA to disclose ingredient differences to generic applicants to speed access to more affordable medicines. The same appropriations package included pharmacy-benefit-manager reforms decoupling PBM compensation from drug list prices.
signals.why_it_matters: Children are a structurally under-served pharmaceutical market because rare pediatric diseases offer little commercial return, so the PRV incentive and PREA enforcement are core governance levers determining whether under-18s ever get approved, affordable treatments. Reviving a lapsed incentive, adding binding pediatric-trial and enforcement authority, and pairing it with generic-access transparency is a concrete child x health-access mechanism that shapes the long-run therapeutic pipeline the current child cohort will depend on - an intergenerational allocation of innovation, not just a spending line.

signals.title: US Advances School-Based Health Centers Reauthorization to 2031 as FY2026 Funds the Programme at $55 Million
signals.source_name: US Congress (H.R. 8209, School-Based Health Centers Reauthorization Act of 2026)
signals.summary: On 6 April 2026, Representatives Paul Tonko and Troy Balderson introduced H.R. 8209, the bipartisan School-Based Health Centers (SBHC) Reauthorization Act of 2026, to extend the federal SBHC grant programme (42 U.S.C. 280h-5) - currently authorized only through 2026 - to 2031 at $55 million a year, with priority for underserved communities and areas with high rates of uninsured children; the House Energy and Commerce Committee advanced the measure in May 2026. In parallel, the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, enacted 3 February 2026) funded the SBHC programme at $55 million for FY2026. More than 2,500 SBHCs currently deliver primary care, mental-health services, substance-use counselling and case management to over 6.3 million K-12 students where they spend their day.
signals.why_it_matters: School-based health centres are the main way many low-income and uninsured children access primary and mental-health care, so whether the federal grant programme is reauthorized rather than allowed to sunset is a decisive child x health governance question. Locating care inside schools reduces access barriers, cuts absenteeism and links health to educational attainment - a compounding investment in the next generation's human capital - making the reauthorization fight a concrete test of whether the state sustains delivery infrastructure for children's health as an intergenerational priority.

signals.title: England Enacts Statutory Mandatory Reporting Duty for Child Sexual Abuse in Crime and Policing Act 2026
signals.source_name: UK Public General Acts (legislation.gov.uk) / Home Office
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 29 June 2026, Home Office Circular 004/2026 recorded that specified public-order provisions of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 came into force in England and Wales, pursuant to the Crime and Policing Act 2026 (Commencement No. 1 and Saving Provision) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/689). The package includes: a new offence of concealing identity in a police-designated protest area (ss.157–159); possession of pyrotechnic articles at a protest (s.160); climbing specified memorials (s.161); a new offence of protesting outside or in the vicinity of a public office-holder's dwelling (s.162); power to impose conditions on processions, assemblies and one-person protests near places of worship (s.164); and section 165, which places a duty on a senior officer, when considering Public Order Act 1986 ss.12 and 14 conditions, to take account of relevant cumulative disruption from any procession or assembly that has taken place or is intended to take place in the same area, regardless of whether the protests share organisers, participants or timing. The circular states that this measure does not allow police to refuse permission for a procession on a particular day. The Act received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. The corpus already records the same statute's child-sexual-abuse mandatory-reporting duty; this candidate is the distinct 29 June commencement of the protest chapter.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a landmark shift in offline child-protection governance: England moves from institutional discretion to a legally enforced duty on adults responsible for children, closing the accountability gap IICSA identified after decades of unreported abuse in schools, care homes and religious settings. The core actor is the Home Office and the mechanism is a statutory reporting obligation backed by barring and a bespoke obstruction offence — deliberately distinct from online age-assurance and platform regulation, locating child safeguarding in professional and institutional duty rather than digital access control. For intergenerational governance it hard-wires a protective floor for the current child cohort and creates a durable enforcement architecture (DBS referral, criminal liability for cover-ups) that reshapes how institutions must behave toward the next generation. It also sets a benchmark against which Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland's parallel IICSA responses will be measured.
signals.update_note: Trusted lab ingest update via cursor on 2026-08-14

signals.title: Wales Launches First UK Ten-Year National Strategy to Prevent and Respond to Child Sexual Abuse
signals.summary: On 11-12 March 2026 the Welsh Government published its Strategy for Preventing and Responding to Child Sexual Abuse in Wales 2026-2036, becoming the first UK nation to adopt a decade-long, whole-system national strategy on the issue, alongside a three-year Delivery Plan for 2026-2029. The strategy is built around four objectives — preventing abuse before it happens (awareness-raising and healthy-relationships education), protecting children when concerns arise (rapid multi-agency information-sharing), supporting children and families with timely counselling and therapy, and supporting adult survivors of childhood abuse across their lifetime. It was co-produced with adult victim-survivors and safeguarding organisations including the NSPCC, Barnardo's, the Centre of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse and the Lucy Faithfull Foundation. The delivery plan commits to concrete actions including national awareness campaigns, a national child sexual abuse pathway for consistent response, a national training framework for frontline professionals, and strengthened multi-agency safeguarding arrangements.
signals.why_it_matters: This is strategic child-protection governance moving from reactive casework to a long-horizon, trauma-informed national framework — the mechanism is a statutory-adjacent government strategy with a rolling delivery plan and monitoring, deliberately spanning a full decade to outlast electoral cycles. It answers IICSA-era criticism that responses to child sexual abuse were fragmented and short-term, and its co-production with victim-survivors embeds lived experience in institutional design. For the mission it is a rare example of a devolved government treating prevention of harm to the youngest cohort as a ten-year planning commitment, complementing England's newly enacted mandatory reporting duty and offering a replicable template of prevention-plus-lifetime-support that other nations can benchmark against.

signals.title: Canada's Protecting Victims Act (Bill C-16) Enacts Sweeping Child Sexual Exploitation Criminal Code Overhaul
signals.summary: Canada's Protecting Victims Act (Bill C-16) received Royal Assent on 18 June 2026, with most reforms coming into force on 18 July 2026, in what the Department of Justice calls one of the most consequential Criminal Code overhauls in a generation for protecting children online and offline. The package creates a new offence of threatening to distribute child sexual abuse and exploitation material, extends the child-luring offence to cover sextortion, and increases penalties for non-consensual distribution of intimate images including sexual deepfakes. It creates a new offence of recruiting, pressuring or grooming youth into criminal activity, strengthens prosecution of Canadians who exploit children abroad, extends the limitation period for offences under the Mandatory Reporting Act from two to five years, and lengthens internet service providers' data-preservation requirements for CSEA material from 21 days to 12 months across all internet services including social media and app-based platforms. Mandatory minimum penalties for serious child sexual offences were also restored.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a comprehensive CSEA legislative package that treats child sexual exploitation as a governance and criminal-justice architecture problem rather than only a platform-moderation issue: the mechanism spans new substantive offences (sextortion, threat-to-distribute, recruitment into crime), extended limitation periods, restored mandatory minimums and mandated data preservation. The extension of the Mandatory Reporting Act limitation window and ISP data-retention duties connects individual accountability with systemic evidence-preservation infrastructure. For intergenerational governance it modernises the state's protective baseline for a cohort facing grooming, sextortion and AI-enabled abuse, and — arriving alongside England's mandatory reporting duty and Wales's prevention strategy — signals a coordinated Anglosphere wave of child-protection statecraft that redefines institutional and corporate obligations toward children.

signals.title: US Kinship Families Act Would Make Relative Placement the Default in Foster Care Reform
signals.summary: The Promoting Permanency Through Kinship Families Act (H.R.5583, 119th Congress), introduced in September 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, would amend Parts B and E of Title IV of the Social Security Act to make kinship (relative and 'fictive kin') placement the preferred permanency option for children who cannot safely remain with their parents. It would require state child-welfare agencies to make and document 'prompt, active, and continuous efforts' to identify and locate relatives (strengthening the current 'shall consider' standard), eliminate age-based disqualifications that block grandparents and older relatives from caring for children, and make participation in the federal kinship guardianship assistance program mandatory rather than optional for states. The bill lowers the time-in-care eligibility threshold for guardianship assistance from six months to three, removes an outdated 1996 income test so more children in foster family homes qualify for federal support, and funds new kinship placement support services (family-finding, crisis stabilisation, case management) through the Promoting Safe and Stable Families program. As of July 2026 the bill remains in committee.
signals.why_it_matters: This is structural foster-care reform aimed at the well-documented harms of the out-of-home care system: children in kinship placements have greater stability and better long-term outcomes than those in non-relative foster care, and the bill's explicit rationale cites the homelessness and criminal-justice risks facing youth who age out without a permanent family. The mechanism reworks federal fiscal levers — mandatory guardianship assistance, removal of the 1996 income test, reimbursable support services — to shift the default of the child-welfare system toward family preservation. For intergenerational equity it targets one of the most vulnerable child cohorts (children removed from home) and reallocates public resources to break intergenerational cycles of instability, complementing existing platform signals on care leavers and foster-youth housing support.

signals.title: Ethiopia Finalises Integrated Child Law With Absolute Ban on Corporal and Mental Punishment of Children
signals.source_name: Capital Ethiopia (reporting Ministry of Women and Social Affairs draft Integrated Child Law)
signals.summary: Ethiopia's Ministry of Women and Social Affairs (MOWSA) announced in early 2026 the completion of a draft Integrated Child Law, a consolidating framework that unifies scattered child-protection provisions from the country's criminal, civil, labour and family statutes into a single instrument and is moving through final legislative approval. Its most significant provision, Article 47, imposes an absolute prohibition on any act intended to punish, correct or control a child that causes physical pain or discomfort — the ban applies regardless of whether the punishment is deemed 'light' or 'severe' — and also prohibits mental punishment such as belittling, mocking or inflicting fear or a sense of inferiority. The prohibition binds parents, guardians, teachers and anyone responsible for a child's care, and the law requires positive-discipline and counselling methods in place of force. The draft defines a child as anyone under 18 and mandates special protection for vulnerable groups including children with disabilities, chronically ill children and displaced minors. The reform follows an MOWSA impact assessment finding that existing laws conflated children's issues with adult perspectives.
signals.why_it_matters: If enacted, this would place Ethiopia among the roughly 70 states worldwide (and a small minority in Africa) that fully prohibit corporal punishment of children in all settings, including the home and school, advancing the UN's SDG target 16.2 for the universal ban that Save the Children estimates is otherwise decades off pace. The mechanism is a codifying national statute that removes the traditional 'reasonable chastisement' defence and reframes discipline around child dignity — targeting the home and classroom, the settings where the youngest children are least able to seek protection. For the mission it is a Global South child-rights governance milestone that diversifies a signal base weighted toward Western digital-protection measures, and it operationalises the CRC principle that freedom from violent punishment is a baseline the current child generation carries into adulthood.

signals.title: California Enacts AB 1230 Reforming Pupil Expulsion Rehabilitation and Guaranteeing Readmission Pathways for Expelled K-12 Students
signals.summary: On 18 November 2025 California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1230 (Bonta), amending Education Code sections 48916 and 48916.1 effective 1 January 2026 to overhaul how school districts handle the expulsion of K-12 pupils and their return to school. The law requires expulsion rehabilitation plans to be individually tailored by a team of educators to the behavior that led to removal, mandates a preliminary readmission assessment at least 45 days before the end of the expulsion term, and obliges districts to help students access needed services and to remove barriers such as cost or transportation. Critically, AB 1230 narrows the grounds for refusing readmission: a district may deny return only if the pupil failed to substantially meet the rehabilitation plan despite having access to resources, or continued the documented conduct - removing the previous discretionary finding that a pupil 'continues to pose a danger to campus safety.'
signals.why_it_matters: Expulsion is the sharpest form of state-sanctioned exclusion from a child's fundamental education entitlement, and California - the largest US school system - is converting expulsion from an open-ended banishment into a time-bound, rehabilitative process with an enforceable right of return. By stripping out the vague 'continuing danger' veto and forcing districts to fund and facilitate reintegration, the reform reallocates institutional responsibility from the excluded child back onto the system, directly countering the school-to-prison pipeline that disproportionately captures disadvantaged and minority under-18s. It is a concrete governance template for treating discipline as a temporary intervention rather than a permanent forfeiture of educational opportunity.

signals.title: New York Enacts Statewide Universal Free School Meals in FY2026 Budget, Becoming Ninth US State to Guarantee Free Breakfast and Lunch to All 2.7 Million Students
signals.source_name: Office of the Governor of New York
signals.summary: Through the FY2026 Enacted Budget, signed in May 2025, New York established a permanent statewide Universal School Meals Program that took effect for the 2025-26 school year, making it the ninth US state to guarantee free breakfast and lunch to every public, charter and nonpublic school student regardless of family income. The measure - sponsored by Senator Michelle Hinchey and Assemblymember Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas - allocates $340 million (a $160 million year-on-year increase), with the state covering the meal costs of roughly 280,000 additional students not previously eligible, reaching all 2.7 million students. By December 2025 the state reported more than 150 million free meals served since September, saving families an estimated $165 per child per month. New York joins California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico and Vermont in providing permanent universal school meals.
signals.why_it_matters: Universal free school meals convert a stigmatized, means-tested benefit into a de facto entitlement of childhood, decoupling a child's daily nutrition - and the attendance, attainment and behavioral gains that flow from it - from parental income and paperwork. New York's move at scale (the largest state yet) consolidates a nine-state bloc that is building a durable, budget-backed precedent for treating school food as core educational infrastructure, and pressures the federal Universal School Meals Program Act debate. As a recurring general-fund commitment rather than a temporary waiver, it is a test of whether states will sustain child-investment entitlements against future fiscal pressure.

signals.title: Wales Completes Statutory Transition to Additional Learning Needs Framework, Replacing SEN Statements With Rights-Based Individual Development Plans to Age 25
signals.summary: In August 2025 Wales completed the four-year statutory transition from the old Special Educational Needs (SEN) framework under the Education Act 1996 to the new Additional Learning Needs (ALN) system created by the Additional Learning Needs and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018, meaning all affected children and young people should now be assessed through the ALN framework. The system replaces SEN statements with statutory Individual Development Plans (IDPs), extends the right to additional learning provision up to age 25 (beyond the old school-age limit), and embeds a duty on local authorities and NHS bodies to have due regard to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. An October 2025 review by the Education Tribunal for Wales documenting the completed transition also flagged a 53% fall in learners formally identified as having ALN, concentrated among those with low-to-moderate needs, despite rising complexity.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a full statutory redesign of how a nation guarantees education rights to disabled children, shifting from a scarce, adversarial 'statement' model toward a broader, rights-anchored entitlement (IDPs) with explicit CRC/CRPD grounding and support extended into young adulthood. It matters as a distinct devolved-jurisdiction counterpoint to England's contested SEND reforms: Wales chose statutory expansion, but the sharp drop in formal identification exposes the central governance risk of any entitlement reform - that thresholds and gatekeeping quietly narrow who actually qualifies. It is a live natural experiment in whether legislated disability-education rights translate into delivered provision.

signals.title: Bihar Bars Government School Teachers From Private Tuition and Coaching to Protect Classroom Learning Time for Public-School Children
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 11 June 2026 the Bihar Education Department issued an order barring all government school teachers from teaching at coaching centres, private tuition classes or other commercial educational institutions - whether on or off school premises - on the grounds that such activity 'adversely affects' the education of children in their own schools. The directive was circulated to District Education Officers, who were instructed to monitor compliance and initiate strict disciplinary action against violators under the teachers' code of conduct. The state framed the move as ensuring that state-paid educators devote their full professional attention to public-school pupils and remain available to students during working hours. It follows related Indian measures, including a March 2025 Directorate of Primary Education directive in Bangladesh banning the use of school classrooms for private tutoring.
signals.why_it_matters: Widespread private tuition by government teachers creates a perverse incentive to under-teach in the free public classroom and up-sell paid instruction, effectively converting a universal education entitlement into a two-tier pay-to-learn system that penalizes the poorest children. Bihar's enforcement-backed ban is a concrete accountability mechanism protecting the quality and integrity of publicly funded schooling for under-18s who cannot afford supplementary coaching, targeting a structural driver of educational inequality across South Asia. Its significance will hinge on monitoring capacity, but it signals states treating teachers' undivided classroom duty as an enforceable child-rights obligation rather than a discretionary norm.

signals.title: India's Supreme Court Rules the Constitutional Right to Education (Article 21A) Requires Gender-Segregated Toilets and Menstrual Hygiene for Schoolgirls
signals.summary: On 30 January 2026, in Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Government of India & Ors. (Writ Petition (C) No. 1000 of 2022, 2026 INSC 97), a Supreme Court of India bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan held that the fundamental right to education under Article 21A of the Constitution and the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 encompass the provision of basic menstrual hygiene management. The Court reasoned that the absence of functional gender-segregated toilets, free menstrual absorbents and safe disposal in schools operates as a structural barrier that excludes menstruating girl children - and disproportionately disabled girls - from the educational process, violating the substantive equality guarantee of Article 14 and the dignity dimension of Article 21. It ruled these measures constitute mandatory 'norms and standards' for schools under Section 19 of the RTE Act and issued directions requiring states and union territories to ensure such provision.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a landmark constitutional interpretation that treats the child's right to education as substantive rather than formal: mere enrolment is insufficient if physical conditions systematically push girls out of the classroom. By anchoring menstrual hygiene in Article 21A and RTE Section 19 norms, the Court converts a facilities and welfare issue into an enforceable, justiciable education-rights obligation on the state for tens of millions of schoolgirls, with intersectional attention to disability. It sets a globally significant precedent that constitutional education guarantees carry positive material duties - a template advocates elsewhere can invoke to compel investment in the enabling conditions of children's schooling.

signals.title: 36-Country Global Charter on Children's Care Reform Drives Deinstitutionalization, Reaffirming CRC and CRPD for Children with Disabilities
signals.source_name: GOV.UK (UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office) / Global Charter on Children's Care Reform
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Global Charter on Children's Care Reform — a UK-led initiative launched by Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy at the UN General Assembly on 24 September 2025 (after a January 2025 campaign launch in Bulgaria) — had by mid-2026 attracted 36 alliance partner governments (including Australia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Ireland, Italy, Kenya, Romania, Rwanda, Ukraine and the UK) plus UNICEF and the UN Special Representative on Violence Against Children. Charter signatories commit to strengthening families to prevent separation, prioritising family-based over institutional care, and 'progressively ending the use of institutions for children', with rolling national commitment windows running through 2026 (October–December 2025, January–March, April–June and July–September 2026). The Charter explicitly builds on the UN CRPD Committee's 2022 Guidelines on Deinstitutionalisation and reaffirms both the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and the parallel Global Coalition on Deinstitutionalization statement (April 2026) stresses that children with disabilities are disproportionately institutionalised and that organisations of persons with disabilities must be involved at all stages of reform.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a live CHILD x DISABILITY governance mechanism turning deinstitutionalization from a treaty principle into a multi-government commitment-and-review campaign. Lens: children with disabilities are the group most likely to be separated from families and placed in segregated institutions, so ending institutional care is a core disability-rights and intergenerational-justice test — whether the youngest, most excluded generation grows up in families and communities rather than closed settings. Mechanism: a signable charter with national commitment windows, technical-assistance guidance and a participating-states register, layered on the CRPD Deinstitutionalisation Guidelines and CRC/CRPD joint implementation. Relationship memory: sits alongside EU/Bulgaria/Romania DI reforms and the CRPD Committee's ongoing guidelines work, and cross-links to national signals (Kenya, Ireland) whose governments are Charter partners, giving a shared accountability spine for children's care reform.

signals.title: WHO, UNICEF and UNDESA Publish Draft Global Road Map for Universal Assistive Technology Access, Flagging Early Access for Children
signals.source_name: World Health Organization (with UNICEF and UN DESA)
signals.summary: WHO, UNICEF and the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA) opened a two-week public review (closing 14 June 2026) of a draft Global road map towards universal access to assistive technology, developed in response to Member State calls to operationalise the Global Report on Assistive Technology and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution WHA71.8. Structured around the WHO-GATE '5P' framework (People, Policy and finance, Products, Provision, Personnel), the road map urges countries to adopt cross-sectoral assistive-technology policies and sustainable financing and to develop and implement National Priority Assistive Product Lists (NAPL) spanning health, early childhood, education, disability services, care and social welfare. The draft stresses that assistive technology is relevant 'across the life course' and that early access for children — many of whom need products such as communication devices, mobility aids and hearing/vision technology to learn and develop — is 'equally critical', tying the agenda to CRPD obligations, universal health coverage and the SDGs.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the leading multilateral attempt to make CHILD x DISABILITY assistive-technology access a planned, financed entitlement rather than an out-of-pocket lottery. Lens: without assistive products, disabled children are locked out of school, play and participation, so early access is a decisive intergenerational-opportunity and equal-rights issue that shapes a whole life trajectory. Mechanism: a shared 5P road map plus National Priority Assistive Product Lists integrated into procurement, workforce and financing systems across sectors, giving ministries a template to embed AT in universal health coverage. Relationship memory: complements the WHO assistive-technology policy brief and CRPD Article 20/education provisions, and connects to national AT commitments (e.g. EU disability strategy AI/AT measures, Brazil's Novo Viver Sem Limite) — but is distinctive as a child-inclusive, life-course global implementation guide.

signals.title: New Zealand Disability Strategy 2026–2030 Adds Child-Specific Actions on Early Intervention, Youth Justice and Residential Safeguards
signals.source_name: Beehive.govt.nz (New Zealand Government) / Whaikaha – Ministry of Disabled People
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: New Zealand launched its third Disability Strategy — the New Zealand Disability Strategy 2026–2030 — on 2 December 2025 (Minister for Disability Issues Louise Upston), shortening the horizon to five years to focus agencies on measurable action across five priority outcome areas: education, employment, health, housing and justice. It carries explicit child-specific provisions: in education, a $26 million investment in early-intervention services so children's learning needs are identified earlier, plus new ways to cut wait times for specialist learning support; in justice, early intervention to reduce the number of disabled children and young people entering the youth justice system and a framework to safeguard disabled people in long-term detention and Disability Support Services-funded residential facilities. The Strategy is aligned with the Enabling Good Lives approach and the UNCRPD (New Zealand ratified in 2008), is designed to progress 14 of 17 remaining UN CRPD Committee recommendations, and commits Whaikaha to improving data and monitoring of outcomes for disabled children and young people, where current data gaps are acknowledged.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a national CHILD x DISABILITY strategy that converts CRPD commitments into funded, time-bound actions for the youngest disabled cohort. Lens: early intervention, keeping disabled children out of youth justice, and safeguarding those in residential care are direct intergenerational-equity levers — they determine whether a disabled child's life chances are shaped by early support or by segregation and detention. Mechanism: a five-year outcomes framework with a dedicated early-intervention budget line, a residential-care safeguarding framework, a monitoring approach, and explicit linkage to outstanding UN CRPD recommendations. Relationship memory: complements New Zealand's earlier Disability Support Services flexible-funding reforms and sits in the same comparative frame as Australia's NDIS/Thriving Kids reforms, showing how CRPD-aligned states are institutionalising child-specific disability provisions.

signals.title: Ireland Launches 'Inclusive Special Class' Model and Signals Section 37A Powers to Compel Places for Children with Disabilities
signals.source_name: Gov.ie – Department of Education and Youth (Ireland)
signals.summary: In April 2026 Ireland's Department of Education and Youth announced special and inclusive class provision for the 2026/2027 school year, including a new hybrid 'Inclusive Special Class' model sanctioned initially in five post-primary schools. The model lets students with additional needs learn alongside peers in mainstream classes while receiving targeted support in a special class during the day, moving flexibly between the two — an attempt to soften the special/mainstream divide and formalise inclusive practice, alongside a Budget commitment to create over 400 additional special classes. The Department is also running pilot inclusion programmes (Towards Inclusion linking mainstream and special schools, a Transitions programme, and Saibhriú), and warned that where schools have not confirmed opening required special classes, the National Council for Special Education can report under Section 37A of the Education Act 1998–2022, after which the Minister may commence a process to compel schools to provide additional capacity for children and young people with special educational needs.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a concrete CHILD x DISABILITY inclusive-education mandate that pairs a new participation model with statutory compulsion. Lens: whether disabled children can attend their local school alongside peers, rather than being placed far away or excluded, is a foundational equal-opportunity and CRPD Article 24 test that shapes lifelong inclusion. Mechanism: a hybrid inclusive-special-class design plus Section 37A powers letting the state override reluctant schools to guarantee places — rights backed by enforcement, not just aspiration.
