signals.why_it_matters: State trust lands are a textbook intergenerational asset: they were granted to Montana at statehood to generate perpetual revenue for public education, binding present governance decisions to future generations of schoolchildren. Every land swap alters the composition, location, and long-term earning potential of that intergenerational portfolio. When the process for approving swaps is streamlined with limited public input, the governance mechanism shifts from multi-stakeholder stewardship toward faster executive decision-making — which may favor short-term transaction value over long-term trust corpus preservation. The Land Board's composition (all statewide elected officials) means electoral cycles rather than fiduciary duty to future beneficiaries can drive decisions. Relationship memory: connects to Montana's coal severance tax trust fund debates, marijuana revenue allocation for conservation, and the constitutional public-land access principles that underpin Held v. Montana's environmental rights jurisprudence.

signals.title: Australia Budget 2026-27 Replaces 50% CGT Discount with Inflation-Based Discount and Caps Negative Gearing to New Builds
signals.summary: In the 2026-27 Federal Budget announced 12 May 2026, the Australian Government unveiled a major tax reform package explicitly framed as restoring intergenerational equity in housing. The 50% Capital Gains Tax discount will be replaced with an inflation-based discount from 1 July 2027, with a minimum 30% tax on gains. Negative gearing will be limited to new builds only, with existing properties held before Budget night grandfathered. A new  Working Australians Tax Offset from 2027-28 will benefit over 13 million workers.
signals.why_it_matters: This is one of the most structurally significant intergenerational fiscal reforms of 2026. By targeting the CGT discount and negative gearing — two mechanisms that disproportionately channel housing wealth to older asset holders while driving up entry costs for younger generations — the reform directly realigns tax incentives with intergenerational equity. The grandfathering design creates a deliberate transition that protects existing owners while shifting future incentives toward new supply.

signals.title: UN General Assembly Adopts Resolution Endorsing ICJ Advisory Opinion on State Climate Obligations with 141 Votes
signals.summary: On 20 May 2026, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution backing the International Court of Justice advisory opinion on state obligations regarding climate change. The resolution, led by Vanuatu, passed with 141 votes in favour, 8 against (including the US, Russia, and Israel) and 28 abstentions. It calls on all UN Member States to avoid causing significant climate and environmental damage and to uphold their Paris Agreement pledges. The resolution follows the ICJ ruling of July 2025 that States have a legal duty to protect the environment from greenhouse gas emissions.
signals.why_it_matters: The UNGA endorsement transforms the ICJ advisory opinion from a judicial statement into a political mandate with near-global backing. By linking climate obligations to rights to life, health, and an adequate standard of living, the resolution reinforces the legal architecture that youth and future generations can invoke in climate litigation. The 141-8 margin signals strong multilateral consensus despite opposition from major emitters.

signals.title: US Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act (H.R.9187) Establishes Fast-Track Solvency Process with Guaranteed Floor Vote
signals.summary: The Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act of 2026 (H.R.9187), introduced by Reps. Tom Cole (R-OK) and Tom Suozzi (D-NY), creates a 13-member Commission on Long-Term Social Security Solvency. The commission must produce bipartisan legislation (requiring 9 of 13 votes) within one year to keep Social Security solvent for at least 75 years. The 2026 Trustees Report projects trust fund depletion in 2032, triggering automatic 22% benefit cuts. The 75-year shortfall exceeds  trillion.
signals.why_it_matters: Social Security solvency is one of the largest intergenerational fiscal questions in any democracy. The 2032 depletion date means workers now in their 20s and 30s face a 22% automatic benefit cut unless Congress acts. The commission fast-track mechanism is designed to overcome gridlock that has prevented reform since 1983. The requirement that all savings stay within Social Security addresses a core trust concern: younger workers contributions should fund their own retirement, not general spending.

signals.title: Norway Deploys ICEYE SAR Satellite System for Nationwide Real-Time Flood Monitoring and Future Hazard Mapping
signals.source_name: The Journal of Space Commerce / ICEYE
signals.summary: In February 2026, Norway's Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE) awarded Finnish satellite intelligence company ICEYE a contract to provide SAR-based flood monitoring across mainland Norway and Svalbard. The system delivers automated flood extent updates every six hours during active events via ICEYE's Flood Rapid Impact service, plus detailed water depth and impact analysis every 24 hours via Flood Insights. The SAR technology images the Earth's surface regardless of cloud cover, terrain, or seasonal darkness — critical for Norway's snowmelt and precipitation-driven flooding challenges. NVE plans to use the data to calibrate hydraulic models, improve flood hazard maps, and support emergency response for years to come.
signals.why_it_matters: This deployment exemplifies climate adaptation governance with strong intergenerational dimensions. Norway is investing in persistent, satellite-based infrastructure that builds institutional capacity to protect communities from worsening flood risks driven by climate change. By calibrating models with real-world flood data and publishing intelligence on the national hazard platform (Naturhendelser.varsom.no), NVE is creating a public good whose benefits compound over time — improving preparedness for future generations while supporting evidence-based spatial planning and insurance decisions today.

signals.title: Save the Children Norway Launches Campaign Proposing Oil Fund Redirect for International Climate Finance
signals.summary: Save the Children Norway launched an advocacy campaign centered on the book 'Hva gjør vi nå?' (What do we do now?), which proposes redirecting a portion of Norway's $1.8 trillion Government Pension Fund Global (Oil Fund) toward international climate finance. The proposal argues that using sovereign wealth accumulated from fossil fuel extraction for climate action abroad would address both Norway's historical responsibility and create fiscal space within the aid budget for broader development objectives, including children's rights and intergenerational equity.
signals.why_it_matters: This campaign advances a concrete proposal at the intersection of sovereign wealth fund governance, climate finance, and intergenerational equity. It challenges Norway to deploy the financial legacy of its petroleum era — explicitly framed as wealth held for both current and future generations — to address the climate crisis that will disproportionately affect the world's children. The campaign tests whether the GPFG's intergenerational mandate can be interpreted to include spending on climate mitigation and adaptation abroad, not just long-term financial returns.

signals.title: Norway's Climate Committee 2050 Publishes Synthesis of Low-Emission Pathways Integrating Sectoral Targets and Social Fairness
signals.source_name: Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment (regjeringen.no)
signals.summary: Norway's Climate Committee 2050 (Klimautvalget 2050) — an independent expert body modeled on the UK Climate Change Committee — delivered its synthesis report of low-emission pathways for Norway's 2050 target. The report integrates cross-sectoral analysis of energy, transport, industry, agriculture and land-use transitions, explicitly assessing distributional impacts and social fairness mechanisms across income groups, regions, and generations. It recommends embedding fairness assessments in annual climate budget processes and calls for a dedicated intergenerational equity monitoring function within Norway's climate governance architecture.
signals.why_it_matters: Klimautvalget 2050's work represents a structural commitment to evidence-based, long-term climate governance in a major fossil-fuel-producing democracy. By explicitly integrating distributional and intergenerational fairness into pathway analysis and recommending institutionalized fairness monitoring, the committee advances the operationalization of intergenerational equity within national climate governance. The synthesis report positions Norway to move beyond target-setting to the harder work of managing the trade-offs, transitions, and political economy of deep decarbonization across generations.
signals.update_note: 2026-08-25 source note: shares regjeringen climate-effort explainer with climate-finance doubling signal.

signals.title: OECD 2026 Trust Survey Finds Youth–Elder Government Trust Gap Persists at Nine Points Across 38 Countries
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Published 29 June 2026, the third OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions reports 2025 fieldwork across 33 OECD member countries and five accession candidates. Overall trust in national government has stabilised at roughly 40% high or moderately high versus 43% low or no trust. Age-disaggregated analysis finds 36.9% of 18–29 year-olds trust national government compared with 45.9% of those aged 50+, a nine-point intergenerational gap present in nearly all surveyed countries. Only 31% feel the political system lets people like them have a say, despite 68% believing voting affects government decisions.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first platform signal on the 2025 OECD trust wave, updating the 2023 baseline already in the database. Stabilised headline trust masks a persistent youth deficit and a widening participation-trust disconnect — young people vote but do not feel heard. That combination is a core foresight indicator for intergenerational governance design: institutions that cannot convert formal participation into perceived voice will struggle to sustain legitimacy among the cohorts who will live longest with today's policy choices.

signals.title: Afrobarometer Round 10: Only 38% of Africans Trust Electoral Management Bodies Despite Strong Election Support
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Afrobarometer Pan-Africa Profile AD1128, released 9 February 2026 from Round 10 surveys (2024/2025), draws on 50,961 face-to-face interviews across 38 African countries. While 74% support choosing leaders through regular elections and 71% report voting — with self-reported turnout highest among older cohorts (82%) — only 38% trust their country's electoral management body 'somewhat' or 'a lot.' Perceptions of free and fair elections have declined seven points across 28 consistently tracked countries since 2014/2015, and substantial minorities fear intimidation (19%) or doubt ballot secrecy (28%).
signals.why_it_matters: On a continent where median age is 19, electoral legitimacy is the primary channel for youth institutional voice — yet the body charged with safeguarding elections is distrusted by nearly two-thirds of citizens. The turnout-trust paradox (high participation, low confidence in electoral integrity) signals a generational contract under strain: young Africans engage formally while doubting the institutions that should translate votes into responsive governance, a pattern that contextualises youth protest mobilisation across Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, and Madagascar already tracked on the platform.

signals.title: Afrobarometer Round 10 Finds Courts and Police Trusted by Only 44% as Access to Justice Stalls
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Afrobarometer Dispatch AD1189, published 2 June 2026, analyses a special Round 10 (2024/2025) access-to-justice module across 38 African countries. On average, only 44% trust courts and 44% trust police 'somewhat' or 'a lot' — well below religious leaders (64%) and traditional leaders (57%). Just 50% are confident they could obtain justice through courts; 51% believe a fair outcome is likely but only 43% expect timely resolution. A majority (51%) believe judges often decide cases based on political influence rather than law, and 81% perceive at least some judicial corruption.
signals.why_it_matters: Courts are the institutional backstop for holding power accountable to future generations — climate litigation, child-rights enforcement, and anti-corruption cases all depend on judicial trust. Continental-scale evidence that formal justice institutions trail informal leaders in public confidence, combined with perceived elite capture of courts, explains why African youth channel political energy through protest and diaspora networks rather than legal remedy. This updates the platform's Afrobarometer trust coverage from Round 9 presidential/police gaps (AD891) to Round 10 justice-system integrity.

signals.title: UN DESA Finds Institutional Distrust Rising Steeply Across Successive Birth Cohorts, Worst Among 1990s Youth
signals.source_name: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: UN DESA Policy Brief No. 184, published 18 December 2025, synthesises UNU-WIDER and World Social Report 2025 data showing institutional trust declining from one ten-year birth cohort to the next. Among 25–34 year-olds, nearly 25% of those born in the 1990s report no trust in government at all, up from 22% of 1980s-born peers and 16% of 1970s-born peers at the same age. More than half the global population now reports little or no trust in government. The brief warns that without policy action, today's teens and young adults will carry these distrust patterns forward as they age, deepening the social-contract crisis.
signals.why_it_matters: Unlike cross-sectional polls that compare today's young and old, this UN synthesis documents a cohort effect — each successive generation enters adulthood with lower baseline institutional trust. That is a structural intergenerational-equity signal: the legitimacy deficit is baked into how younger cohorts relate to the state, not a life-cycle stage they will outgrow. Future-generations institutions and redistributive social policy are framed here as trust-repair mechanisms, giving advocates a UN-backed foresight baseline for long-horizon governance planning.

signals.title: British Council G20 Survey: Youth Trust in Authoritarian Governments Rises as Established Democracies Slip
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Global Perceptions 2025, published 18 November 2025 by the British Council, surveyed 20,957 people aged 18–34 across 18 G20 countries (fieldwork April–July 2025). The UK ranks first for government trust among G20 nations at 55% (+1 point since 2023), while Canada fell three points to third place. Since 2016, youth trust in government has risen sharply for Saudi Arabia (+17 points), Türkiye (+15), and China (+13), while Canada dropped from 62% to 52% and Australia, Canada, and the US all saw attractiveness declines. The report finds liberal democracies' ten-point attractiveness lead over emerging powers has nearly vanished.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the largest recent age-capped (18–34) cross-national government-trust survey in the G20, capturing a geopolitical trust realignment among the cohort that will dominate 21st-century governance. Rising youth trust in non-democratic states alongside declining trust in established democracies reframes the intergenerational trust gap as a global competition for legitimacy — not merely domestic institutional failure. The data complicates simple 'Gen Z withdrawal' narratives and signals that youth trust follows perceived delivery and stability, making intergenerational fairness in economic outcomes a strategic variable in democratic renewal.

signals.title: Harsant PhD Synthesis Finds Local Government Youth Impact Depends on Decision-Maker Buy-In and Feedback Loops, Not Council Structure Alone
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Published 7 April 2026, Josh Harsant (University of Huddersfield PhD, 2025) synthesises qualitative case studies across four London borough participatory mechanisms — an elected youth council, a non-elected youth council, a young mayor and young advisors programme, and a remunerated young advisors project. The study asks how young people's participation impacts local government decision-making and finds impact is understood in three ways: shifting individual decision-maker behaviour, embedding youth input in routine processes, and raising awareness of youth issues. Six interrelated conditions — decision-maker buy-in, agenda negotiation, mutual learning, adult mediating roles, meaningful sustained opportunities, and recognition — determine whether participation produces influence or symbolic inclusion. Harsant proposes a seven-component framework for assessing impactful youth participation in constrained local-authority governance environments.
signals.why_it_matters: This is one of the few recent empirical studies explicitly designed to measure whether youth councils and advisory bodies change local government decisions rather than participation quality alone — the mission's core Naides gap. Its finding that impact is relational and contingent on adult responsiveness and institutional feedback loops directly challenges the assumption that creating youth councils satisfies intergenerational equity obligations. For foresight, it offers an evaluative checklist: track buy-in, agenda-setting power, and feedback mechanisms, not just council existence.

signals.title: Shelby County Youth Council Documents County Commission Resolution Adopting Youth Voice Recommendations as Policy Priorities
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: A 13 April 2026 Evidence & Policy article co-authored by Shelby County Youth Council (SCYC) youth co-researchers and BRIDGES staff documents a county-funded youth council's youth participatory action research (YPAR) project across the 2023–2024 academic year. SCYC surveyed 344 youth, held focus groups with 265 more, and synthesised recommendations on mental health, violence prevention, and public safety. After initial elected-official non-response, sustained commissioner engagement led SCYC to present at a County Commission meeting in July 2025; in September 2025 the Commission accepted a resolution to officially consider SCYC Youth Voice Summit recommendations as part of its policy and funding priorities. The article candidly notes most officials did not respond to the initial report and that durable intergenerational relationships were prerequisite to policy uptake.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare positive case where a municipal youth council's research-led recommendations were formally adopted into county policy and funding priorities — not merely heard in consultation. It demonstrates that youth council impact requires sustained YPAR, stipended youth researchers, pre-existing adult allies in elected office, and repeated public presentation rather than one-off forums. The September 2025 commission resolution is a traceable policy-outcome anchor for the participation-to-impact evidence base that remains thin globally.

signals.title: Systematic Review of 34 Studies Finds Municipal Child Participation Research Lacks Longitudinal Policy-Impact Evaluation
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Riádigos-Couso, García-Vinuesa and Gradaílle-Pernas publish a PRISMA 2020 systematic review in Children and Youth Services Review (volume 170, 2025) synthesising 34 peer-reviewed empirical studies on citizen participation of childhood and adolescence in local government. The review finds scientific interest has grown since 2012, research is predominantly qualitative and Spain-centred, and seven thematic categories dominate the literature. It concludes the field lacks longitudinal and evaluative research on impacts on governance, public policies, and power relations between children, adolescents and adults — calling explicitly for studies measuring whether municipal participation mechanisms change policy outcomes and inclusion, not just describe participation processes.
signals.why_it_matters: This meta-evidence directly confirms the platform's identified gap: even the academic literature on municipal youth and child councils rarely measures policy influence. By mapping 34 studies and naming missing evaluative methods, it provides a bibliometric baseline for tracking whether new youth-council reforms are accompanied by impact measurement or remain descriptive. Relationship memory: complements the LSE 48-study scoping review and Augsberger municipal youth-council scoping review already in the database.

signals.title: Sida Evaluation Finds GoFor Expanded Youth Decision-Making Participation in Türkiye Despite Shrinking Civic Space
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Sida published a 2026 decentralised evaluation (publication 2025:15) of the Expanding Space for Youth's Political Participation project implemented by Gençlik Örgütleri Forumu (GoFor) in Türkiye. The evaluation assessed progress on four objectives: strengthening youth organisations, expanding youth participation in decision-making, increasing sector networking, and institutional development. Despite rapidly shrinking civic space, evaluators found GoFor gave member organisations voice and safe spaces, with youth voices heard at local and national levels within Türkiye and in European and UN fora. The report recommends Sida and other donors provide core bridging funding while GoFor builds alternative revenue, noting domestic funding challenges leave a gap in rights-based youth participation advocacy.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a donor-commissioned impact evaluation in a high-constraint authoritarian-democracy context where youth participation is often assumed impossible to scale — testing whether advisory and advocacy networks can expand real decision-making access versus performative inclusion. For intergenerational governance foresight, Türkiye offers a stress-test case: when civic space contracts, measured participation gains depend on intermediary institutions (GoFor) rather than government-created youth councils alone. The evaluation's decision-making objective distinguishes it from generic youth-empowerment programming.

signals.title: Global Scoping Review of 72 Studies Finds Youth Advisory Councils Improve Wellbeing When Youth Can Observe Programme Impact
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Donohoe-Bales et al. publish a youth-co-produced systematic scoping review in Child and Adolescent Mental Health (2025; 30(4):375–391) synthesising 72 resources covering 69,297 young people aged 15–24 on mental health and wellbeing outcomes of youth participation. Participation in civic engagement, volunteering, leadership and governance, and youth advisory councils generally produced positive outcomes (empowerment, reduced anxiety/depressive symptoms), while activism and political engagement showed mixed results. Key components shaping outcomes included clear communication, supportive environments, skill-building opportunities, and — critically — observing programme impact. The review identifies knowledge gaps in underrepresented populations and geographies and argues participation design must enable youth to see their input change outcomes, not only attend meetings.
signals.why_it_matters: Although measuring wellbeing rather than policy change directly, this review supplies cross-national evidence that government-initiated youth advisory councils fail the meaningful-participation test when young people cannot observe impact — a proxy indicator for tokenistic consultation. 'Observing programme impact' as a design variable bridges the mental-health and governance literatures: participation without visible influence harms as well as excludes. For the platform's impact-measurement gap, it reinforces that advisory bodies need traceable feedback loops to count as consequential intergenerational governance, not just seat-at-the-table presence.

signals.title: OECD Employment Outlook 2025: Young People Have Borne the Brunt of Intergenerational Disparities as NEET Rates Exceed 15% in Nine OECD Countries
signals.summary: The OECD Employment Outlook 2025, published 9 July 2025 under the title Can We Get Through the Demographic Crunch?, frames population ageing as a labour-market and fiscal challenge while explicitly naming intergenerational disparities as a live policy problem. Its editorial states that young people have borne the brunt of current intergenerational disparities and face potential competition from AI for entry-level jobs. In nine OECD countries — Colombia, Costa Rica, Greece, Italy, Korea, Lithuania, Mexico, Spain and Türkiye — more than 15% of people aged 15–29 are NEET. The report calls for mobilising youth, migrants, women and older workers as untapped labour pools and links intergenerational wealth gaps to booming asset markets that have left younger cohorts facing barriers to wealth accumulation and homeownership.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a flagship OECD labour-market release that treats youth NEET not as a side indicator but as central to intergenerational fairness. By pairing NEET concentration in Southern and emerging OECD economies with explicit language on intergenerational disparities and housing-driven wealth gaps, it gives policymakers a quantitative bridge between labour exclusion and the participation-capacity problem: young people locked out of work, education and assets have less economic slack to engage in civic life. The AI-entry-job warning adds a forward-looking mechanism where technological change may compound existing generational disadvantage.

signals.title: ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026: Global Youth NEET Rate Reverses Downward Trend, Reaching 257 Million in 2025
signals.summary: ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026, published 14 January 2026, reports that progress in youth labour-market conditions is stagnating. In 2025 the global youth unemployment rate reached 12.4%, while the share of youth not in employment, education or training (NEET) reached 20.0% — meaning 257 million young people missed opportunities to build skills and experience. Following a low of 19.7% in 2023, the report warns that the recent reversal in youth NEET rates is projected to continue increasing modestly until 2027. NEET rates stood at 10.9% in high-income countries versus 27.9% in low-income countries in 2025. The report also notes that AI and automation could compound entry-level job challenges, especially for educated youth in high-income countries.
signals.why_it_matters: Where the 2024 Global Employment Trends for Youth report documented recovery, this 2026 flagship marks a structural warning: global youth exclusion is worsening again after a brief improvement. For intergenerational equity, 257 million NEET youth represent a generation losing human-capital formation at scale — and therefore losing the time, income and security that underpin meaningful civic participation. The 17-point NEET gap between high- and low-income countries shows the intergenerational contract fraying fastest where youth populations are largest.

signals.title: OECD Education at a Glance 2025: Youth NEET Rates Diverge Sharply Across Countries Despite OECD Average Holding at 14%
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Education at a Glance 2025, published 9 September 2025, dedicates Chapter A2 to youth transitions from education to work. It finds that NEET rates are below pre-pandemic levels in about half of OECD and partner countries with trend data, but have risen in almost as many — with six countries seeing increases of more than 2 percentage points. The OECD average NEET rate for 18–24 year-olds was 14% in 2024, unchanged from 2019, but national outcomes diverged sharply: Italy fell 8 percentage points while Lithuania rose 7 points. NEET exceeds 25% among 18–24 year-olds in Colombia, Türkiye and South Africa. The chapter links prolonged NEET spells to scarring effects on earnings, mental health and long-term social exclusion.
signals.why_it_matters: Stable OECD averages mask a bifurcating youth labour market in which some countries are repairing post-pandemic damage while others are accumulating a new cohort of disengaged young adults. That divergence is an intergenerational equity signal: national policy choices on school-to-work bridges, second-chance education and mental-health support determine whether young people enter adulthood with employability and civic capacity or with long-term exclusion. The report's emphasis on inactive NEETs — not just unemployed ones — highlights material and psychological barriers beyond job vacancy counts.

signals.title: Eurofound: EU Housing Affordability Crisis Disproportionately Blocks Young Adults from Independent Living and Household Formation
signals.source_name: Eurofound (European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions)
signals.summary: Eurofound's report Foundational challenges: The housing struggles of Europe's youth, published 17 December 2025, finds that young adults aged 18–39 experience Europe's housing affordability crisis more acutely than older cohorts because of lower incomes, insecure employment and concentration in high-demand urban and tourist areas. Survey evidence shows many young adults remain in the parental home when they would prefer independent or partnered living. Eurofound briefing materials note that EU property prices have risen more than 55% since 2010 while rents have tracked a similarly steep path, and that in Bulgaria, Ireland, Poland, Portugal and Spain a standard two-room rental can require more than 80% of a young worker's median wage — exceeding 100% in some coastal regions. The report links delayed independence to consequences for education, employment mobility, mental wellbeing and regional cohesion.
signals.why_it_matters: Housing precarity is one of the clearest material barriers to youth participation: young Europeans spending most of their income on rent or unable to leave the parental home have less geographic mobility, less household stability and less discretionary time for civic engagement. Eurofound's EU-agency status and cross-country rental-burden data make this a primary source for connecting intergenerational housing inequality — older cohorts benefited from earlier affordability and asset appreciation — to the participation-capacity squeeze already visible in OECD and FEPS/TASC research on youth political disengagement.

signals.title: Global Youth Participation Index 2025: Socio-Economic Barriers Score Highest but Strong Economy Does Not Guarantee Civic or Political Inclusion
signals.source_name: European Partnership for Democracy (GYPI / WYDE Civic Engagement)
signals.summary: The Global Youth Participation Index (GYPI) 2025, launched mid-June 2025 by the European Partnership for Democracy under the EU WYDE Civic Engagement programme with University of Birmingham-linked researchers and a nine-member Youth Panel, is the first systematic global index scoring 141 countries (85%+ data coverage of 41 variables) on youth participation. Four unweighted dimensions average to an overall 0–100 score: Socio-Economic (6 vars, global avg ~77), Civic Space (11, avg 62), Elections (13, avg 54) and Political Affairs (11, avg 51—the weakest). Global overall average is 61; Norway and New Zealand lead at 84; Afghanistan is last at 14. The index draws multi-source data (including the Youth Progress Index) plus 66 country consultants. Core claim: low scores measure structural barriers and closed opportunity structures, not youth apathy—youth legislative representation averages only about 12/100 and 28 countries have zero youth MPs. High socio-economic scores do not guarantee high overall GYPI (e.g. Czechia, Singapore). Nuance: GYPI measures enabling structures more than absolute activism levels; social-movement and online-debate volume remain gaps; influence of participation on policy is not scored.
signals.why_it_matters: GYPI operationalises the intergenerational-equity agency layer: material and socio-economic conditions can improve while young people remain locked out of legislatures, parties and elections. That is the same pattern the Youth Progress Index shows as Opportunity/Rights lag, and that trust-gap analyses describe as participation without power. For the platform it supplies a global country baseline for Layer B (agency and voice), reform trackers (age thresholds, quotas, automatic registration, youth party wings), and an anti-apathy interpretive rule for youth-governance signals. Pair with foresight items on youth protests, Youth Checks and future-generations institutions rather than treating GYPI as a full IE score.
signals.update_note: 2026-07-13: Primary-sourced to GYPI 2025 Final Report PDF; added methodology (4 dimensions, 41 vars, no weighting, 15–30 age band), averages, top/bottom, anti-apathy rule and structure-vs-behaviour nuance; confidence High.

signals.title: Indonesia Launches National Transfer Accounts Policy Book as Intergenerational Planning Instrument
signals.source_name: Ministry of National Development Planning (Bappenas) / UNFPA Indonesia
signals.summary: On 6 April 2026, Bappenas and UNFPA held a national dialogue titled 'Towards Intergenerational Prosperity: A New Direction for Indonesia's Policy at the End of the Demographic Transition' and officially launched a Policy and Analysis Book based on National Transfer Accounts (NTA). Ministers framed the sandwich-generation burden (12% elderly share in 2024, demographic-dividend window closing in the 2040s) as an intergenerational fiscal challenge requiring lifecycle human-capital investment aligned across youth and elder protection. Coordinating Minister Pratikno and Population Minister Wihaji emphasised intergenerational equity and 'intergenerational family resilience' (ketahanan keluarga antargenerasi) as planning prerequisites for Indonesia Emas 2045.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a Global South national planning instrument that embeds intergenerational resource-flow analysis in central development policy—not OECD 'fairness' branding but operational cross-generational budgeting. NTA reveals hidden generational economies and gives planners a measurable basis for sandwich-generation relief and fiscal sustainability as Indonesia ages.

signals.title: Canarias Launches Programa Auchón Intergenerational Cohousing as Explicit Solidarity Policy
signals.summary: On 29 August 2025, the Canarias government presented the Programa Auchón de Cohabitabilidad Intergeneracional—a non-profit social housing-cesión model pairing older people living alone with vulnerable youth (students, care-leavers, single-parent families). Consejera Candelaria Delgado framed the programme as converting elder loneliness and youth housing vulnerability into 'una oportunidad compartida,' with six-phase matching, supervised cohabitation, and monthly community activities. The official release states the programme aims to become 'un referente de solidaridad intergeneracional' replicable across the archipelago.
signals.why_it_matters: A subnational government operationalises reciprocal intergenerational solidarity through housing and loneliness policy—not rhetorical TEU language but a governed cohabitation protocol with legal backing and multidisciplinary follow-up. Useful comparator to EU fairness strategy tools and to one-way elder-care models.

signals.title: Chile Promulgates Comprehensive Older-Persons Law Naming Solidarity and Intergenerational Cooperation
signals.source_name: Diario Oficial de la República de Chile
signals.summary: Law No. 21.822 (Ley Integral de las Personas Mayores y de Promoción del Envejecimiento Digno, Activo y Saludable) was published in the Diario Oficial on 1 June 2026. Article 3(k) lists 'La solidaridad y fortalecimiento de la protección familiar y comunitaria' as a general principle; Article 3(e) mandates 'participación, integración e inclusión intergeneracional plena y efectiva.' Articles 15–16 require employers and Chile's civil service to adopt lifecycle people-management policies with 'cooperación intergeneracional' and knowledge transfer across working ages. The law creates a National Ageing Policy framework and 15 enumerated older-person rights.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a binding national statute—not a programme announcement—that constitutionalises solidarity language alongside intergenerational inclusion and obliges public and private employers to institutionalise intergenerational cooperation in HR policy. Fills a Latin American gap distinct from Ecuador's equality-council agenda already in the DB.

signals.title: European Parliament Intergenerational Forum Demands Solidarity Frame Over Fairness Duplication
signals.source_name: AGE Platform Europe / EP Intergenerational Forum
signals.summary: On 6 March 2026, co-chairs of the European Parliament Intergenerational Forum (MEPs Mendia, Szczerba, Bosanac, with AGE Platform Europe) responded to the Commission's Intergenerational Fairness Strategy. They welcomed the initiative but warned the proposed November 'Intergenerational Fairness Day' duplicates the existing European Day of Solidarity between Generations (29 April, rooted in Decision 940/2011/EU and the 2012 European Year). They urged that the Fairness Index 'strengthen solidarity and avoid unintended competitive narratives between generations,' called for a public awareness campaign 'to challenge age stereotypes and promote intergenerational solidarity,' and asked the Commission to celebrate the April solidarity day consistently.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first cross-party EP stakeholder pushback on the EU's fairness-vs-solidarity terminology split—directly testing whether COM(2026) 110's fairness branding erodes the treaty-anchored solidarity norm (TEU Article 3(3)). Tracks institutional discourse, not just Commission messaging.

signals.title: Basque Government Publishes Official Intergenerational Solidarity Population Survey Feeding Zubiak Pact
signals.source_name: Gobierno Vasco / Departamento de Bienestar, Juventud y Reto Demográfico
signals.summary: The Basque Department of Welfare, Youth and Demographic Challenge published the Ikerfiel report 'Solidaridad intergeneracional en la población vasca / Belaunaldien arteko elkartasuna euskal herritarren artean' (48 pages, Vitoria-Donostia, 2025). The official documentation page presents results showing broad social consensus on strengthening independent living across life stages, expanding opportunities for youth and older people, and designing policies with fair distribution between generations. The report underpins the Zubiak intergenerational pact strategy subsequently presented in Brussels (June 2026).
signals.why_it_matters: Distinct from the June 2026 EESC conference signal: this is the official regional evidence base that names intergenerational solidarity in policy research and feeds a subnational intergenerational pact model. Shows how solidarity framing is being quantified and institutionalised at regional level ahead of the 2027 Bilbao international congress.

signals.title: China Expands Personal Pension Early-Withdrawal Grounds Ahead of Longer Contribution Periods
signals.source_name: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security of China (gov.cn)
signals.summary: On 13 July 2025, China's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security, Ministry of Finance, State Taxation Administration, National Financial Regulatory Administration and China Securities Regulatory Commission issued Notice No. 2025-39 on personal pension withdrawals, effective 1 September 2025. The notice adds hardship-based early withdrawal grounds—including serious illness, qualifying unemployment and subsistence-allowance receipt—alongside existing retirement-age, total disability and emigration triggers, while clarifying application channels via social-insurance agencies and bank platforms. It sits atop the December 2024 nationwide rollout of the voluntary third-pillar personal pension (annual contribution cap RMB 12,000) and the January 2025 statutory retirement-age increase that will raise minimum contribution years from 15 to 20 between 2030 and 2039.
signals.why_it_matters: China is layering third-pillar pension choice onto a mandatory system that is shifting contribution burdens onto younger workers before benefit adequacy is assured. Expanded early-withdrawal routes acknowledge liquidity stress among contributors facing youth unemployment and longer pay-in periods, but they also test whether voluntary long-term savings can survive when the generational pension contract is under strain.

signals.title: Japan's Koki Town Adopts Sixth Comprehensive Plan Built Through Future Design Workshops
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In March 2025 Koki Town, Miyazaki Prefecture, formally adopted its Sixth Comprehensive Plan (2025–2034) together with the third Local Creation Comprehensive Strategy, after a three-year deliberation process that embedded Tatsuyoshi Saijo's Future Design method. From FY2022 the town ran five Future Design workshops—including imaginary-future-generation sessions with residents, staff, U23 youth and middle-school students (up to 68 participants in one session)—alongside resident surveys and a population-decline 'saki-gake' project. The adopted plan treats depopulation as the top priority and integrates Future Design outputs into its basic philosophy, sector targets and ten-year municipal strategy, following staff training that began in 2022.
signals.why_it_matters: Future Design is moving beyond pioneer towns like Yahaba into statutory comprehensive planning for shrinking municipalities. Koki shows how imaginary-future-generation deliberation can be institutionalised in Japan's top-tier local master plans—not just one-off workshops—offering a replicable bridge between Saijo's method and formal intergenerational foresight as national future-generations legislation is debated.

signals.title: Bank of Korea Finds Youth Job-Search Delays and Housing Costs Permanently Scar Lifetime Earnings
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-2, published 12 February 2026, quantifies how delayed labour-market entry and housing-cost burdens compound across young Koreans' lifetimes. BOK estimates that a one-year non-employment spell cuts the probability of regular employment five years later from 66.1% to 56.2% and reduces current real wages by 6.7% per extra year of past joblessness; a 1 percentage-point rise in housing costs lowers total assets by 0.04%, and a 1 percentage-point rise in housing expenditure share cuts education spending share by 0.18 points. The note argues youth employment and housing strains are structural growth constraints, calling for labour-market dualism reform, small-housing supply expansion and short-term work-experience and minimum-housing-stability support.
signals.why_it_matters: South Korea's 'Hell Joseon' discourse is often anecdotal; BOK's central-bank analysis supplies institutional metrics linking youth exclusion from decent jobs and housing to lifetime human-capital loss. That makes intergenerational unfairness measurable in fiscal and growth terms—not only in protest rhetoric—and raises the stakes for pension and housing reforms that already shift costs onto younger cohorts.

signals.title: Bank of Korea Warns Korea Faces Compound Asset–Income Polarization Entrenching Youth Exclusion
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-14, published 11 June 2026, diagnoses 'compound polarization' in which widening household asset gaps and re-expanding income inequality reinforce each other. Net-asset Gini rose from 0.584 in 2017 to 0.625 in 2025 as real-estate gains concentrated among older cohorts; the share of households in the bottom quintile for both net assets and income who are aged 20–39 jumped from 7.9% in 2020 to 15.2% in 2025. BOK links asset concentration among the top 10% to lower total-factor productivity (a 1 percentage-point rise in top-decile asset share cuts TFP by 0.16%) and warns that ageing-driven 'wealth lock-in' and renewed income inequality are weakening social mobility, labour motivation and domestic demand.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the clearest official Korean framing of generational asset exclusion as a macroeconomic pathology—not just a housing grievance. It validates 'lost ladder' narratives behind Hell Joseon while arguing that income-targeted redistribution alone cannot fix intergenerational wealth concentration in a real-estate-heavy economy, with direct implications for pension, tax and housing policy design.

signals.title: South Korea Plans 90,000 Greater-Seoul Purchase-Rental Units for Youth by 2027
signals.source_name: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport / Yonhap News Agency
signals.summary: On 22 May 2026 the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport announced it will supply 90,000 purchase-rental (매입임대) units in the greater Seoul area over 2026–2027—roughly 2.5 times the 36,000 units supplied in 2024–2025—with 66,000 targeted to Seoul and 12 regulated Gyeonggi cities. Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol told a real-estate ministers' meeting the package prioritises fast-supply non-apartment stock (multifamily, officetels, studio units) to ease youth jeonse/wolse instability. Measures include partial-building purchases, lower minimum lot sizes (10 units), waived building-age limits for existing stock in regulated zones, expanded LH land-cost support (up to 80%), stronger HUG project-financing guarantees and modular construction to shorten delivery timelines.
signals.why_it_matters: After loan caps that critics said hurt asset-light young buyers, Seoul is pivoting to supply-side youth housing at scale—a direct response to generational housing precarity driving Hell Joseon politics. The scale (90,000 units in two years) and focus on non-apartment rentals test whether public purchase-rental can restore a 'housing ladder' when homeownership remains out of reach for renters without inherited property.

signals.title: Nigerian Senate Passes Constitutional State Police Bill With Safeguards Against Political Weaponisation
signals.summary: On 24 June 2026, the Nigerian Senate passed the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Alteration) (State Police) Bill, 2026 (SB. 1055), establishing a dual Federal Police Service and State Police Services framework. More than two-thirds of senators voted in favour after clause-by-clause consideration. The bill empowers governors to appoint state commissioners subject to state assembly confirmation, prohibits using state police against government critics, requires stated cause and two-thirds assembly approval to remove commissioners, and mandates State Police Service Commissions for recruitment, discipline and complaints oversight. Existing regional outfits such as Amotekun and Hisbah cannot automatically become state police or bear firearms. The amendment still requires concurrence and ratification by at least 24 of 36 state assemblies.
signals.why_it_matters: State policing is the most consequential structural response to Nigeria's EndSARS-era demand for police accountability since the 2020 protests. Mechanism memory: constitutional decentralisation with explicit anti-partisan firewalls, judicial review of federal interventions, and independent commissions attempts to convert protest grievances into enforceable governance architecture rather than another unimplemented panel report. Lens memory: youth who bore the cost of centralised policing failures are the primary constituency for whether reform restores trust or merely relocates abuse. Relationship memory: pairs directly with the database's EndSARS five-year accountability signal and #EndBadGovernance prosecution signals as the legislative counter-move.

signals.title: South African Parliament Raises Alarm Over NYDA Whistleblower Retaliation and Governance Breakdown
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 3 June 2026, the Portfolio Committee on Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities briefed members on worsening governance at the National Youth Development Agency (NYDA). Chairperson Liezl van der Merwe said whistleblower complaints referred earlier had received no formal response and raised concern that the entity may be using public funds to identify whistleblowers rather than address allegations — conduct she warned would breach the Protected Disclosures Act. Members also flagged internal board discord, disputed oversight authority claims, and possible misuse of agency legal budgets. The committee said it would consider reviewing the NYDA legislative framework, including a possible committee Bill to strengthen oversight and accountability.
signals.why_it_matters: NYDA is South Africa's primary youth-development delivery vehicle at a moment of documented youth voter disengagement and unemployment above 45%. Mechanism memory: whistleblower retaliation at a Schedule 3 public entity undermines the accountability infrastructure Cabinet is simultaneously building through the National Youth Policy 2030 M&E framework. Lens memory: when the institution meant to serve young people is accused of silencing dissent, it reinforces the intergenerational fairness critique that youth are consulted in rhetoric but excluded from trustworthy governance. Relationship memory: contrasts sharply with June 2026 Youth Parliament and PYEI scale-up signals already in the database.

signals.title: Kenya Postpones National Youth Council Elections Indefinitely Over Compliance Failures
signals.source_name: The Eastleigh Voice (National Steering Committee statement)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Gazette Notice No. 10421 of 10 July 2026, issued by Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya under the National Youth Council Act (Cap. 132) and the 2021 election regulations, postponed the July NYC polls and set ward elections for 9 October, constituency elections for 16 October, and National Youth Congress elections for 30 October 2026. The notice cites Regulation 19(3) and voter-education duties under Regulation 21. Days earlier the High Court in Kisumu (Justice Alfred Mabeya, petition by Austine Ogalo) issued conservatory orders stopping the remaining phases until a verified public voters' register is published and the 2021 regulations are complied with. The National Youth Council confirmed the new dates on 13 July. This follows the 3 July indefinite postponement already in the corpus.
signals.why_it_matters: Kenya's Gen Z movement has shifted from street protest toward ballot-box and institutional channels, yet the formal youth governance body remains dormant. Mechanism memory: postponement after gazetting exposes a participation-to-delivery gap — constitutional youth representation rights without operational electoral machinery. Lens memory: young Kenyans who mobilised on Finance Bill 2026 and Niko Kadi voter registration face another state institution failing to open on schedule, risking further disillusionment. Relationship memory: substantive development after the database's April 2026 gazetting signal; distinct event warranting a new record or update.
signals.update_note: Trusted lab ingest update via cursor on 2026-08-14

signals.title: African Peer Review Mechanism Recruits 20 Youth Technical Experts to Appraise African Youth Charter at 20
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 10 April 2026, the APRM Continental Secretariat — with YouLead Africa and Restless Development — issued terms of reference calling for twenty Youth Technical Experts to appraise implementation of the African Youth Charter (AYC) ahead of its 20th anniversary. Applications closed 30 April 2026; selected experts were to conduct continental consultations from May through 30 June 2026, submit appraisal reports by 17 July 2026, and feed a consolidated policy brief for launch on International Youth Day (12 August 2026). Findings will also inform the Africa Governance Report 2027 on the theme 'Youth in Governance: From Promise to Prosperity,' endorsed at the 35th APR Summit in February 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: Agenda 2063 and the African Youth Charter set continental youth empowerment targets, but implementation tracking remains weak. Mechanism memory: youth-led, APRM-governed appraisal converts Aspiration 6 rhetoric into evidence that can feed amendment proposals at the July 2026 AYC@20 summit. Lens memory: with more than 75% of Africans under 35, a charter review led by young technical experts is an intergenerational governance innovation — youth as auditors of commitments made to youth. Relationship memory: operationalises the database's Agenda 2063 Aspiration 6 and STYIP youth-target signals with a 2026 accountability process.

signals.title: UNECA Pilots Continental Initiative to Convert National Youth Policies Into Decent Jobs and Entrepreneurship Pathways
signals.source_name: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa
signals.summary: On 28 May 2026, UNECA announced a pilot initiative, 'Strengthening Youth Policy Implementation and Employment Pathways in Africa,' to accelerate delivery of existing national youth policies for Africa's 400+ million people aged 15–35. The programme built on a Dire Dawa local workshop (11–13 February 2026) on Ethiopia's National Youth Policy and a regional Expert Group Meeting in Addis Ababa (22–24 March 2026) with IGAD member states, Djibouti, academia and youth-led businesses. ECA is co-producing a diagnostic study with Oxford Economics to help countries strengthen policy-to-livelihood linkages, with IGAD peer-learning to follow.
signals.why_it_matters: The demographic dividend framing shifts from policy design to delivery — ECA explicitly states the challenge is no longer drafting youth policies but connecting skills, finance, markets and jobs. Mechanism memory: a continental diagnostic tool targeting implementation gaps is the fiscal-governance counterpart to AU STYIP's 14% youth unemployment and 15% elected-youth targets. Lens memory: without accelerated delivery, Africa's youth bulge becomes an intergenerational liability rather than dividend — the core equity trade-off Agenda 2063 was meant to resolve. Relationship memory: complements Nigeria's NALTF youth-policy dialogue, Kenya's NYC reboot attempt, and South Africa's NYP 2030 M&E framework as the multilateral delivery layer.

signals.title: Mexico Proposes Public Pension Insurer and PENSIONISSSTE Strengthening to Reverse 2007 Individual-Account Shift
signals.source_name: La Jornada (reporting ISSSTE / Secretaría de Gobernación)
signals.summary: On 4 June 2026 ISSSTE director Martí Batres presented CNTE teacher-union representatives a federal package to strengthen PENSIONISSSTE — Mexico's only fully public Afore — and create a dedicated public, non-profit pension insurer to administer monthly retirement payouts in coordination with PENSIONISSSTE. The proposal explicitly frames the 2007 ISSSTE Law reform, which replaced a public solidarity intergenerational pension regime with individual accounts mostly managed by private Afores, as having produced negative consequences for retirees. Secretaría de Gobernación said the public insurer is the most significant element because no public entity currently performs that function. The offer was made during CNTE strike negotiations attended by Gobernación secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez and Education secretary Mario Delgado.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a live intergenerational fiscal governance signal: the Sheinbaum administration is testing whether Mexico can partially re-socialize pension payout infrastructure without immediately repealing the 2007 individual-account architecture teachers reject. A public insurer alongside PENSIONISSSTE would give workers a non-profit alternative to private Afore-linked insurers, directly addressing the generational trade-off embedded in Mexico's shift from solidarity pensions to marketized accounts — and could become a template for broader Latin American debates on reversing neoliberal pension privatization without triggering massive transition liabilities.

signals.title: Brazil Senate Files Complementary Bill PLP 58/2026 Mandating Actuarial Balance Across State and Municipal Pension Systems
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 16 March 2026 Senator Jorge Kajuru (PSB/GO) filed Complementary Bill PLP 58/2026, amending Law 9.717/1998 to improve organization and functioning of Regimes Próprios de Previdência Social (RPPS) for federal, state, Federal District, and municipal civil servants. The bill establishes mandatory actuarial deficit equilibration, strengthens collection and governance mechanisms, and improves regulation and supervision instruments. The measure was autuado in the Senate plenary and published in the Diário do Senado Federal on 17 March 2026. It arrives as Ministry data show 54.8% of Brazil's 2,131 subnational pension systems — overwhelmingly municipal — have not completed broad reforms aligned with the 2019 federal pension overhaul.
signals.why_it_matters: Brazil's 2019 federal pension reform shifted retirement burdens onto younger cohorts through higher ages and contribution rules, but more than half of municipal pension systems remain unreformed — meaning intergenerational fiscal risks are being pushed down to city-level taxpayers and future workers. PLP 58/2026 is federal legislation attempting to force actuarial discipline across 2,000+ local systems, making the generational cost of pension promises visible and legally enforceable rather than deferred. For intergenerational equity tracking, it marks the next wave after EC 103/2019: from national rule-setting to binding subnational solvency governance.

signals.title: Philippines LCOY 2025 Delivers 12-Point National Youth Statement on Climate Action to Government Ahead of COP30
signals.summary: On 11 October 2025 young people from Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao convened in Quezon City under the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY) 2025 process and issued a National Youth Statement on Climate Action, published by UNICEF on 4 November 2025. The statement — representing 38.5 million Filipino children — explicitly frames climate change as intergenerational injustice and demands a National Climate Emergency declaration, grant-based climate finance, passage of the National Land-Use Act and Coastal Greenbelt Bill, institutionalized youth seats on disaster risk reduction councils (amending RA 10121 Section 11 for Sangguniang Kabataan representation in LDRRMCs), and protection for youth environmental defenders. Government agencies including the Climate Change Commission, DENR, DepEd, and Council for the Welfare of Children committed to carrying youth recommendations to COP30 negotiations in Belém.
signals.why_it_matters: This is one of the most institutionally connected youth climate mobilizations in Southeast Asia: not a protest alone but a YOUNGO-recognized pipeline producing a formal national mandate with explicit intergenerational injustice framing, delivered to multiple ministries before COP30. The SK/LDRRMC seat demand links grassroots climate youth power to the Philippines' existing barangay-level youth governance architecture — a rare attempt to convert the world's largest youth council system into climate decision-making seats rather than parallel consultation forums.

signals.title: Bangladesh Updates National Population Policy to Prioritize Demographic Dividend Over Population Control
signals.summary: On 14 July 2025 Health Adviser Nurjahan Begum inaugurated Bangladesh Population Policy-2025 at Osmani Memorial Auditorium on World Population Day, replacing the 2012 policy after 13 years. The updated policy — prepared by the Health and Family Welfare Ministry with implementation across 29 ministries — shifts primary emphasis from fertility reduction to harnessing the demographic dividend while Bangladesh remains in its dividend window. Six objectives include transforming the population into skilled human capital through healthcare, nutrition, demand-based education, and social protection; reducing unmet family-planning need and harmful practices; expanding technology for the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions; equalizing urban-rural services; achieving gender equality and gender dividends; and addressing climate disaster impacts. Directorate General of Family Planning officials said the policy takes effect once an implementation strategy now under development is approved.
signals.why_it_matters: Bangladesh's policy pivot is a structural intergenerational equity signal: the state is explicitly reframing population governance from controlling today's birth rates to investing in the current youth bulge before the window closes — the classic demographic-dividend race against ageing. With 29 ministries tasked, success or failure will determine whether today's largest young cohort becomes an economic asset or an abandoned generation as dependency ratios rise; this is the South Asian counterpart to Africa-focused demographic-dividend finance signals already in the platform.

signals.title: Indonesia Reactivates Climate and Carbon Collaboration Hub with Carbon Youth Lab Under Ministerial Decree 2211/2026
signals.summary: On 4 June 2026 Environment Minister Moh Jumhur Hidayat relaunched the Climate and Carbon Collaboration and Consultation Hub (RKKIK) at KLH/BPLH headquarters in Jakarta, operationalized under Ministerial Decree No. 2211 of 1 June 2026. Deputy Ary Sudijanto said RKKIK connects government, business, academia, civil society, development partners, and young people to support NDC implementation and carbon economic value governance, including the National Registry System for Climate Change Control and Carbon Unit Registry. Flagship public programs include Climate Corner, Climate Clinic, Climate Dialogue Forum, the National Carbon Forum, and the Carbon Youth Lab — explicitly designed to expand youth engagement in climate action and carbon-economy development.
signals.why_it_matters: Indonesia is embedding youth participation inside national carbon-governance infrastructure rather than treating young people as outreach audiences. The Carbon Youth Lab within a decree-backed NDC/carbon-registry hub creates an institutional bridge between Gen-Z climate concern (80%+ per ministry-cited surveys) and Indonesia's low-carbon development and carbon-market rollout — a governance model distinct from both Western youth panels and prior youth statements alone. For intergenerational equity, it tests whether carbon-economy rules that will bind future generations include structured youth input at the registry and finance layer.

signals.title: WHO Europe Publishes First Regional Child and Youth Mental Health Baseline With Nine Quality-of-Care Actions
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 12 November 2025 WHO/Europe launched its first consolidated regional report on child and youth mental health, finding one in seven children and adolescents aged 0–19 lives with a mental health condition — prevalence up one-third over 15 years. One in four girls aged 15–19 is affected; suicide remains the leading cause of death for ages 15–29. The report documents governance gaps: one in five countries lacks dedicated CAY mental health policy, one in four lacks community services, and care quality varies sharply. It proposes nine actions spanning national plans, financing, quality standards, service redesign, youth engagement, workforce investment, and outcome measurement.
signals.why_it_matters: This converts youth mental health from anecdotal crisis reporting into a measurable regional governance baseline — the kind of evidence infrastructure that can drive policy convergence across 53 Member States. The explicit policy-gap data (countries without CAY mental health legislation or community services) reframes youth distress as an institutional failure to protect future generations, not only a clinical problem. Relationship memory: complements EU youth-friendliness Council work and UK Youth Matters mental-health delivery pledges with supranational quality-of-care standards.

signals.title: UN DESA Launches World Youth Report on Mental Health Framing Inequality as Root Cause of Youth Distress
signals.source_name: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs
signals.summary: On 10 February 2026 UN DESA formally launched the World Youth Report on Youth Mental Health and Well-being, convening Member States, UN entities, and youth delegates including UN Youth Delegates from Switzerland and Finland. The report applies a youth-informed social-determinants lens across education, employment, family dynamics, poverty, technology, societal attitudes, and climate-related stress. Launch speakers framed structural inequality — not individual pathology — as the driver of rising youth distress and called for preventive, cross-sectoral, youth-responsive policies feeding into the Commission for Social Development and World Programme of Action for Youth.
signals.why_it_matters: A UN flagship report elevates youth mental health from a health-ministry silo to an intergovernmental equity question: who gets opportunity, voice, and care across generations. By centring youth lived experience and linking climate stress to mental health outcomes, it creates a replicable framing for national wellbeing frameworks that treat distress as a governance failure. Relationship memory: extends ECOSOC Youth Forum mental-health rhetoric into a permanent evidence product routing into 2026–2027 social-development processes.

signals.title: Nature Mental Health Synthesis Links Youth Eco-Anxiety to Government Inaction and Political Participation
signals.summary: Published 10 December 2025, a Nature Mental Health systematic review synthesises 69 studies on social, political, and geographic determinants of eco-anxiety among children and young people. Political factors — especially perceived government inaction and distrust — emerge as consistent drivers alongside media exposure, gender, and developmental stage. Young adults and young women report the highest levels. The review notes children's mental health remains largely invisible in national climate-adaptation policies and calls for strategies that channel eco-anxiety into adaptive civic engagement rather than functional impairment.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the strongest peer-reviewed evidence bridge between climate governance failure and youth mental health — treating eco-anxiety as a political-attitudes signal, not only a clinical symptom. For intergenerational equity advocates, it legitimises policy accountability for youth distress caused by inadequate climate action. Relationship memory: underpins UKHSA's November 2025 climate–mental health assessment and connects to youth climate litigation and participation arcs already in the database.

signals.title: UK Publishes First National Climate–Mental Health Assessment Flagging Youth and Eco-Anxiety as Priority Risks
signals.source_name: UK Health Security Agency / Centre for Climate and Health Security
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 12 November 2025 UKHSA's Centre for Climate and Health Security published the Climate Change and Mental Health thematic assessment report — the first in a National Adaptation Programme series. The umbrella and systematic reviews map pathways from extreme weather, housing instability, and climate awareness to mental health harm, identifying children, young people, and those with pre-existing conditions as disproportionately affected. Companion GOV.UK guidance on climate communication and eco-anxiety notes 26% of UK young people report eco-anxiety affecting daily functioning and calls for age-appropriate, action-oriented framing co-designed with youth.
signals.why_it_matters: This institutionalises youth mental health inside national climate-adaptation governance — a concrete wellbeing-framework move that shifts eco-anxiety from media debate to public-health planning. By mandating integration of mental health into adverse-weather and adaptation planning, it creates enforceable evidence infrastructure for long-horizon policy. Relationship memory: pairs with England's Youth Matters Action 8 (school MHSTs, Young Futures Hubs) and Wales's prevention-through-Future-Generations logic as a UK-wide climate–youth wellbeing stack.

signals.title: Australia Opens Consultation on headspace Plus and Youth Specialist Care Centres to Close Youth Mental Health 'Missing Middle'
signals.source_name: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
signals.summary: From 21 May to 11 June 2026 the Australian Government consulted on draft models of care for headspace Plus (30 enhanced centres) and 20 Youth Specialist Care Centres, backed by more than A$700 million committed from 2025–26. Developed by headspace National and Orygen, the models target young people aged 12–25 whose needs exceed primary headspace care but do not require state-funded acute treatment — covering psychosis, eating disorders, personality disorder, and severe mood/anxiety conditions. Consultation sought feedback on target populations, workforce, pathways, safety, and integration; final models are expected mid-2026 with staged rollout from 2027–28 to full operation by 2029–30.
signals.why_it_matters: This operationalises youth mental health governance as tiered public infrastructure — moving from crisis rhetoric to codified models of care with federal funding, jurisdictional working groups, and a planned National Institute for Youth Mental Health. The 'missing middle' framing directly addresses intergenerational unfairness where young people bear rising distress costs but lack proportional service access. Relationship memory: Australia's world-leading youth mental health architecture now enters a new reform phase distinct from generic health-budget signals.

signals.title: CFR Analysis: Asia Gen Z Protests Intense but Chenoweth Data Shows Post-2010 Nonviolent Success Rate Below 34%
signals.summary: In an October 23, 2025 CFR analysis, Joshua Kurlantzick assesses Gen Z-led uprisings in Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Thailand, and Sri Lanka, arguing that digitally organised, leaderless protests rarely convert disruption into durable reform. Citing Erica Chenoweth's research, the piece notes nonviolent revolutionary success rates fell from above 40% (1960s–2010) to below 34% since 2010, with violent revolutions succeeding only 8% of the time. Exceptions—Thailand's People's Party and Sri Lanka's NPP electoral breakthrough—show protest-to-institutional conversion requires sustained grassroots organisation and party alliances.
signals.why_it_matters: This CFR regional synthesis complements the global CFR Gen Z piece already in the database by applying Chenoweth's success-rate threshold to Asia's 2025 wave specifically. For early-warning governance, it frames the risk: youth crossing into disruptive action without institutional conversion pathways produces regime change without reform—raising cycles of renewed protest, as seen in Bangladesh's post-Hasina interim-government fractures.

signals.title: Chenoweth and Cebul: 80% of Nonviolent Regime-Change Campaigns 1990–2020 Had Substantial Youth Participation
signals.summary: In the January 2026 issue of Journal of Democracy, Harvard's Erica Chenoweth and Matthew Cebul synthesise the global Gen Z protest wave, citing survey evidence of youth democratic disillusionment alongside mobilisation data showing 80% of nonviolent campaigns to topple national leaders (1990–2020) featured substantial youth participation, with under-30s comprising at least a quarter of frontline actors. The essay traces anticorruption diffusion from Sri Lanka (2022) and Bangladesh (2024) through Indonesia, Nepal, Peru, and Madagascar, and argues durable change requires converting protest momentum into electoral and institutional politics—yet many activists remain deeply sceptical of parties.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the flagship academic institutional synthesis of the participation→protest→institutional-conversion dilemma, directly linking survey-documented disillusionment with longitudinal campaign data. For intergenerational equity foresight, it establishes that youth disruption is structurally potent but institutionally fragile—the key design challenge for future-generations governance bodies seeking to absorb youth energy before it hardens into extra-institutional repertoires.

signals.title: Jamaica and Netherlands Launch UN Group of Friends on Future Generations to Implement Declaration
signals.source_name: School of International Futures / Declaration on Future Generations co-facilitators network
signals.summary: On 13 November 2025, the Permanent Missions of Jamaica and the Kingdom of the Netherlands — co-facilitators of the intergovernmental Declaration on Future Generations process — launched the Group of Friends on Future Generations at UN headquarters. The cross-regional coalition of Member States and civil-society partners aims to drive Declaration implementation, share national models (including Kenya's Senate Futures Caucus, Portugal's intergenerational justice tools, and the EU intergenerational fairness portfolio), and keep future-generations governance on the multilateral agenda while the proposed UN Special Envoy remains unfunded.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the primary diplomatic implementation vehicle for the Declaration while the Special Envoy appointment is on hold — a member-state-led workaround for the gap between Pact for the Future commitments and UN budgetary refusal to create the envoy post. It signals that future-generations institutionalisation is advancing through coalitions of the willing rather than waiting for a single UN centre of leadership.

signals.title: Portugal Publishes Updated Intergenerational Justice Index Across Six Policy Dimensions
signals.source_name: Institute of Public Policy Lisbon / Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In November 2025 the Institute of Public Policy (IPP–Lisbon), with Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation support, published the updated Intergenerational Justice Index (IJI) for Portugal (presented 4 December 2025 at the Gulbenkian Foundation). The annual composite tracks six equal-weight dimensions—environment and natural resources, health, labour market, housing, poverty and living conditions, and public finances—normalised to (0,1], with movement toward 1 meaning relative improvement for younger and future cohorts. After mild aggregate improvement through about 2020, the 2016–2023 update shows a reversal in 2022–23 driven mainly by housing (price-to-income accessibility and share of 25–34-year-olds living with parents; housing sub-index reported falling from roughly 0.46 in 2019 to 0.23 in 2023) and health (unmet needs, household out-of-pocket spending, anxiolytic/antidepressant use), with a milder public-finance drag. Labour market and poverty dimensions improve modestly; environment shows slight net gain. Nuance: the index is diachronic for Portugal only, not a cross-country ranking; absolute levels matter less than annual change; public-finance methodology was redesigned in 2025 (from generational accounts toward explicit debt plus implicit pension liabilities and capital stock) and back-applied for series consistency; many indicators are youth-age or trend proxies rather than full-life cohort microdata.
signals.why_it_matters: Portugal offers a national multi-domain measurement model for intergenerational equity without a future-generations commissioner: a public dashboard that makes housing, fiscal liabilities, environment, health, labour and poverty jointly visible. The 2025 reversal—especially the housing collapse—shows IE can deteriorate even when some social indicators improve, reinforcing the platform rule that aggregates must be read component-wise. For GYC framework design, the IJI supplies equal-weight geometric aggregation practice, the sustainability-vs-justice distinction, and Layer C–D indicators (housing autonomy, implicit pension liabilities) that complement the Youth Progress Index (global youth rights) and JRC same-age cohort income/housing method. It was cited as a replicable member-state tool around the Group of Friends of Future Generations and parallels the EU Intergenerational Fairness Index under construction.
signals.update_note: 2026-07-13: Primary-sourced to IPP November 2025 report PDF; expanded summary with six dimensions, 2022–23 reversal, housing 0.46→0.23, public-finance method redesign; confidence raised to High.

signals.title: Welsh Government Issues Initial Written Response to Future Generations Report 2025
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 17 July 2025, Cabinet Secretary Jane Hutt issued Welsh Government's initial written statement responding to Commissioner Derek Walker's Future Generations Report 2025, laid alongside the statutory Section 23 report. The statement acknowledges the Act's transformative impact over ten years, commits to detailed consideration of all 50 recommendations over autumn 2025, and signals support for post-legislative evaluation of the Act coordinated with the Auditor General's No time to lose report and forthcoming Senedd Equality and Social Justice Committee inquiry. It also commits to publishing the statutory Future Trends Report 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first executive accountability beat in the Section 23 report-response cycle — distinct from the March 2026 itemised annex accepting or deferring each recommendation. It shows how Wales's commissioner model converts statutory reporting into a sequenced government response architecture that other jurisdictions studying Wales's Act must replicate or improve upon.

signals.title: Kenya Senate Futures Caucus Adopts Strategic Plan 2025–2028 at Inaugural Foresight Retreat
signals.summary: Kenya's Senate Futures Caucus convened its inaugural Strategic Foresight Retreat in the Maasai Mara in April 2025 to embed future-oriented thinking in lawmaking, fiscal planning, and devolution.
