For GYC, the forum is a high-leverage venue to push measurable youth participation, Declaration on Future Generations delivery, and cross-track intelligence across Pact, UN80, and Article 109.

signals.title: C4UN Information Clearinghouse Publishes 2025 Annual Follow-up Report on Pact for the Future
signals.source_name: Summit of the Future Information Clearinghouse / C4UN
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The C4UN Information Clearinghouse team published the 2025 Annual Follow-up Report on the Pact for the Future, an independent civil-society assessment of the first year of implementation after the September 2024 Summit of the Future. Covering 22 September 2024 to 16 September 2025, the report reviews developments across the Pact five chapters and two annexes (Global Digital Compact and Declaration on Future Generations). Lead author Ishaan Shah and co-authors from the ICH team aim to capture how commitments translated into action, highlight achievements and challenges, and offer recommendations for stronger implementation. The report is explicitly framed as an accountability product for Member States, UN entities, and civil society.
signals.why_it_matters: This is one of the few civil-society-owned year-one scorecards for the entire Pact package, including DFG and GDC annexes. It fills the gap left by delayed official institutional machinery and gives youth and intergenerational advocates a baseline for the 2028 review. Pairing it with Stimson GGI 2026 and regional futures outcomes creates a multi-source accountability stack.

signals.title: C4UN Stakeholder Monitoring Report Maps Civil Society and Youth Engagement on Pact Implementation
signals.source_name: Summit of the Future Information Clearinghouse / C4UN
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Bulletin No. 68 from the C4UN Information Clearinghouse presents findings from the second Stakeholder Mapping Survey on engagement with the Pact for the Future and its annexes. More than 100 organizations and individuals participated between April and August 2025, with strong representation from Africa, global networks, and Asia. Respondents include CSOs, youth-led groups, think tanks, academia, UN entities, private sector actors, and independent researchers. The report finds a cautiously hopeful outlook but stresses that the Pact must move beyond symbolism toward inclusive, accountable, and action-oriented implementation. Recommendations call for systemic reforms, stronger youth and marginalized-community participation, long-term funding and capacity-building, meaningful accountability frameworks, digital inclusion, and integration of human rights, gender equality, and sustainability.
signals.why_it_matters: This is rare demand-side evidence from implementers and monitors, not only institutional self-reporting. The explicit youth-led participation and accountability recommendations make it a direct input for GYC briefing products and for Pact tracker stages that currently lack civil-society engagement metrics.

signals.title: C4UN Pact for the Future Follow-up Dashboard Tracks Commitments Toward 2028 Review
signals.source_name: Coalition for the UN We Need / Information Clearinghouse
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Pact for the Future Dashboard, developed by the Information Clearinghouse team, is a dynamic monitoring framework for commitments and action items under the Pact and its annexes. It aims to provide a transparent breakdown of implementation status, corresponding intergovernmental processes, and stakeholder roles, including responsible UN entities, civil society partners, and Member State champions. Contents cover monitoring requests to the Secretary-General and follow-up action items for the Pact, Global Digital Compact, and Declaration on Future Generations. The dashboard is framed as a tool for accountability, coordination, and collective action on the road to the General Assembly 2028 formal review, and is also described as an archive of Summit of the Future engagement.
signals.why_it_matters: Without a public action-level tracker that civil society trusts, Pact accountability defaults to narrative. This dashboard is a primary reference layer GYC can mirror or deep-link from the intelligence platform UN Pact tracker, especially for DFG and GDC follow-up items that currently sit as sparse or unknown milestones.

signals.title: C4UN 2026 Pact Moments Timeline Maps Action-Linked Intergovernmental Windows Across the Year
signals.source_name: Coalition for the UN We Need
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: C4UN 2026 Pact Moments timeline is a curated calendar linking months and events to specific Pact chapters and actions, GDC paragraphs, and Declaration on Future Generations references. Key 2026 windows include DFG para 32c inputs for the SG DFG implementation report (before March); SG reports on concessional finance, sovereign debt architecture, and credit rating agencies (before March); ECOSOC Youth Forum (14-16 April); SG report on the future of peace operations (before May); GDC progress-report data collection (before June); AI for Good and WSIS sessions in July; Beyond GDP expert group final report (before August); Youth, Peace and Security second independent progress study (September); Partner2Connect USD 100 billion mobilisation (before December); and Internet Governance Forum in Nairobi (14-18 December). Additional moments include SG candidate interactive dialogue, tax cooperation INC sessions, and cultural property restitution dialogues under DFG para 15.
signals.why_it_matters: This is operational briefing material: it turns the Pact from a static document into a calendar of pressure points. For the intelligence platform, these moments should power a what-matters-this-month briefing strip and overdue or upcoming milestone chips on the Pact tracker, especially DFG 32c, youth participation, and financing actions.

signals.title: C4UN Global Synthesis Report Consolidates Six Regional Futures Forums on Pact, UN80, and Governance Reform
signals.source_name: Coalition for the UN We Need
signals.summary: On 7 July 2026, C4UN released a draft Global Synthesis Report consolidating civil society perspectives from the 2026 Regional Futures Forums across Africa, Arab States, Asia, Europe and North America, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Pacific. The report, authored by Eliane El Haber with C4UN reviewers, draws on 1,151 participants representing more than 1,000 organizations. It synthesizes regional views on Pact commitments most relevant to SDG delivery, accountability and implementation gaps, civil society engagement strategies, and UN80 and global governance reform. Cross-cutting themes include structured multi-stakeholder participation beyond states alone, stronger institutions and coordination, and adequate financing and international cooperation. Regions also elevate youth participation and intergenerational responsibility, while differentiating priorities such as anticipatory governance and digital or AI governance in Europe and North America, debt and fiscal constraints in the Arab States, and structural reform of global governance in Africa.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the civil society baseline for GFF 2026 and the 2028 Pact review: a multi-region, multi-organization synthesis. It is especially useful for briefing because it maps where youth and future-generations language is strong, where accountability gaps dominate, and how UN80 is being read as either enabler or risk relative to Pact delivery.

signals.title: Africa Futures Forum 2026 Outcome Document Demands Structural Multilateral Reform and Pact Domestication
signals.source_name: Coalition for the UN We Need / Africa Futures Forum partners
signals.summary: The 2026 Africa Futures Forum, convened in two parts on 5 and 26 May 2026 by Article 109, Building Blocks for Peace, Centre for Global South Initiatives in Development, Nigeria Network of NGOs, Oxfam International, SDGs Kenya Forum, and C4UN, engaged more than 400 civil society organisations from 29 African and 25 non-African countries. The outcome document consolidates expert briefings, consultations, and over 25 written submissions on Pact implementation, UN80, and the UN We Need. Speakers included the Director of Pact for the Future Implementation in EOSG and Africa policy specialists. The forum frames a USD 4 trillion annual development financing gap and argues Africa must shift from passive recipient to active architect of multilateral reform, with domestication of the Pact as the critical priority alongside structural equity, human security, and resilience.
signals.why_it_matters: Africa is the region where Pact delivery, financing justice, and UN structural reform are most tightly coupled. The outcome document is a high-value regional accountability input for the Pact tracker and for GYC positioning on youth, peace and security, digital governance, and future generations annexes.

signals.title: Arab Regional Futures Forum 2026 Outcome Links Pact Delivery to Debt, Fiscal Space, and Inclusive Multilateralism
signals.source_name: Arab NGO Network for Development / Coalition for the UN We Need
signals.summary: The Arab Regional Futures Forum: Reflections from the Arab Region was held online on 11 May 2026, co-organized by the Arab NGO Network for Development (ANND) and C4UN. The draft regional outcome document captures civil society, UN, regional institution, academia, and youth-network perspectives on implementing the Pact for the Future in the Arab context and feeding into GFF 2026, the 2027 SDG Summit, the 2028 Pact review, and UN80 debates. The dialogue explored interlinkages among the Pact, Agenda 2030, UN80, and broader reform, with emphasis on accountability, sustainable development, peace, and inclusive multilateralism. Related synthesis materials highlight debt burdens, fiscal constraints, unequal access to development finance, and the need for more equitable international economic governance.
signals.why_it_matters: Arab regional priorities show that Pact implementation is inseparable from financing architecture and civic space. For briefing products, this is a counterweight to New York-centric reform talk and a reminder that future-generations commitments will fail without fiscal and debt pathways that free policy space for youth and long-term investment.

signals.title: Europe Regional Futures Forum 2026 Puts Accountability, Civic Space, and Institutionalised Youth Participation at Centre of Pact Delivery
signals.source_name: ECE-RCEM / Peace Child International / SDG Watch Europe / C4UN
signals.summary: The Europe Regional Futures Forum was held online on 16 and 24 April 2026, co-organized by ECE-RCEM, Peace Child International, SDG Watch Europe, and C4UN. It convened 280 representatives from 25 European countries plus participants from 48 countries worldwide, with an interactive policy sprint on sustainable development; peace, security and conflict prevention; Global Digital Compact and digital governance; and youth engagement and future generations, plus 20 written contributions. Regional priorities centre on accountability, inclusion, and resilience; protection of human rights and civic freedoms amid shrinking civic space; and moving youth participation beyond symbolic consultation toward institutionalised roles in national, regional, and international decision-making. The Pact is framed as needing to function as an operational framework, not only a political declaration.
signals.why_it_matters: Europe is where anticipatory governance, democratic resilience, digital and AI governance, and youth institutionalisation are most clearly articulated as Pact delivery tests. This outcome is a direct source for best-practice standards on youth participation actions and DFG commitments in the intelligence platform Pact tracker.

signals.title: C4UN 2026 Regional Futures Forums Series Channels Six-Region Civil Society Input into GFF and 2028 Pact Review
signals.source_name: Coalition for the UN We Need
signals.summary: C4UN convened the 2026 Regional Futures Forums as a series of civil society-led consultations between February and May 2026 covering Asia, the Pacific, Africa, the Arab States, Europe, and Latin America. The series is designed to surface regional perspectives on Pact implementation, identify priorities, and feed a People Framework to inform the 2028 High-Level Review of the Pact for the Future. Insights were intended to flow directly into Global Futures Forum 2026 on the margins of HLPF in New York. The process is explicitly situated alongside UN80 and post-2030 and UN centenary (2045) debates.
signals.why_it_matters: The series is the production line behind GFF 2026 and the civil society 2028 review strategy. Tracking it as a process signal, not only as discrete PDFs, helps the platform explain provenance of regional recommendations and avoid treating New York convenings as freestanding events.

signals.title: Hawaii Enacts HB 1802 Creating Conservation Mitigation Bank Framework for Species Offsets (Act 208)
signals.summary: On 8 July 2026, Governor Josh Green signed House Bill 1802 into law as Act 208, establishing a statutory conservation mitigation bank framework in Hawaii. The measure authorizes the Department of Land and Natural Resources and certain public or private entities to seek Board of Land and Natural Resources approval to operate conservation banks that generate compensatory mitigation credits when a person or entity must offset adverse impacts to threatened, endangered, candidate, or proposed species under an approved incidental take license and habitat conservation plan. The framework is designed to consolidate fragmented project-by-project mitigation into larger, banked conservation sites under state oversight.
signals.why_it_matters: Conservation banks encode intergenerational equity into permitting: present development that harms listed species must finance durable habitat outcomes rather than one-off, poorly monitored offsets. By tying bank credits to incidental take and habitat conservation plans, Act 208 hardens the link between today's land-use decisions and long-term species survival obligations that future residents inherit. Relationship memory: complements Act 203 co-management (community stewards as potential bank operators/managers) and the Green Fee climate-revenue stack as a dedicated-legislation mechanism for permanent habitat finance.

signals.title: Hawaii Enacts HB 1728 Requiring Counties to Allow Rainwater Catchment on All Properties (Act 209)
signals.summary: On 8 July 2026, Governor Josh Green signed House Bill 1728 into law as Act 209, relating to rainwater catchment systems. Per the enacted measure's description, counties must allow installation and operation of rainwater catchment systems for potable and nonpotable uses on all properties, while retaining authority to require registration, inspection, or notification and to enforce standards. The law removes local bans or connection-based restrictions that previously blocked catchment even where municipal water is available, expanding decentralized water resilience options statewide.
signals.why_it_matters: Distributed catchment reduces future generations' exposure to drought, aquifer stress, and centralized infrastructure failure by making household- and property-scale water security a default right rather than a zoning exception. The county-standard carve-out keeps public-health safeguards while preventing local rules from locking communities into single-source dependence. Relationship memory: pairs with Act 204 cesspool-conversion finance as a dual water-cycle intervention (cleaner wastewater disposal plus diversified supply) and with Green Fee resilience spending for community-scale systems in fire- and drought-exposed areas.

signals.title: Hawaii Creates Banyan Drive Community Development District Under HCDA With Lineal Descendant Seat (Act 206)
signals.source_name: Big Island Video News / Office of the Governor of Hawaii
signals.summary: On 8 July 2026, Governor Josh Green signed Senate Bill 2001 into law as Act 206, establishing the Banyan Drive Community Development District within the Hawaii Community Development Authority and creating a dedicated Banyan Drive Community Development District Special Fund. HCDA membership for the district is amended to include district representatives, the chairperson of the Banyan Drive Hawaii Redevelopment Agency, and a lineal descendant of the Waiakea Ahupuaa. The statute frames revitalization of the historic Hilo waterfront resort corridor around cultural and public facilities, recreation, education, and entertainment while protecting natural and cultural resources.
signals.why_it_matters: Act 206 is dedicated place-based legislation that institutionalizes intergenerational and Indigenous representation in redevelopment governance: a lineal-descendant seat and special fund make long-horizon cultural stewardship a structural input, not an optional consultation. That design reduces the risk that short-term visitor-economy gains permanently alienate public-trust and ahupuaa interests for future Hilo residents. Relationship memory: sits alongside Act 203 community co-management and Act 121 ALOHA Homes leasehold expansion as Hawaii's 2026 pattern of embedding multi-generational land governance into statutory vehicles.

signals.title: Senate Armed Services FY2027 NDAA Directs Negotiated Army Lease Renewals for Pohakuloa and Kahuku, Rejecting Condemnation Path
signals.summary: In mid-June 2026, the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee advanced Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act language directing the Army to seek negotiated renewal of expiring training-land leases covering roughly 19,700 acres of state land at Pohakuloa Training Area on Hawaii Island and 450 acres at Kahuku Training Area on Oahu, rather than pursue condemnation. The draft also requires the Army to resubmit environmental impact statements addressing deficiencies identified by the Hawaii Board of Land and Natural Resources and to report progress to Congress. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, Governor Green, and Hawaii's congressional delegation framed the shift as movement toward fair-market, conditioned leases that keep public-trust lands in the public trust; leases dating to $1 terms expire in 2029.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare federal-state international/defense commitment signal for Hawaii: it constrains how present military use of public-trust lands can lock in future generations' options. Rejecting condemnation while mandating renegotiated leases and repaired environmental review keeps alienation of trust lands off the table and reasserts that Native Hawaiian beneficiaries and future Hawaii residents retain residual claims over lands leased for $1 decades ago. Relationship memory: connects the ACLU Public Land Trust stewardship analysis, Governor Green's Military Leased Lands Advisory Committee, BLNR's May 2025 EIS rejection, and OHA's planned Ka Paakai cultural analysis for Pohakuloa into one multi-level governance arc.

signals.title: OHA Allocates $60,000 and Prepares DLNR MOU for Ka Paakai Cultural Analysis of Pohakuloa Training Area
signals.source_name: Big Island Video News / Office of Hawaiian Affairs
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In June 2026, concurrent with Senate Armed Services Committee NDAA action on military land leases, the Office of Hawaiian Affairs reported that its Board of Trustees approved a Permitted Interaction Group allocation of $60,000 to support a comprehensive Ka Paakai analysis of Pohakuloa Training Area and that OHA is finalizing a memorandum of understanding with the Department of Land and Natural Resources to complete the work. OHA states the analysis will document cultural, historical, and community connections to create a fuller decision-making record for evaluating impacts, identifying protections, and fulfilling Hawaii-law public-trust responsibilities as lease renewal talks proceed.
signals.why_it_matters: Ka Paakai analysis is Hawaii's doctrinal tool for ensuring traditional and customary Native Hawaiian practices are assessed before government actions affect public resources — a direct intergenerational equity mechanism that forces present decision-makers to account for cultural continuity. Funding and institutionalizing that analysis for Pohakuloa before 2029 lease deadlines raises the evidentiary bar for any renewed military use and strengthens OHA's ability to insist that benefits from public-trust lands flow to Native Hawaiian beneficiaries and future generations. Relationship memory: operational follow-through on the NDAA negotiation track, BLNR EIS rejection, and ACLU public-land-trust legal framing.

signals.title: Youth Progress Index 2025: Global Opportunity and Rights Stagnate While Basic Needs Rise Across 169 Countries
signals.source_name: European Youth Forum / Social Progress Imperative
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The fourth Youth Progress Index (YPI 2025), published November 2025 by the European Youth Forum with Social Progress Imperative, ranks 169 countries on 61 social and environmental indicators of youth wellbeing over 2015–2024, without using GDP as an input. The world average rose only from about 61.9 to 64.6. Basic Needs improved most (global level ~75.5), Foundations of Wellbeing mid (driven by information and communications +9.4), while Opportunity barely moved (~56.9) and the Rights & Voice component fell roughly four points. North America is the only region with net overall regression, led by an Opportunity drop of about 4.1 points; the United States (−2.1) and Canada (−1.4) appear among the largest national score declines. This edition overlays a rights-based reading of the indicators and calls for a UN Convention on the Rights of Young People plus coordinated global youth-disaggregated data infrastructure. Nuance: YPI measures present youth cohort outcomes as a rights proxy, not future-generations institutions or intergenerational fiscal transfers; some civic indicators are adult-level proxies; authors state it is not a comprehensive rights audit.
signals.why_it_matters: YPI is the largest global youth-wellbeing composite and a measurement template for intergenerational equity debates that often stop at GDP or youth participation rhetoric. The pattern it quantifies — rising survival floors with stagnant opportunity and eroding civic rights — is the structural diagnosis the platform already tracks qualitatively (Naides trust gap; GYPI socio-economic vs civic split). For foresight, it supplies peer-relative (GDP-controlled) performance, component-level alerts, and a beyond-GDP architecture. For GYC framework-building it anchors Layer A–C (present outcomes, agency conditions, material preconditions) while exposing what still must be measured separately: future-generations institutions, fiscal/climate transfers, and participation influence rather than presence. Italy is already piloting YPI methodologies in its 2026 Youth Voluntary Review, so the index is moving from advocacy dataset toward policy tooling.

signals.title: JRC 2025: EU Young Cohorts Stagnate on Income and Lose Homeownership Versus Same-Age Predecessors
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In December 2025 the Joint Research Centre published Intergenerational fairness in the EU: income and housing dynamics in the context of demographic change (JRC144437). Using Luxembourg Income Study and EU-SILC microdata, the report compares generations at the same age over the life course rather than only cross-sectional age groups. It finds that recent cohorts—especially at younger ages—face stagnant disposable income relative to previous generations at the same age, higher poverty risk and low-pay exposure, rising within-generation inequality, falling homeownership, and higher rental cost overburden (notably in cities), amplified by urban migration of young adults and a sharp rise in single households at ages 25–29. Post-2004 Member States show less pronounced income deterioration. The report was produced to inform the EU Intergenerational Fairness Strategy, Affordable Housing Plan, Anti-Poverty Strategy, and related monitoring tools including the Intergenerational Fairness Index. Nuance: coverage is incomplete for full EU27 on long series; it measures living-cohort material outcomes, not future-generations institutions or climate liability; excluding co-resident young from ownership stats avoids parental bias but understates dependence on parents.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the EU’s clearest official template for measuring intergenerational fairness as same-age cohort outcomes—the method that separates normal life-course gaps from true generational decline. It operationalises the material side of intergenerational equity (income, poverty, housing wealth channel) that youth-rights composites like the Youth Progress Index do not resolve, and it supplies the empirical backbone the Commission’s Intergenerational Fairness Index and Strategy need. For the platform, the same-age cohort rule should become a standing analytical standard in country and fiscal IE work: age cross-sections alone misdiagnose fairness.

signals.title: JRC 2024: EU Life-Fairness Perceptions Fall 51% to 38%, Sharpest Among Young People and Students
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: JRC summary report Fairness, inequality and intergenerational mobility (JRC138713, DOI 10.2760/048970) analyses Eurobarometer Special surveys on Fairness, Inequality and Inter-generational mobility for 2017 (Special 471, n≈26,693) and 2022 (Special 529, n≈26,395) across the EU-27. Agreement that things that happen in life are fair fell from 51% to 38%, with the largest declines among young people and students; perceived equality of opportunity also fell (about 57% to 47%), again steepest for 15–24/students. Concern that income inequality is too high stayed very high (85% to 81%). Redistribution support remains around 77%. Parental education is the strongest predictor of tertiary attainment; more than 40% of respondents underestimate their relative income position, with younger people misperceiving more. Groups that received public COVID support showed less fairness decline. Nuance: subjective perceptions, not an objective IE composite; 2022 mode mix may affect comparability.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the EU’s primary official Layer F (legitimacy) battery for intergenerational equity: cohort-sensitive fairness and opportunity sensors that move differently from raw inequality concern. The youth-specific fairness collapse while inequality worry stayed high matches Naides trust-gap and GYPI/YPI opportunity stagnation narratives. For the platform it wires scorecard indicator #18 and warns that objective housing/fiscal metrics alone do not drive politics—perceived fairness does. Relationship memory: pairs with WISER subjective wellbeing, JRC 2025 same-age income/housing outcomes, and EU Intergenerational Fairness Strategy monitoring.

signals.title: Intergenerational Foundation 2016: EU28 Fairness Index Deteriorates +5.5 Points as Debt and Youth Unemployment Drive Post-Crisis Loss
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Intergenerational Foundation’s European Intergenerational Fairness Index 2016 tracks EU28 fairness 2005–2014 with 13 Eurostat/ESS indicators (debt, youth unemployment, pensions and ageing health costs, housing burden, poverty risk, education spending, tertiary attainment, R&D, GHG, democratic participation, incomes, dependency). Aggregate EU index rose to 105.5 by 2014 (base 2005=100)—a +5.5 deterioration after pre-crisis improvement. Critical polarity: higher score means worse for young people. Government debt was the largest driver; youth unemployment rose roughly 15% to 22% post-crisis. Southern Europe (Greece, Italy, Romania, Cyprus) worst; Eastern Europe often better on debt/youth ratios. Foreword by Laurence Kotlikoff calls for explicit youth and future-citizen impact assessment of all policies. Nuance: age-group snapshot not same-age birth cohorts; pre-2015 data; polarity opposite modern higher=better indices (Portugal IJI, YPI, GYPI).
signals.why_it_matters: Classic EU composite ancestor of Portugal IJI and EU IGF Index debates. Establishes the Layer C–D indicator menu (debt, pensions vs education, youth unemployment, housing, environment) still used in IE measurement. For the platform it is a historical baseline that IE is measurable and was deteriorating in post-crisis Europe, plus a standing polarity-hygiene warning when comparing indices. Kotlikoff’s assessment demand prefigures Youth Check / SOIF toolkit logic. Relationship memory: Vanhuysse IJI (debt-per-child upgrade), JRC cohort method, EU Strategy Index commitment.

signals.title: SOIF–Gulbenkian Framework for Intergenerational Fairness: Institutions, National Dialogue, and Five Unfairness Tests for Policy Assessment
signals.source_name: School of International Futures / Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: School of International Futures and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation co-designed a Framework for Intergenerational Fairness (Pilot Report Dec 2020; Specialist Report 2021) with more than 400 experts and citizens in Portugal, built for global adaptation. Fair policies must allow people of all ages to meet needs now and meet present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland-auditable). The system has three required elements: institutional ownership/legitimacy; national dialogue for a shared future vision; and a policy assessment toolkit applying five unfairness tests ex-ante and ex-post across alternative futures—disadvantage to a life stage; disadvantage to a time period; inequality transmission through time; restriction of future choices; drift from shared future vision. Not a scored country ranking. Authors stress politicians lack long-term distributional information and a constituency for unborn/young non-voters, and that change often requires civil-society pressure. Nuance: process tool, not outcome index; toolkit alone insufficient without institutions and dialogue.
signals.why_it_matters: Best Layer E process framework in the measurement library: how to assess policies for IE, not only rank countries. Complements Portugal IJI (same Gulbenkian lineage, outcome dashboard) and the EU Strategy Youth Check/foresight tools. For platform signals and country briefs it supplies a reusable five-test checklist for why_it_matters and mechanism analysis. Relationship memory: Wales FG commissioner models; EU Youth Check; Portugal IJI 2025.

signals.title: Vanhuysse 2013 Bertelsmann IJI: OECD Intergenerational Justice via Ecological Footprint, Child Poverty, Debt-per-Child, and Elderly Spending Bias
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Pieter Vanhuysse’s Intergenerational Justice in Aging Societies (Bertelsmann Stiftung, 2013) builds a synthetic Intergenerational Justice Index for 29 OECD countries at a late-2000s/early-2010s snapshot. Four dimensions: ecological footprint; child poverty (including relative to old-age poverty); public debt per child; and EBiSS—the Elderly Bias Indicator of Social Spending, demography-adjusted. Dual weighting schemes (researcher-imposed and benefit-of-the-doubt). Top cluster included Estonia, Korea, Israel, New Zealand, Hungary and Nordics; bottom included USA, Japan, Italy, Greece and Canada. Debt per child ranged extremely (e.g. Japan hundreds of thousands of dollars per child vs low-debt peers). No OECD country met a ~1.8 gha/cap sustainable footprint benchmark. Core claim: aging is ethically neutral; the policy package is the justice variable. Nuance: cross-sectional snapshot not full cohort life-course accounts; pre-crisis residual timing for some series; ranks are historical structure not live 2026 scores.
signals.why_it_matters: Canonical OECD IE measurement model and still underused Layer D toolkit: debt-per-child beats raw debt/GDP, and EBiSS shows demography does not fully explain pro-elderly spending skew. Foundational citation for later national IE indices (Portugal IJI lineage). For the platform it upgrades scorecard fiscal liability metrics and frames aging as constraint not automatic injustice. Relationship memory: IF 2016 EU menu; Portugal IJI public-finance redesign; JRC same-age income/housing method.

signals.title: Galasso Age-It 2025: European Index of Intergenerational Justice Finds Economic and Political Skew Toward Older Adults, Relational Edge for Young
signals.source_name: Journals of Gerontology / Age-It / Bocconi University
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Vincenzo Galasso and Age-It collaborators published An index of intergenerational justice: main concepts and preliminary evidence (Journals of Gerontology Series B, 2025; doi 10.1093/geronb/gbaf192), with a Bocconi/Age-It 2025 report applying the index across 19 EU countries. The snapshot compares younger adults (25–34) with older adults (55–64 labour; 65+ broader) on four dimensions: economic fairness (poverty, unemployment, contracts, wages, housing, financial resilience); access to services/public goods (healthcare, non-pension transfers, environment, safety, digital); relational equality (networks, leisure, discrimination, mental wellbeing); and political equality (interest, voting, party ID, manifesto saliency, parliamentary age composition). Coding: more=better; positive values favor older adults, negative favor younger; three weighting schemes (equal, empirical via life satisfaction, normative). Findings: older adults dominate economic and political dimensions; younger adults dominate relational equality; services mixed; aggregate balance often masks offsetting inequalities (Ireland/Italy lean elderly; Croatia/Lithuania/Slovenia lean young). Age-group not birth-cohort design by deliberate choice. Nuance: living-generation justice, not unborn FG welfare; not the official EU Intergenerational Fairness Index.
signals.why_it_matters: Most recent academic European multi-dimension IE index, bridging generational-accounting politics with measurable age-group fairness across economy, services, relationships and political power. Complements JRC same-age cohort income/housing (method purity) and Vanhuysse/IF (liabilities) by adding relational and political equality into one frame. For GYC it supplies Layer B political under-representation metrics next to GYPI and Layer C–D economic skew evidence for Southern Europe. Relationship memory: Age-It NRRP research; Population Europe policy insights; EU Strategy measurement track.

signals.title: Global Carbon Budget 2025: Fossil CO2 at Record High; Remaining 1.5°C Carbon Budget Virtually Exhausted
signals.source_name: Global Carbon Project / Global Carbon Budget
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Global Carbon Budget 2025 (Global Carbon Project; 20th edition), synthesised in official FAQs and building on the peer-reviewed ESSD carbon-budget accounting series (Friedlingstein et al.), projects fossil CO2 emissions at a record ~38.1 GtCO2 in 2025 (+1.1%), with land-use-change emissions ~4.1 GtCO2. The remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5°C is described as virtually exhausted; at current rates there is roughly a one-in-two chance that about four more years of current CO2 emissions would bring multi-year 1.5°C breach. Remaining budgets for 1.7°C and 2°C are given as ~525 GtCO2 (~12 years) and ~1055 GtCO2 (~25 years) at 2025 emissions levels. Climate change is already weakening land and ocean sinks (~8% of atmospheric CO2 rise since 1960 attributed to sink weakening). 35 countries cut emissions over 2015–2024 while growing GDP. Novel CDR methods remain negligible vs fossil emissions. Nuance: budgets depend on probability choices and non-CO2 pathways; GCB is scientific accounting not a justice composite; equity of budget allocation across countries/cohorts is a policy layer on top of the physical stock.
signals.why_it_matters: Remaining carbon budget is the core Layer D climate-stock metric for intergenerational equity: cumulative CO2 left is what present generations can still emit without foreclosing safe climate for younger and unborn cohorts. GCB is the operational standard updating IPCC AR6 remaining-budget figures annually and should anchor scorecard climate-liability signals alongside Portugal IJI GHG paths and Vanhuysse ecological footprint. Relationship memory: Paris Agreement NDC/stocktake cycle; youth climate litigation; EU IGF environmental measurement debates.

signals.title: Naides / UNU-CPR: Intergenerational Trust Gap Framework — Recognition, Representation, Redistribution as Governance Test of the Era
signals.source_name: United Nations University Centre for Policy Research / UNICEF Innocenti
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Shai Naides (Global Policy Manager for Intergenerational Governance and Participation, UNICEF Innocenti), published via UNU Centre for Policy Research, diagnoses an intergenerational trust gap: when authority operates in short electoral/budget cycles while exposure accumulates over decades, younger cohorts experience governance as done to them not with them. Nearly half the world is under 30 while leadership stays older; OECD and trust surveys show eroded youth confidence and widespread belief children will be worse off than parents. Core distinction: participation volume is widespread (youth councils, consultations) but participation agency is rare—presence without decision-shaping power erodes legitimacy. Three interdependent conditions for meaningful participation: Recognition (youth perspectives treated as relevant to long-term risk), Representation (embedded decision pathways not parallel consultative spaces), and Redistribution (material conditions—education, work, security—that enable participation). Youth act as informal early-warning sensors when legitimacy fractures; where channels fail, willingness for more disruptive action rises. Closing claim: intergenerational governance is a key governance test of this era. Nuance: analytic essay, not a scored index; cites Edelman, OECD, ILO, IPU, CFR as evidence base.
signals.why_it_matters: Primary Layer B/F theory frame for the platform: agency over presence, material preconditions for voice, and trust/legitimacy as early-warning. Maps directly onto GYPI (structures), YPI Opportunity lag, JRC fairness collapse, and protest-threshold signals already in the database. For scorecard and thematic synthesis it supplies the Recognition–Representation–Redistribution checklist and the barrier-not-apathy interpretive rule. Relationship memory: already referenced across dozens of IE signals; this record makes the primary source itself a first-class intel object.

signals.title: SOIF March 2025: EU LTG/IGF Ecosystem Agenda — Foresight Governance Prism and Five Recommendation Blocks Ahead of Strategy
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In March 2025 the School of International Futures published Advancing Long-Term Governance and Intergenerational Fairness in the European Union, a policy paper converting EU IGF momentum—including the first Intergenerational Fairness Commissioner (Glenn Micallef, Nov 2024), the Strategy process kickoff, and the UN Declaration on Future Generations—into an actionable ecosystem agenda. Core device is the Transformative Foresight Governance Prism: citizens involved, leaders with incentives for intergenerationally fair decisions, and organisations/sectors ready—isolated interventions are judged insufficient and risk performative results. The brief maps the EU foresight legacy from Delors Forward Studies Unit through ESPAS and Better Regulation foresight, mentions an Intergenerational Fairness Assessment Framework at the March 2025 kickoff, and sets five recommendation blocks: DFG implementation; holistic MS/EU foresight governance; institutional capacity (IGF assessments, Eurostat generational data, parliamentary Committee for the Future, ECA long-term audit); citizen dialogues and FutureCheck; partner-country LTG via Global Gateway, INTPA and Youth4Foresight. Nuance: pre-dates the March 2026 Strategy text; does not publish Index indicator lists; complements rather than replaces the 2020/21 SOIF–Gulbenkian five unfairness tests.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the missing SOIF link between the 2020/21 policy-assessment toolkit and the live EU institutional agenda. For the platform it supplies the Layer E ecosystem inventory structure (citizens/leaders/organisations), an EU mechanism checklist (assessments, Eurostat, Committee for the Future, RSB/ECA, MFF scrutiny), and language distinguishing transformative from performative youth engagement that pairs with Naides agency>presence. Relationship memory: EU Strategy 2026 delivery track through 2028 DFG review; Portugal/Wales pioneer models; Youth Check and foresight tools already on the platform.

signals.title: Fiji Youth Councils Urge Constitutional Youth Seats, Intergenerational Responsibility and Climate Justice
signals.source_name: FijiVillage / National Youth Council of Fiji
signals.summary: In early July 2026 submissions to Fiji's Constitution Review Commission, the National Youth Council of Fiji, Provincial Youth Forum and Youth Assemblies of Fiji called for four dedicated youth seats in Parliament and for Chapter 1 of the Constitution to enshrine intergenerational responsibility—requiring the State to consider the rights, welfare and future security of children, young people and future generations in major public decisions. They also proposed expanding Section 40 environmental rights to include climate justice and intergenerational equity, youth participation in climate decision-making, guaranteed budget funding for the NYCF Secretariat, youth impact assessments before major legislation, and stronger civic education.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare package of constitutional design proposals that links youth representation, future-generations duties and climate justice in a Pacific small-island state already exposed to sea-level rise. Distinct from the parallel FICA debt-stewardship submission, it treats young people as present rights-holders and seeks hard institutional seats rather than consultative soft power. If any elements enter the review draft, Fiji would join a small set of jurisdictions experimenting with constitutional intergenerational equity language beyond environmental preambles.

signals.title: UNICEF, France and Spain Launch Global Coalition for Children's Rights in the Age of AI
signals.summary: On 7 July 2026 at the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva, UNICEF with the Governments of France and Spain and UN partners (including OHCHR, ITU, UNESCO, the Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies and DGC) launched the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. The coalition frames children as rights-holders whose voices should shape how AI is designed, not merely as users to be protected after harm. It aims to turn CRC-based principles into practical multi-stakeholder action on safe, rights-respecting AI systems for children.
signals.why_it_matters: Coming one day after UNESCO floated a new normative instrument on children and AI, this coalition is the implementation vehicle that could convert soft standards into coordinated state and industry practice. Anchoring AI governance in the CRC rather than consumer-safety framing strengthens intergenerational digital equity arguments: today's design choices lock in harms or capabilities for cohorts who will live with AI for decades. Watch for national adoption packages, procurement rules and youth co-design requirements as the real test of substance.

signals.title: OECD France Survey 2026 Urges Pension Reform Restart and Tax Alignment for Intergenerational Equity
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In its Economic Survey of France 2026 (released around 30 June 2026), the OECD warned that France faces rising debt without deeper consolidation and urged resumption of the suspended 2023 pension reform raising the statutory retirement age from 62 toward 64, with eventual linkage to life expectancy. Beyond sustainability, the survey explicitly flags intergenerational equity challenges in the pay-as-you-go system and recommends aligning tax treatment of retirees and workers—including phasing out the 10% income-tax allowance on pension income—to share ageing costs more fairly across generations while raising revenue.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a high-authority fiscal signal that names intergenerational equity as a design criterion for pension and tax reform in a major EU economy, not only deficit arithmetic. The proposed removal of retiree tax privileges and age-linked retirement rules reallocate burdens between current older cohorts and younger/future workers. For foresight, it reinforces a 2026 pattern of OECD surveys (also Norway, Korea) treating ageing costs as intergenerational fairness problems rather than pure technocratic finance.

signals.title: OECD Korea Survey 2026 Frames Semiconductor Boom as Chance for Intergenerational Fiscal Contract
signals.summary: The OECD Economic Survey of Korea 2026 (published early July 2026) and accompanying Ecoscope analysis argue that booming semiconductor-related tax revenues should underpin an intergenerational fiscal contract: using temporary windfall revenues and structural reform to align current tax and spending with long-term sustainability amid extreme low fertility and rapid ageing. Without a prudent fiscal framework, further pension reform, revenue increases and productivity measures, ageing-driven spending could put public debt on a sharply rising path if costs are debt-financed.
signals.why_it_matters: Korea is a leading case of demographic headwinds colliding with a cyclical fiscal windfall. Framing the semiconductor super-cycle as capital for an intergenerational contract—rather than permanent spending expansion—is exactly the mechanism-level intergenerational equity logic the platform tracks: who captures boom revenues now versus who inherits pension and care liabilities later. Complements parallel OECD France messaging and regional signals on youth housing and skills mobility.

signals.title: Wales Future Generations Commissioner Opens Section 20 Energy Review (Project Ynni)
signals.source_name: Business News Wales / Future Generations Commissioner for Wales
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 15 July 2026, Future Generations Commissioner for Wales Derek Walker announced Project Ynni, a Section 20 review—the strongest power under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act—into energy policy and decision-making. The review will examine how Welsh ministers and public bodies plan and deliver renewable energy and infrastructure so communities share benefits and long-term well-being is protected. An initial involvement phase runs July–August 2026 before the formal review focus is set in October.
signals.why_it_matters: Section 20 reviews are rare, high-leverage uses of Wales's flagship future-generations institution on a concrete sector (energy) rather than abstract strategy. Linking renewable acceleration to community ownership, land use and public-body practice tests whether future-generations duties can reshape infrastructure politics. Outcomes will be a reference case for other jurisdictions debating commissioners, energy justice and intergenerational benefit-sharing.

signals.title: Lancet CAP-2030 Paper Distills Eight Lessons for Putting Children and Future Generations in All Policies
signals.summary: In a July 2026 Health Policy paper in The Lancet, authors linked to the WHO–UNICEF–Lancet Commission and Children in All Policies 2030 (CAP-2030) report five years of implementation experience. They diagnose systemic prejudice against children in policymaking and set out eight lessons: creative child involvement, patient coalition-building, seizing political windows, harmonising global data, national political-technical platforms, media for cultural change, strategic framing across sectors, and joint learning—aimed at embedding children and future generations in cross-sector policy design.
signals.why_it_matters: CAP-2030 is one of the few global implementation networks explicitly pairing child rights with future-generations framing. Codifying what works (and what fails) after the 2020 Commission turns aspiration into transferable governance practice for national platforms, UN partnerships and civil-society coalitions. Useful baseline for the platform's child-rights and futures-governance themes as states claim to mainstream youth and children without delivery mechanisms.

signals.title: OECD Italy 2026: Youth Engagement and Fiscal Consolidation Framed Against Ageing and Future Generations' Debt Burden
signals.source_name: OECD EcoScope / OECD Economic Survey of Italy 2026
signals.summary: In July 2026 OECD EcoScope posts tied to the Economic Survey of Italy 2026, the OECD argues Italy must convert NRRP-driven resilience into long-term growth while ageing shrinks the workforce and raises pension and care costs. It notes generous support measures have inflated already-high public debt 'on current and future generations' (debt ratio above 137% of GDP) and urges sustaining fiscal consolidation, containing pension spending (including maintaining life-expectancy links to retirement age), and enabling youth, women and other under-represented groups to work. A companion 6 July piece stresses Italy's high youth NEET rate and emigration risk, calling for stronger school-to-work pathways and more attractive domestic jobs as youth become a scarcer resource.
signals.why_it_matters: Italy joins France, Korea and Germany in the mid-2026 OECD-centred wave treating fiscal sustainability, pension design and youth labour-market inclusion as one intergenerational package. High public debt framed as a claim on future generations plus extreme youth disengagement is a dual mechanism: costs roll forward while productive capacity of younger cohorts is underused. For the platform's Italy deep-dive and intergenerational-fiscal trend, this is a high-authority baseline for NRRP endgame choices on education, pensions and climate/energy investment.

signals.title: 17th European Youth Parliament for Water Set for Strasbourg on Cross-Border Watershed Governance
signals.source_name: SIE-SEE / European Youth Parliament for Water
signals.summary: The 17th European Youth Parliament for Water is scheduled for Strasbourg, France, from 20–26 September 2026, under the theme of uniting across borders toward sustainable watershed governance. The recurring youth parliament format brings young people into structured deliberation on water policy, climate-linked hydrology and cross-border basin management, producing recommendations aimed at European and national water institutions.
signals.why_it_matters: Water governance is a classic intergenerational commons problem—allocation today locks in drought, flood and ecosystem outcomes for later cohorts. A dedicated European youth parliament focused on watersheds is a concrete participation channel beyond one-off climate COPs, testing whether youth deliberative institutions can influence river-basin and EU water acquis implementation. September outcomes (recommendations, institutional uptake) are the next checkpoint.

signals.title: Wales Future Generations Commissioner Publishes Statutory 2025 Report With 38 Recommendations Ahead of Senedd Election
signals.summary: Wales' Future Generations Commissioner Derek Walker published the statutory Future Generations Report 2025 on 29 April 2025, the five-yearly assessment required by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. The report makes 38 recommendations across seven missions, including ending short-term fixes, ringfenced prevention funding, a Real Living Wage commitment, a national food resilience plan, and a review to strengthen the Act itself. It serves as advice to the next Senedd after the 2026 election and calls for the Act's scope to be expanded to additional public bodies.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive assessment of Wales' world-leading future generations legislation since its implementation, providing the clearest evidence yet of what a statutory future-generations institution produces in practice. The Commissioner's call to 'review and strengthen the WFG Act' signals that even the gold-standard model requires evolution. The emphasis on prevention spending and wellbeing economy offers concrete policy levers for other jurisdictions considering similar legislation, including Scotland, Australia, Ireland, and the EU.

signals.title: Coalition of 70+ Irish Civil Society Groups Calls for Future Generations Commissioner as Bill Returns to Agenda
signals.summary: Coalition 2030, representing over 70 civil society groups and trade unions, called for Ireland to appoint a commissioner for future generations. Green Party leader Roderic O'Gorman confirmed that the Commission for Future Generations Bill has been restored to the Government's legislative agenda. The Bill would establish a commission to advise on creating a full ombudsman for future generations, with broad cross-sectoral backing including trade unions, youth groups, environmental NGOs, and the UN Youth Delegation.
signals.why_it_matters: Ireland is actively reconsidering a Future Generations Commissioner model with government-level commitment. The broad coalition backing demonstrates strong cross-sectoral demand for long-term governance institutions. Ireland's potential move would add to a growing cluster of future generations institutions across Europe, including Wales, Scotland (proposed/rejected), the Netherlands, and Finland, creating critical mass for regional diffusion of the commissioner model.

signals.title: Amsterdam UMC Appoints World's First Academic Hospital Future Generations Commissioner
signals.summary: Amsterdam UMC appointed Professor Tessa Roseboom as Future Generations Commissioner, the first academic medical centre in the world to create such a role. Roseboom, a professor of Early Development and Health, uses insights from the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort study to advocate for long-term thinking in healthcare and institutional decision-making. The role includes experimenting with Future Design methodology for the hospital's long-term strategy.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a novel institutional innovation demonstrating that the future-generations commissioner model can scale beyond national government into sectoral institutions. Roseboom's scientific evidence base on transgenerational health impacts provides a powerful, measurable argument for why today's decisions affect generations yet unborn. The role creates a replicable template for embedding intergenerational advocacy within healthcare, research, and other public institutions.

signals.title: Third World Summit of Parliamentary Committees for the Future Held in Chile With 42 National Parliaments
signals.summary: The Third World Summit of Parliamentary Committees for the Future took place in Santiago, Chile in January 2025, hosted by the Senate of Chile. Delegates from 42 national parliaments adopted motions calling on member states to strengthen anticipatory governance capacities, encourage future-oriented reporting, and promote inter-parliamentary cooperation on long-term challenges. The summit followed previous gatherings in Helsinki (2022) and Uruguay (2023).
signals.why_it_matters: The growing World Summit series demonstrates that parliamentary foresight committees are becoming a global movement, not isolated experiments. The Santiago declaration's language that Committees for the Future are 'necessary components of national and global resilience' marks a significant normative shift. IPU case study data shows 43 parliaments now engage in some form of institutionalised foresight activity, providing critical mass for inter-parliamentary learning and standard-setting.

signals.title: National Media Debate Erupts on Whether Canada Needs a Future Generations Commissioner
signals.summary: CBC News published a major feature examining whether Canada should establish a Future Generations Commissioner, drawing on Wales' experience and interviewing Commissioner Derek Walker. The piece notes growing Canadian interest: Generation Squeeze has campaigned for a federal Generational Fairness Task Force, the Commissioner of Environment and Sustainable Development has advocated for long-term thinking institutions, and the government publishes annual well-being metrics through the Canadian Index of Wellbeing.
signals.why_it_matters: Canada's debate reflects growing policy interest in future generations institutions beyond Europe. Canada already has relevant infrastructure including the Commissioner of Environment and Sustainable Development and well-being measurement frameworks that could form the basis for a broader future generations mandate. The CBC feature signals the idea is entering mainstream Canadian policy discourse and provides a potential pathway for institutional adoption in a federal system.

signals.title: Nauru Intergenerational Trust Fund Reports Continued Capital Growth, Model for Climate-Vulnerable States
signals.source_name: Government of the Republic of Nauru
signals.summary: Nauru's Intergenerational Trust Fund (NTF), established in 2015 to convert finite resource revenues into permanent intergenerational wealth, published its 2025 annual report showing continued capital growth under a long-term investment horizon. The fund is designed to provide revenue for education, health, environment, and infrastructure post-2035, with governance by a committee including Australia, New Zealand, and Taiwan representatives. An IMF 2025 Article IV consultation noted the fund as key to Nauru's long-term fiscal sustainability.
signals.why_it_matters: The NTF is a rare example of a small island state using sovereign wealth fund architecture specifically structured around intergenerational equity, with explicit constitutional and treaty backing. As climate-vulnerable nations face existential fiscal challenges, Nauru's model including deep-sea mining revenues directed to the fund offers a concrete case study in intergenerational resource governance directly relevant to debates about the Loss and Damage Fund and climate finance for future generations.

signals.title: Bhutan Launches 5th National Biodiversity Strategy With Intergenerational Equity Framework Grounded in Gross National Happiness
signals.summary: Bhutan launched its 5th National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan with 20 targets explicitly grounded in intergenerational language and Bhutan's Gross National Happiness philosophy. The plan integrates biodiversity with climate action, mainstreams conservation across agriculture, tourism, energy, and finance sectors, and dedicates Target 15 to gender-responsive biodiversity governance. It is embedded in the country's 13th Five-Year Plan.
signals.why_it_matters: Bhutan is a global leader in constitutional intergenerational equity, with a constitutional mandate to maintain 60% forest cover for future generations. This NBSAP operationalises that commitment in a measurable, sector-crosscutting framework. The explicit alignment of biodiversity governance with GNH, a wellbeing economy framework, and integration into national five-year planning cycles make this a model for how intergenerational sustainability can be embedded in national development governance.

signals.title: UN DESA Releases Policy Brief on Institutionalising Foresight With Modular Integration Framework for Governments
signals.source_name: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs
signals.summary: UN DESA released a comprehensive policy brief providing a modular Foresight Integration Framework that embeds strategic foresight into government planning, budgeting, and SDG implementation cycles. The framework operates across four dimensions: institutional architecture, capabilities and skills, policy-cycle integration, and culture and leadership. It draws on successful models from Singapore, Finland, Guyana, Flanders, and the US.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the most concrete operational guide yet from the UN system on how to institutionalise foresight within governments, moving from episodic exercises to continuous governance capability. It directly answers the Pact for the Future's call for long-term anticipatory governance and provides a replicable template that any national or local government could adopt ahead of the post-2030 agenda.

signals.title: OECD Report on Building Anticipatory Capacity Identifies Structural Barriers and Pathways for Strategic Foresight in Government
signals.summary: The OECD published a major report examining how governments can build anticipatory capacity through strategic foresight, analysing practices across OECD member countries. It identifies structural barriers including bureaucratic inertia, short-term electoral cycles, and annual budget horizons, and showcases promising cases where governments have successfully integrated futures thinking into routine operations and decision-making.
signals.why_it_matters: As the OECD's most comprehensive treatment of anticipatory governance to date, this report provides the evidence base and comparative analysis needed to make the case for foresight institutionalisation globally. It bridges the gap between conceptual support for long-term governance and practical implementation pathways that governments can adopt.

signals.title: UK Office for National Statistics Launches Quarterly Beyond GDP National Wellbeing Measures
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The UK ONS launched a quarterly headline set of seven national well-being measures including life satisfaction, health, governance trust, social capital, material well-being, environment, and education and opportunity. The February 2026 release shows GDP recovered post-pandemic while life satisfaction remained below pre-pandemic peaks, and the share of adults reporting good health fell from 76.0% in 2020 to 70.9% in 2025.
signals.why_it_matters: The UK is one of the first G7 countries to move beyond GDP to regular, official quarterly well-being metrics that can directly inform policy decisions. This creates a governance infrastructure for measuring intergenerational outcomes, tracking whether current prosperity is coming at the expense of future well-being, and provides a replicable model for other national statistical offices aligning with the UN Beyond GDP agenda.

signals.title: Loss and Damage Fund Board Warns of Capital Depletion by 2027 as Only $456M of $822M Pledged Is Paid
signals.summary: The FRLD Executive Director warned the Board at its 8th meeting in Livingstone, Zambia that the Fund faces liquidity issues by end of 2027, with only $456M of $822M pledged actually paid into the trust fund. With 10 project proposals already requesting $166M against only $250M allocated for the start-up phase, the Fund is already oversubscribed. Annual loss and damage finance needs are estimated at $937 billion, making current pledges a fraction of 1% of needs.
signals.why_it_matters: The funding gap directly threatens the credibility of the international loss and damage architecture created at COP27 and COP28. If the Fund cannot sustain disbursements beyond 2027, it risks becoming a symbolic failure rather than the operational justice mechanism vulnerable countries were promised. The gap between needs and resources represents a fundamental challenge to intergenerational climate justice: current generations are pledging far too little to compensate for climate harms locked in for future generations.

signals.title: Ninth Circuit Dismisses Lighthiser v. Trump Youth Climate Challenge to Energy Executive Orders on Standing Grounds
signals.summary: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed Lighthiser v. Trump, a lawsuit by 22 young Americans challenging Trump executive orders to expand fossil fuel development. The court ruled the youth lacked standing because their climate injuries bore too tenuous a connection to the executive orders, and that granting the requested injunction would constitute impermissible judicial supervision of executive energy policy. Ten of the plaintiffs had previously prevailed in the landmark Held v. Montana case.
signals.why_it_matters: The ruling illustrates continuing judicial barriers youth plaintiffs face in federal court despite establishing overwhelming evidence of climate harm. The decision reinforces that separation-of-powers doctrines can block youth climate cases even when plaintiffs demonstrate concrete injuries, highlighting the gap between constitutional rights rhetoric and judicial remedies in US federal courts. The involvement of Held v. Montana veterans makes this a direct test of whether state-level climate precedent translates to federal forums.

signals.title: Wisconsin Youth Appeal Dunn v. PSC Dismissal on Constitutional and Public Trust Grounds
signals.summary: Fifteen Wisconsin youth filed Dunn v. Wisconsin Public Service Commission challenging state laws that limit the PSC from considering air pollution when approving fossil fuel plants. The Dane County Circuit Court dismissed on political question grounds in April 2026. The youth plaintiffs appealed in May 2026, arguing the laws violate their constitutional rights to life, liberty, and the public trust doctrine protecting navigable waters for present and future generations. Indigenous youth plaintiffs added claims about threats to traditional lifeways including harvesting wild rice and maple sugar.
signals.why_it_matters: The case raises novel legal questions about whether statutes that structurally exclude climate considerations from regulatory decision-making violate state constitutional rights. The appeal tests whether state courts will enforce intergenerational public trust obligations against legislative limitations on agency authority. The Indigenous youth claims add a dimension of cultural and intergenerational heritage rights not typically present in youth climate litigation.

signals.title: Utah Supreme Court Dismisses Youth Climate Lawsuit Natalie v. State for Lack of Redressability
signals.summary: The Utah Supreme Court dismissed a youth climate lawsuit brought by seven Utahns aged 9-18 challenging state statutory provisions and government conduct promoting fossil fuel development. The Court held that declaring challenged provisions unconstitutional would not redress plaintiffs' injuries because it would not require the government to curb fossil fuel development, and that challenges to government conduct were not tied to specific concrete actions, making them non-justiciable.
signals.why_it_matters: The ruling demonstrates that even when youth plaintiffs can show climate harm, redressability remains a critical barrier when the causal chain between state law and emissions is diffuse. The decision adds to growing case law across US states where courts express sympathy but dismiss youth climate cases on justiciability grounds, while the dismissal was without prejudice, preserving potential for reformulated claims.

signals.title: Swedish Supreme Court Dismisses Aurora Youth Climate Case but Opens Pathway for Association-Led Claims
signals.summary: The Swedish Supreme Court dismissed the Aurora case brought by over 600 young Swedes seeking stronger climate action under the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court ruled individual plaintiffs lacked standing under ECtHR KlimaSeniorinnen criteria, but explicitly left the door open for climate cases brought by qualified associations seeking declarations of rights violations rather than specific policy orders. The case was remitted to district court for possible continuation as an association claim.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first systematic application of the ECtHR KlimaSeniorinnen precedent by a national supreme court in domestic climate litigation, establishing important boundaries for climate cases across Europe. The distinction between permissible declarations of rights violations and impermissible orders for specific government action will influence climate litigation strategy throughout the Council of Europe, creating both barriers and pathways for future youth climate cases.

signals.title: Brazil Adopts Updated National Adaptation Plan With Intergenerational Climate Justice as Core Principle
signals.summary: Brazil submitted its updated National Climate Adaptation Plan to the UNFCCC on February 27, 2026, formally approved by the Interministerial Committee on March 23, 2026. The Plan establishes climate justice as its central axis encompassing four dimensions: procedural, distributive, restorative, and intergenerational. It includes 16 Sectoral and Thematic Plans developed through co-production involving 25 ministries and civil society, including Indigenous and traditional community representatives.
signals.why_it_matters: Brazil's NAP is among the first national adaptation plans to formally incorporate intergenerational climate justice as a guiding principle with explicit dimensions. As the Amazonian host of COP30 and a major developing country, Brazil's approach sets a precedent for how large developing economies can embed intergenerational equity into adaptation governance. The co-production model with Indigenous and traditional communities also provides a replicable participation framework.

signals.title: First Institutionalised Youth-Led Climate Forum Held Within COP30 Blue Zone Sets Precedent for UNFCCC Participation
signals.summary: The COP30 Youth-Led Climate Forum was held across four sessions in November 2025 within the Blue Zone of COP30 in Belém. Co-organised by the COP Presidency and YOUNGO, the forum covered intergenerational equity in the energy transition, food security and climate resilience, and climate justice. It culminated in the official launch of the Global Youth Statement presented to the COP30 Presidency. The forum was supported by the Glasgow Climate Pact and the Sharm El-Sheikh Implementation Plan.
signals.why_it_matters: The YCF represents the first institutionalised youth forum within the UNFCCC formal negotiation space, transforming youth participation from parallel side events to an integrated component of the COP agenda. The emphasis on monitoring and evaluation of youth recommendations through YOUNGO's Youth Stocktake process marks a shift from participation-as-presence to participation-as-accountability. The forum's demand for binding youth roles rather than consultation spaces reflects a growing maturity in youth climate advocacy.

signals.title: Global Youth Call to Action on Adaptation Launched at COP30 With 10 Priorities for NDCs and NAPs
signals.summary: The Global Center on Adaptation and young people from 90 countries launched the Global Youth Call to Action on Adaptation at COP30, presenting 10 priority recommendations for integrating youth perspectives into NDCs and NAPs. Priorities include scaling adaptation finance access, recognising youth as agents of change, embedding climate education, creating adaptation jobs, integrating Indigenous knowledge, and strengthening intergenerational partnerships.
signals.why_it_matters: This represents the largest coordinated youth input into national adaptation planning processes, directly linking grassroots youth priorities to formal UNFCCC instruments. The 10-priority framework provides concrete benchmarks for governments to assess whether their adaptation plans are intergenerationally responsive, and creates accountability mechanisms for youth monitoring of NDC and NAP implementation across 90 countries.

signals.title: Global Indigenous Youth Caucus Advances Direct Funding and Structural Inclusion Demands at UNPFII 24th Session
signals.source_name: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
signals.summary: During the 24th session of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues in April 2025, the Global Indigenous Youth Caucus called for permanent recognition of Indigenous youth in decision-making processes, specific direct funding mechanisms, and structural inclusion. These demands were incorporated into the UNPFII 24th Session Report. The GIYC also co-led the first Global Youth Declaration on Mercury, highlighting mercury pollution as an intergenerational human rights violation.
signals.why_it_matters: The GIYC is the only Indigenous Youth-led collective within the UN Major Group for Children and Youth, representing all seven socio-cultural regions. Its sustained advocacy for direct funding mechanisms addresses a critical structural barrier: between 2022 and 2024 only 0.96% of major climate foundation grants supported youth-led climate initiatives, with Indigenous youth receiving an even smaller share.

signals.title: UN Youth Office and ITU Sign Joint Declaration on Youth-Inclusive Digital Policies
signals.summary: The United Nations Youth Office and the International Telecommunication Union signed a Joint Declaration on 16 July 2026 to strengthen collaboration on youth-inclusive digital policies and increase young people's participation in shaping digital governance. UN Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs Felipe Paullier announced the agreement, which focuses on promoting digital policies inclusive of young people, advancing youth digital well-being, and ensuring meaningful youth roles in technology governance.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first formal institutional partnership between the UN's youth affairs body and its primary digital governance agency, signalling recognition that youth digital inclusion is a cross-cutting governance priority. As 82% of global youth are digitally connected yet remain marginalised in digital policy forums, this declaration creates a framework for systematically embedding youth perspectives into ITU's standard-setting and digital policy work.

signals.title: Nigeria 30% Youth Quota Bill Passes First Reading in House of Representatives With IPAC Endorsement
signals.summary: A bill seeking to reserve 30% of seats in Nigeria's National and State Legislatures for youths under 35 passed its first reading in the House of Representatives in November 2025. The Inter-Party Advisory Council formally endorsed the bill in April 2026 at the Dialogue4Change Policy Roundtable. The bill complements the existing Not-Too-Young-To-Run Act by creating a structural quota to translate eligibility into actual representation. Advocates aim for at least 20% youth representation in the 11th National Assembly.
signals.why_it_matters: If passed, this would be one of the most ambitious youth quota laws globally, reserving nearly a third of legislative seats for under-35s across all levels of Nigeria's federal system. It directly addresses the gap between formal eligibility and actual representation, recognising that removing age barriers alone is insufficient without structural mechanisms. With Nigeria's youth population being one of the largest demographics globally, this could set a precedent for youth quotas across Africa.

signals.title: Navajo Nation Youth Advisory Council Presents Historic First Report to 25th Navajo Nation Council
signals.summary: The 25th Navajo Nation Council received the first official report from the reestablished Navajo Nation Youth Advisory Council on 21 April 2026, marking the first time a youth advisory body has formally presented before the Navajo Nation Council. The council voted unanimously to accept the report, which outlined the NNYAC's Plan of Operations and Diné Fundamental Law-compliant Rules of Order, focusing on mental health, youth development, and strengthening youth representation across all five agencies of the Navajo Nation.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a landmark moment for Indigenous youth governance within the largest Native American reservation in the United States. The NNYAC's formal integration into the Navajo Nation Council's legislative process creates a structural mechanism for Indigenous youth voices in tribal self-governance, grounded in Diné Fundamental Law. It demonstrates how Indigenous youth advisory bodies can be institutionalised within tribal sovereignty frameworks.

signals.title: Malaysia Revamps Youth Parliament With Proportional Representation and Online Voting Starting 2026
signals.summary: Malaysian Dewan Rakyat Speaker Johari Abdul announced a major reform of the Malaysian Youth Parliament introducing a Proportional Representation and Closed Party List electoral system for voters aged 18-30. The PBMy elections will be conducted entirely online starting from the first sitting in June 2026, with seven parties competing for 222 seats aligned with Dewan Rakyat constituencies. PBMy sittings will occur three times annually, with resolutions channeled to the Parliamentary Special Select Committee for consideration as national agenda.
signals.why_it_matters: This reform transforms the Youth Parliament from a training ground into a strategic platform with direct policy influence, creating an institutional pipeline for youth-led legislative proposals to enter national parliamentary discourse. The use of online voting for youth elections is an innovative approach to reducing participation barriers, while the PR-Closed Party List system encourages programmatic politics among youth.

signals.title: Pan-African Youth Ambassadors for Internet Governance Launches 2026 Fellowship in AI Governance and Cyber Diplomacy
signals.summary: The Pan-African Youth Ambassadors for Internet Governance, recognised under the ITU's WSIS Champion 2025, announced its 2026 Fellowship with targeted tracks in Cyber Diplomacy, Digital Rights, and AI Governance. The initiative has brought together over 1,000 young leaders from 52 African countries, with women representing more than half of participants. Operating across five language cohorts, PAYAIG creates pathways for African youth to engage with global processes including the Global Digital Compact and Internet Governance Forum mechanisms.
signals.why_it_matters: Africa is the world's youngest continent with over 60% of the population under 25, yet its voice in global digital governance remains limited. PAYAIG addresses this structural imbalance by building a pipeline of informed young digital policy leaders across 52 countries and five language groups. The shift to specialised tracks in AI Governance and Cyber Diplomacy reflects recognition that youth need domain-specific expertise to influence emerging technology governance.

signals.title: California AB 1899 Proposes Office of Youth Homelessness Prevention to Reduce Youth Homelessness to Functional Zero
