signals.title: New Zealand Launches 2026–2036 Mental Health Strategy With Co-Designed Youth Roadmap and Under-18 Seclusion Ban Path
signals.source_name: New Zealand Ministry of Health / Beehive
signals.summary: On 6 August 2026 Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey launched New Zealand’s Mental Health and Wellbeing Strategy 2026–2036 and a three-year Implementation Plan (2026/27–2028/29). The strategy states that nearly half of mental health challenges emerge before age 18 and that 22.9% of people aged 15–24 report high or very high psychological distress; Priority 1 includes expanding age- and developmentally tailored child and youth supports with flexible age-range eligibility. The Implementation Plan commits to collaboratively develop by 30 June 2027 and implement a youth mental health and addiction action plan (integrated services designed with young people, stronger transitions, flexible age bands, school-based supports), a national seclusion-elimination plan, and a child-and-youth prevalence survey to be completed in 2028. The Beehive release ties the seclusion pathway to the recently passed Mental Health Bill, which prohibits seclusion for people under 18. Delivery is to be met from existing health resources, including a mental health and addiction ringfence of about $2.982 billion in 2026/27.
signals.why_it_matters: Youth mental health is treated here as future-capacity infrastructure: untreated distress before 18 compounds into adult workforce, care and fiscal costs borne by later cohorts. The mechanism is a 10-year statutory-adjacent strategy plus a dated youth co-design instrument (roadmap by 30 June 2027) and a child-specific seclusion prohibition—shifting who designs services (young people) and who is protected from coercive care (minors) rather than leaving lifetime harm as a private residual.

signals.title: Ontario Opens Enhanced HST Rebate Worth Up to $130,000 on New Primary Homes for 2026–27
signals.summary: Ontario’s Enhanced New Housing Rebate (ENHR) and Enhanced New Residential Rental Property Rebate, implemented by federal regulations made 12 June 2026, rebate 100% of the 8% provincial HST on eligible new or substantially renovated homes used as a primary residence, up to $80,000 on homes valued to $1 million (tapering to the legacy $24,000 at $1.85 million). The Ontario New Home Affordability Payment then tops up the 5% federal GST portion (up to $50,000), for combined relief of up to $130,000. Purchase agreements must be signed between 1 April 2026 and 31 March 2027. The official backgrounder, updated 23 July 2026, states applications are now available through CRA. A separate Ontario first-time-home-buyer rebate of the full 8% provincial HST on new homes up to $1 million (agreements 20 March 2025–31 December 2030) can be claimed alongside ENHR, but total 8% relief is capped at $80,000.
signals.why_it_matters: Transaction-tax relief on new primary residences cuts the cash barrier that hits first-time and younger buyers hardest, while assignment-sale and investor-limitation rules try to keep the subsidy from flipping to asset-holders. Mechanism: time-limited HST rebate plus a first-home overlay, shifting fiscal cost from today’s new-home occupiers onto general revenue rather than onto existing owners’ wealth.

signals.title: Portugal Enacts Decreto-Lei 97/2026 Housing-Tax Package for First Homes, Moderate Rents and Non-Resident Buyers
signals.summary: On 20 May 2026 Portugal published Decreto-Lei n.º 97/2026, using the authorisation in Lei n.º 9-A/2026 of 6 March, as a fiscal package to expand first-home and rental supply. The law applies a temporary 6% VAT rate to construction and rehabilitation of housing; raises the IRS deduction for residential rents to €900 in 2026 and €1,000 from 2027; sets a 10% special IRS rate through 31 December 2029 on rental income at or below a ‘moderate monthly rent’ (capped at 2.5 times the 2026 minimum wage); reduces IMT and stamp duty for controlled-cost homes; and imposes a flat 7.5% IMT, with no exemption or reduction, on urban housing bought by non-residents. Buyers who do not put a home to owner-occupation within six months face a 10% IMT surcharge. Investment-for-rental contracts (CIA) and a simplified affordable-rental regime (RSAA) start 1 September 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: The preamble names first permanent home (HPP) access as the policy problem. The package simultaneously cheapens construction and moderate rents for occupiers, claws back IMT if a buyer does not live in the home, and taxes non-resident purchasers more heavily—shifting fiscal incidence from young first-home and renter cohorts toward non-resident and non-occupying capital.

signals.title: Rhode Island Non-Owner Occupied Property Tax Takes Effect on Homes Over $1 Million Left Empty
signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 Rhode Island began collecting a new state Non-Owner Occupied Property Tax (R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 44-72), enacted in the FY2026 budget (House Bill 5076, Article 5, § 18). The tax applies to municipally classified residential property assessed above $1 million that the owner does not occupy as a primary residence for at least 183 days in the preceding privilege year (1 July 2025–30 June 2026 for the first year). The rate is $2.50 per $500 of assessed value above $1 million (0.5% of the excess); the threshold indexes to CPI-U from tax years beginning 1 July 2027. Exemptions cover long-term or short-term rentals actually rented 183 days or more. Tax is billed in four instalments (15 September, 15 December, 15 March, 15 June). From 1 July 2026, sales of residential property assessed over $1 million require a Division Certificate of No Tax Due (Advisory 2026-17).
signals.why_it_matters: This is a state-level vacant/second-home levy that prices unused high-value housing held by asset-owners rather than lived in or rented. Incidence falls on current wealth holders of empty or seasonal stock; the intended transfer is toward local housing supply and younger households locked out of ownership. Mechanism: occupancy-conditioned property tax plus a closing-certificate gate, distinct from baby-bond wealth architecture already in the corpus.

signals.title: Sámi Youth Gávnnadeapmi 3 Declaration Demands FPIC, Climate Emergency Fund and Undivided Sápmi
signals.summary: Sámi youth gathered in Ohcejohka / Utsjoki, Finland, from 15–18 June 2026 and issued the Gávnnadeapmi 3 Youth Declaration – Oktasaš Sápmi, delivered by Elle-Rávdná Näkkäläjärvi on behalf of participants and published by the Saami Council. The declaration frames an undivided Sápmi across colonial borders, states that healthy ecosystems are required for present and future Sámi generations, and condemns renewable-energy siting on Sámi territories as green colonialism. It demands Sámi community-led monitoring and Rights of Nature implementation; legal recognition of Sámi reindeer herding as a distinct Indigenous practice in Finland; a Sámi-governed emergency fund for climate-driven livelihood loss; full FPIC for any activities on Sámi lands including military presence and mass tourism; alignment of national law with UNDRIP, ILO 169, ICCPR and ICERD; a cross-border Sámi curriculum and resources for all Sámi languages; and reclamation of the siida system. It also calls for permanently funded culturally based youth mental-health services.
signals.why_it_matters: This is Indigenous youth climate governance in the form of a cross-border political mandate, not a consultation quote. The asked-for instruments are FPIC as a land-use veto/process, a Sámi-governed climate loss fund, legal recognition of herding, and language education—each allocating who pays for green-transition infrastructure now versus who inherits degraded grazing lands, salmon rivers and living languages. Young Sámi explicitly refuse to carry both climate damage and land dispossession for renewable energy.

signals.title: Sri Lanka Certifies National Environmental (Amendment) Act No. 15 of 2026 Mandating Strategic Environmental Assessment of Government Policies
signals.source_name: Parliament of Sri Lanka / Government Gazette (Department of Government Printing)
signals.summary: The National Environmental (Amendment) Act, No. 15 of 2026, certified on 21 July 2026 and published as a supplement to Part II of the Gazette of 24 July 2026, amends the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980. New Part IVD (section 23KK) requires any government policy, plan or programme likely to have a significant environmental effect to undergo strategic environmental assessment before adoption, with a national-security/emergency exception. The Central Environmental Authority gains an explicit power (section 10(ha)) to require SEAs. The Act also adds wetland conservation (Part IVE), extended producer responsibility, stronger licensing and local-authority enforcement, and reconstitutes the Authority’s membership. The certified text states it may be downloaded from documents.gov.lk.

Mechanism: a gazetted statutory SEA duty plus wetland and EPR powers, shifting residual environmental risk from future residents onto current ministries before they lock in plans.

signals.summary: On 27 May 2026 Governor Greg Abbott sent a letter to all Texas public higher-education presidents stating that his November 2024 directive remains fully in effect: no undergraduate tuition or fees may increase for academic year 2026-27. signals.title: UK House of Lords Gives Second Reading to Nature's Rights Bill Creating Guardianship Council and Tribunal
signals.summary: On 3 July 2026 the House of Lords held second reading of the Nature's Rights Bill [HL] (session 2026-27), a private member's bill introduced 1 June 2026. The bill as introduced would recognise Nature as a legal subject, impose a duty of care on public bodies, businesses and individuals, create an Integrated Rights Framework, and establish a Nature Guardianship Council, Bioregional Councils and a Nature's Rights Tribunal, with phased implementation and parliamentary scrutiny. Official parliamentary records show the bill then moved to committee stage. As a Lords private member's bill it remains procedurally fragile and is not government legislation.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first time rights-of-nature architecture has entered the UK parliamentary process, proposing guardianship institutions that would represent ecosystems against present-day extraction. Mechanism: a Nature Guardianship Council plus tribunal would shift standing and duty of care so future ecological integrity is not only a policy target but a justiciable interest. Because it is a PMB, the intergenerational mechanism is still prospective, not enacted.

signals.title: UK Work and Pensions Committee Calls for a Youth Employment Strategy, Under-25 NICs Relief and 10-Year Youth Guarantee Funding
signals.source_name: UK House of Commons Work and Pensions Committee
signals.summary: On 22 July 2026 the Work and Pensions Committee published its Third Report of Session 2026-27 (HC 180) on youth employment, education and training. It records 1.01 million NEETs in January-March 2026 (13.5% of 16-24s), of whom 61% are economically inactive, and estimates the direct cost at about £47 billion. The Committee says current Youth Guarantee schemes mainly reach benefit claimants even though 44% of NEETs are not claiming, and that the Guarantee must not become another 'here-today-gone-tomorrow' youth policy. Binding recommendations include a cross-departmental youth employment strategy with NEET-reduction targets; extending the National Insurance Upper Secondary Threshold so all employees under 25 attract no employer Class 1 NICs until they earn more than £967 a week; and a minimum Youth Guarantee funding level for the next 10 years, including matching long-term settlements with local government. The government has two months to respond. The Milburn review's final recommendations remain outstanding.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a parliamentary demand to convert short-cycle youth employment schemes into a decade-long fiscal commitment and a tax-side hiring subsidy for under-25s. The mechanism is explicit: employer NICs currently make 21-24-year-old non-apprentices more expensive to hire than under-21s, while time-limited Youth Guarantee money leaves later cohorts exposed when the 2026/27-2028/29 envelope expires. The Committee frames the task as preventing today's NEET spike from becoming a scarred future generation.

signals.title: US 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act Bans Large Institutional Investors from Buying Existing Single-Family Homes
signals.summary: H.R. 6644 became Public Law 119-101 on 11 July 2026. Section 1001 (‘Homes Are for People, Not Corporations’) prohibits a ‘large institutional investor’—a for-profit entity that, alone or in concert, has investment control of at least 350 single-family homes after enactment—from purchasing or contracting to purchase any single-family home. Exceptions include newly built sale inventory, build-to-rent, substantial renovate-to-rent, specified rent-to-own and first-look homeownership programmes, and pre-enactment stock (no forced divestiture). Treasury, in consultation with HUD, FHFA and the SEC, may issue implementing rules but may not raise the 350-home threshold. Civil penalties are up to $1 million per violation or three times the purchase price, whichever is greater, with amounts from FY2027 transferable to HUD homeownership-expansion activities. HUD must open a renter-outreach resource within 180 days.
signals.why_it_matters: The Act draws a statutory line between household buyers and scaled corporate landlords in the existing single-family stock—the inventory first-time and younger buyers compete for. Mechanism: a prospective purchase ban on large funds, with penalties recycled toward homeownership, rather than a tax on vacant or inherited wealth.

signals.title: US Education Department Finalises Workforce Pell for 8-15 Week Programmes, Effective 20 July 2026 With Early Start 1 July
signals.source_name: U.S. Federal Register / Department of Education
signals.summary: On 19 May 2026 the Department of Education published a final rule (FR 2026-10013; 34 CFR 600/668/690; Docket ED-2026-OPE-0133) implementing Workforce Pell Grants under the Working Families Tax Cuts Act. Eligible workforce programmes must last at least 8 but less than 15 weeks, comprise 150-599 clock hours (or credit-hour equivalents), be Governor- and Secretary-approved, meet completion and job-placement rates, and keep published tuition and fees at or below a value-added earnings metric (completer median earnings minus 150% of federal poverty for a single person). Students in these programmes may receive Pell only, not other Title IV aid; bachelor's-degree holders may receive Workforce Pell, but graduate-credential holders may not. The rule is effective 20 July 2026, with Secretary-authorised early implementation from 1 July 2026. It also limits Pell for students whose non-federal grants or scholarships already cover cost of attendance.
signals.why_it_matters: Workforce Pell redirects the main US need-based grant toward short, employer-aligned credentials with an earnings-minus-tuition test, instead of traditional degree programmes that load younger cohorts with loans. That can open a non-debt skills pathway for students who would otherwise borrow, but it also tightens conventional Pell just as RAP/Grad PLUS changes make graduate and professional borrowing more private. Future cohorts' mobility then depends on whether Governors actually certify high-wage programmes rather than low-quality short courses.

signals.title: Waitangi Tribunal Finds Crown in Treaty Breach Over 2026 Clause Review Covering Climate and Child Acts
signals.summary: On 31 July 2026 the Waitangi Tribunal released Te Tinihanga o ngā Mātāpono, the urgent Wai 3565 report on Cabinet’s 23 February 2026 decision to repeal or downgrade Treaty of Waitangi / te Tiriti provisions in 18–19 statutes. Affected laws include the Climate Change Response Act 2002 (s 3A, including converting it toward a purely descriptive provision), the Crown Pastoral Land Act 1998, the Environment Act 1986, the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Act 2012, the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, and Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022. The Tribunal found Cabinet proceeded without Māori consultation, largely disregarded officials’ advice, and prioritised coalition commitments; it held the process already breached the principles of partnership, active protection and good government, and that enactment without co-design would also breach equity and redress. It recommended an immediate pause, no repeals or downgrades, co-design with Māori, and consultation with post-settlement governance entities on settlement impacts. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith told media the Government’s position is unchanged and the review will continue, while stating the bill will not pass before the November 2026 election.
signals.why_it_matters: The intergenerational mechanism is statutory Treaty weighting inside climate, land, environment and child-welfare law. Weakening those clauses shifts who can require the Crown to protect Māori land, forests returned in settlements, coastal marae and tamariki now versus who bears later climate, conservation and care costs. The Climate Change Response Act provisions were originally sold as protecting iwi forestry returned in Treaty settlements from ETS surprises; their repeal or dilution would lock present political preferences over future kaitiakitanga. Oranga Tamariki Treaty duties are the child-rights counterpart: present care decisions shape the next generation of land stewards.

signals.title: Washington Opens WA Cares Benefits, Launching the First US Public Long-Term Care Insurance Paid by Current Workers
signals.source_name: WA Cares Fund / Washington State Department of Social and Health Services
signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 Washington began paying benefits from the WA Cares Fund, the first public long-term care insurance programme in the United States. Workers have contributed 0.58% of wages via automatic payroll deduction since 1 July 2023; approved beneficiaries can access up to $36,500 in lifetime covered services (inflation-adjusted), including in-home care, paying a family caregiver, home modifications, meals and transportation. Governor Bob Ferguson’s 30 June 2026 release stated that nearly half a million Washingtonians will need long-term care within ten years, that fewer than 3% of Americans hold private LTC insurance, and that more than one million Washington renters cannot tap home equity. Qualification requires both a contribution history and a care-needs assessment (help with daily activities such as bathing, eating, medications and mobility); even workers or recent retirees who contributed only part of a year since July 2023 may have earned usable benefits.
signals.why_it_matters: WA Cares is a state-level intergenerational LTC levy: today’s working-age payroll funds a social-insurance floor so ageing and disability care does not strip housing wealth from the next household generation. Younger contributors pay now for benefits they may draw decades later, while near-retirees can access partial benefits after a short contribution window—an explicit now-versus-later bargain that also lets benefits pay family caregivers, converting unpaid kin labour into a covered service.

signals.title: Western Australia Lifts First-Home Duty and Grant Caps in a $297 Million 2026–27 Housing Tax Package
signals.summary: On 7 May 2026 Western Australia announced a $297 million housing-taxation package. For transactions from that date, the first-home owner rate of duty (FHOR) exempts newly built or established homes up to $600,000 (was $500,000) with a concession to $800,000 (was $700,000), and vacant land up to $450,000 (was $350,000) with a concession to $550,000. The first-home owner grant cap south of the 26th parallel rises to $800,000, and FHOR eligibility is unlinked from the grant cap so buyers above the grant ceiling can still get a duty concession. A new foreign-transfer-duty exemption is created for build-to-sell projects that add at least one net dwelling. RevenueWA’s official page, last updated 29 July 2026, states the FHOG, FHOR and off-the-plan concession changes are now live, with refunds available for settlements between announcement and 28 July; the foreign-duty exemption awaits Royal Assent of the Finance Legislation Amendment (Housing Affordability) Bill 2026.

The Senate gist requires the Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism to designate large-share housing suppliers (about one-quarter of the market in the earlier MLIT bill note) as upper-tier housing top-runners who must file medium- to long-term energy-performance plans and annual implementation reports, with ministerial recommendations if progress is seriously inadequate. Building owners, architects, contractors and materials producers receive effort duties to cut whole-life (embodied plus operational) carbon; owners of specified-use buildings above a size set by Cabinet order must prepare a design-stage whole-life carbon plan, carry out an assessment, and notify the Minister  — who may recommend improvements. A registered-body environmental-performance certification and labelling scheme is created, and equivalent-performance ministerial certification can unlock floor-area-ratio exceptions. Most provisions take effect on a Cabinet-order date within two years of promulgation. Buildings account for about 40% of Japan's greenhouse-gas emissions in the 27 March 2026 MLIT Cabinet-decision note.
signals.why_it_matters: Housing and commercial buildings lock in carbon for 30–80 years, so today's design choices are a physical transfer of mitigation cost onto children who will occupy and retrofit the stock. Mechanism: statutory whole-life carbon assessment plus top-runner planning duties on the largest housing suppliers, so embodied emissions from materials and construction cannot be left as an uncounted residual for later cohorts after operational energy standards were already tightened.

signals.title: Korea Announces Future Response Fund to Ring-Fence Windfall Tax Revenue for Youth, Regions and Skills
signals.source_name: Korea Policy Briefing / Ministry of Planning and Budget
signals.summary: On 13 July 2026 President Lee Jae-myung chaired Korea's first National Fiscal Strategy Meeting of the current administration at Cheong Wa Dae. Planning and Budget Minister Park Hong-keun presented a 2027 budget and medium-term fiscal direction that would create a Future Response Fund (미래대응기금) as a strategic investment platform: tax receipts above the long-term trend, including the semiconductor boom, would be accumulated in the fund and concentrated on four fields — youth, growth engines, regions, and talent — rather than absorbed into ordinary current spending. Mechanism: above-trend tax receipts parked in a dedicated fund earmarked for youth, skills, regions and future productive capacity, instead of financing present consumption or ageing-related mandatory spending — the opposite incidence of a tax-cut or basic-pension expansion paid by later taxpayers.

signals.title: Peru Publishes DS 009-2026-MINEDU, Creating One-Year State Boards to Keep Students in Unlicensed Associative Universities
signals.source_name: Diario Oficial El Peruano / Ministerio de Educación
signals.summary: On 24 June 2026 (El Peruano 25 June) President José María Balcázar Zelada and Education Minister María Esther Cuadros Espinoza signed Decreto Supremo Nº 009-2026-MINEDU, the 19-article regulation of Ley 32494. The statute covers only non-profit associative universities created by law, with a final SUNEDU licence denial, already in cese de actividades, and with enrolled students harmed by that wind-down. MINEDU must install a Comisión Técnica de Gestión Excepcional (CTGE) for each such campus: a MINEDU-designated chair plus elected teacher and student members. The board takes temporary government, administration and legal representation, automatically displacing sitting authorities, for one year from installation unless the university obtains a SUNEDU licence or has no remaining enrolled students. University assets may not be transferred or encumbered; cash-flow may be used only to keep teaching, payroll and tax obligations running. CTGE costs are charged to the university’s own resources. The decree implements the Ley Universitaria ‘interés superior del estudiante’ rule so that a failed private licence does not strand the current student cohort.
signals.why_it_matters: When a private university loses its licence, the cost usually falls on the students already enrolled—lost years, stranded fees, and a weaker credential—while founders exit. The CTGE is a one-year public stewardship overlay that keeps those students on a completion path instead of treating institutional failure as a private loss. Later cohorts are not promised new places at the failed campus; the instrument protects the generation already inside the system.

signals.title: Serbia Enacts €4/t Greenhouse-Gas Emissions Tax, Applicable from 1 January 2026
signals.source_name: National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia
signals.summary: The National Assembly’s adopted-laws archive now publishes the Law on the Tax on Greenhouse Gas Emissions (2230-25), which wave 2 could not verify as enacted on parlament.gov.rs. The Tax Administration cites Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia No. 109/25. Article 1 introduces a tax on CO2, N2O and PFCs. Article 2 limits taxpayers to operators required to hold a GHG-emissions permit in fertiliser and nitrogen compounds, cement, crude iron/steel/ferroalloys, aluminium, or electricity production. Article 3 sets the base as verified total emissions minus a reference quantity for best available technology, multiplied by four euros per tonne of CO2 or CO2-equivalent in dinars at the National Bank middle rate on the last day of the tax period (normally the calendar year). Article 4 grants electricity producers that earned at least 80% of prior-period revenue from power a tax credit of 20% of qualifying decarbonisation investment, capped at 80% of the tax due. Article 7 authorises budget incentives for renewable energy, efficiency, low-carbon technology, industrial decarbonisation, energy-transition infrastructure, green building and just-transition support for vulnerable households. Articles 9–11 apply the credit and incentive provisions for ten years from application, require implementing by-laws within 180 days of entry into force, and provide that the law enters into force eight days after gazette publication and applies from 1 January 2026. The same sitting adopted a sister Law on the Tax on Import of Carbon-Intensive Products (2231-25), also applicable from 1 January 2026. signals.title: UNPFII 25 Official Report Calls for Binding FPIC in Just-Transition Pathways by 2027
signals.source_name: UN Economic and Social Council / Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues
signals.summary: The official report of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues on its twenty-fifth session (20 April–1 May 2026), issued as ECOSOC Official Records 2026 Supplement No. 23, document E/2026/43–E/C.19/2026/6 (8 May 2026), is now on documents.un.org (N2611013). The Forum held an interregional, intergenerational dialogue on Indigenous Peoples and climate change (UNDRIP arts. 3, 4, 25 and 26). Paragraph 14 welcomes the UAE just-transition work programme and calls on UNFCCC Parties, by the end of 2027, to reflect it in binding national frameworks operationalising FPIC in all just-transition pathways, including transition minerals, renewable energy and biofuels, and to report to UNPFII 26. Paragraph 17 calls on UN entities to require FPIC as a mandatory condition for all just-transition programmes; to establish by 2027 monitoring of health and cultural-continuity impacts, with particular attention to women and children; and to operationalise by 2027 direct-access funding mechanisms for Indigenous Peoples without intermediary requirements. Paragraph 16 asks States by 2027 to designate territories of Peoples in isolation as exclusion zones, halt projects lacking FPIC, and suspend fast-tracked critical-minerals projects pending Indigenous-led impact assessments. Paragraph 56 reiterates that national law must align with FPIC and that consultation is not a substitute for consent. Draft decision II sets UNPFII 26 for 10–21 May 2027 at UN Headquarters.
signals.why_it_matters: The intergenerational mechanism is a time-bound UN recommendation that just-transition minerals, renewables and carbon markets must run through FPIC and direct-access finance rather than intermediary climate funds. Without it, present extraction on Indigenous lands locks in loss of territory, language and health for the next generation while States claim a green transition. Isolated Peoples in the Amazon are named as needing exclusion zones before contact-forced development proceeds.

signals.title: Czech Environment Ministry Reports Nearly 3,000 Responses to Public Consultation on Draft National Restoration Plan
signals.summary: The Czech Environment Ministry's official NPOP consultation page states that a public consultation on the first working version of the National Restoration Plan (Narodni plan na obnovu prirody) ran from 21 April to 15 May 2026, opened by a public seminar on 21 April. The ministry reports almost 3,000 respondents; more than 2,700 agreed that the landscape and biodiversity are deteriorating, citing drought and water scarcity, insect and bird decline, and worsening forests as top problems; more than 2,900 supported introducing restoration measures and treated restoration as a public interest on a par with other development priorities. Open-text comments called for stronger agricultural-landscape measures, wetlands and reduced drainage, cross-sector links to farming and spatial planning, and involvement of landowners and municipalities. The ministry published the questionnaire results spreadsheet (dated 25 May 2026) and a 1 June 2026 chat transcript from the online seminar. The parent NPOP page still used future tense for an April consultation even after the results page was live; the dedicated results page is the verified record. The draft remains due to the Commission by 1 September 2026 after inter-ministerial comment and summer government approval.
signals.why_it_matters: Czechia has generated a mass public mandate for restoration before locking the 2030/2040/2050 NRP. Mechanism: feeding nearly 3,000 consultation responses into the legally required National Restoration Plan decides which ecosystems (especially water in the landscape and agricultural features) are restored this decade and how restoration costs and land-use rules are shared across generations.

signals.source_name: Finnish Government / Ministry of the Environment and Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry
signals.summary: On 2 July 2026 Finland's Ministry of the Environment and Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry opened a request for views on a summary of the draft national restoration plan (ennallistamissuunnitelma), with comments due 27 August 2026 on Lausuntopalvelu.fi (diaari VN/25123/2024-YM-313). signals.title: Kosovo Enacts Law 10/L-021 on Financing Water-Resource Management with User-Pays and Polluter-Pays Charges
signals.source_name: Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure of Kosovo / Official Gazette
signals.summary: The ministry-hosted Official Gazette text of Law No. 10/L-021 on Financing Water-Resource Management records Assembly adoption, proclamation by acting President Albulena Haxhiu (decree DL-53/2026 of 5 May 2026), publication in GZ No. 9 of 13 May 2026, and entry into force 15 days after publication. Article 1 aligns the statute in part with the EU Water Framework Directive 2000/60/EC. Article 4 finances water-resource management from water charges paid by users and polluters, treats water as having an economic value, and writes in the ‘user pays’ and ‘polluter pays’ principles. Charges cover abstraction (including hydropower, irrigation, bottling, process water), wastewater discharge, mineral-fertiliser and plant-protection-product production/import, and alluvial extraction. Article 12(5) sets a floor: the wastewater charge may not be lower than treatment cost. A Water Resource Management Agency calculates charges; until it is established, the competent ministry unit acts (Art. 32). By-laws on metering are due in six months and on charge levels in twelve months (Art. 30). Existing abstractors without meters have twelve months to install them or lose their water permit (Art. 31).
signals.why_it_matters: Kosovo’s rivers and aquifers are the water stock later cohorts will drink, irrigate and generate from; unpriced abstraction and untreated discharge shift scarcity and pollution onto them. Mechanism: a gazetted user-pays/polluter-pays charging statute, in force 15 days after 13 May 2026, that funds water-resource management from today’s abstractors and dischargers rather than from general taxation alone, with a WFD cost-recovery alignment.

signals.title: Maldives Enacts Sixth Pension Act Amendment 4/2026 Targeting Basic Pension and Opening Self-Employed Coverage
signals.source_name: Attorney General's Office / Government Gazette of the Maldives
signals.summary: The Gazette of the Maldives Volume 55, Issue 82 of 21 May 2026 publishes Act No. 4/2026, the Sixth Amendment to the Maldives Pension Act 8/2009, passed by the Majlis on 14 May 2026 and ratified on 21 May 2026, in force on gazette. The amendment retargets Basic Pension: persons whose other pension and income exceed the Basic Pension amount lose the old-age Basic Pension (new s.11(c-1)); elected or appointed public office-holders and government/SOE employees lose Basic Pension while in those posts (new s.11(r-1)). It expands self-employed participation in the Maldives Retirement Pension Scheme (s.14(c) contribution rules). Investment duties are tightened (ss.3, 6, 16): assets must be invested solely for members and beneficiaries, with life-stage funds and a statement of investment principles. The Maldives Pension Administration Office English notice of the same day also records RSA collateral for house construction/renovation loans, early RSA access for terminal illness, and Hajj-place reservation from pension savings. signals.source_name: Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Serbia
signals.summary: On 25 June 2026 the National Assembly adopted the Law amending the Law on Establishing a Guarantee Scheme and Subsidising Part of the Interest as a Measure of Support to Young People in Purchasing a First Residential Property. The Assembly’s enacted-laws register lists adoption on 25 June 2026 and publication in Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia No. 56/26. The Ministry of Finance notice of the same day states that the ceiling of loans covered by the state guarantee rises from €600 million to €900 million (a further €300 million after a prior rise from €400 million to €600 million). The programme remains for Serbian citizens resident in Serbia aged 20–35 at application, employed or not, including farmers, the self-employed and independent artists; maximum covered loan €100,000; banks must offer 1% down-payment and a one-year grace period; state interest subsidy 2 percentage points for the first six years (user rate 1.5% vs 3.5% fixed). The Government bill of 7 May 2026 (still listed among bills in procedure on the live tracker) is the same instrument now recorded as enacted in the doneti-zakoni register.

Mechanism: a gazetted 2026 amendment (SG RS 56/26) that raises the statutory guarantee envelope by €300 million to €900 million without changing the age gate or the 40% bank-cover architecture of the parent 2025 law.

signals.title: Serbia Ratifies the CRC Optional Protocol on a Communications Procedure (Official Gazette MU 6/26)
signals.source_name: National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia
signals.summary: The National Assembly’s enacted-laws register records that on 10 July 2026 it adopted the Law on Confirmation of the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a Communications Procedure, on a Government proposal submitted 4 June 2026, published in Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia — International Treaties No. 6/26. The Protocol, which Serbia signed in 2012, lets a child, group of children or representative file an individual communication with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child after domestic remedies are exhausted, and allows a confidential inquiry into grave or systematic violations. The Committee’s views trigger a six-month state reply. Tanjug, quoting the Ministry for Human and Minority Rights and Social Dialogue on 10 July 2026, frames ratification as completing Serbia’s CRC treaty set and as a Chapter 23 interim benchmark. Complaints cannot be filed until the instrument of ratification is deposited with the UN Secretary-General and three months elapse; the Committee has jurisdiction only over violations after that date (and continuing ones).
signals.why_it_matters: Individual access to the CRC Committee is the last-instance accountability channel for today’s children when Serbian courts and administration fail — a governance lock that later cohorts inherit only if the instrument is deposited and used. Mechanism: a gazetted 2026 ratification law (SG RS — MU 6/26) opening the UN communications procedure after domestic remedies, contingent on deposit and a three-month entry-into-force clock.

signals.title: Bolivia Submits NDC 3.0 With Intergenerational Approach and 80% Deforestation Cut by 2035
signals.source_name: UNFCCC NDC Registry / Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia
signals.summary: The Plurinational State of Bolivia submitted NDC 3.0 to the UNFCCC on 29 September 2025 (registry timestamp 16:33) covering 2026–2035. The fetched official PDF sets 36 sectoral targets (13 mitigation, 16 adaptation, 7 joint). Headline mitigation includes cutting deforestation outside protected areas by 80% versus baseline by 2035 and adding 1 million hectares of forest cover through restoration, afforestation and reforestation. Agriculture pledges conservation of 1 million hectares of soils and climate-resilience support for at least 400,000 producers. Average conditionality is 74%, so most ambition depends on international climate finance. Section 10.3 (‘Enfoque intergeneracional’) treats children, adolescents and youth as agents of change, not only vulnerable groups, and lists youth climate-governance leadership, green skills, differentiated child/youth impact assessment, and intergenerational participation mechanisms. On 11 February 2026 the Ministry of Planning and the Autoridad Plurinacional de la Madre Tierra convened sectoral tables in La Paz to write those NDC targets into the PDES 2026–2030.
signals.why_it_matters: Bolivia has no prior record in the corpus. NDC 3.0 is the Paris-cycle instrument that allocates who cuts deforestation and who pays for it through 2035: present extractive and agricultural cohorts versus children who will inherit the remaining forest, soils and water. The named intergenerational approach and 74% finance-conditionality make later delivery a test of whether youth participation and land restoration actually reach the next cohort or stay on paper until donors pay.

signals.title: Canada Enacts National School Food Program Act, Locking Long-Term Federal Funding for Child Meals
signals.source_name: Justice Laws Website / Statutes of Canada
signals.summary: On 26 March 2026 Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent and enacted the National School Food Program Act as section 599 of chapter 3 of the Statutes of Canada, 2026, in force on assent. The Act’s vision is that all children and youth in Canada have access to nutritious food at school in an inclusive, non-stigmatizing setting that strengthens connections with local food systems, the environment and culture. It commits the Government of Canada to maintaining long-term funding through agreements with provinces, territories or Indigenous governing bodies, guided by accessibility, health promotion, inclusivity, flexibility, sustainability and accountability, and requires an annual report tabled in Parliament. Finance Canada’s 26 March release states the Act helps provide meals for up to 400,000 more children annually. ESDC’s 27 May 2026 release records that Budget 2025 also committed $216.6 million per year from 2029–30 to make the programme permanent, and that all provinces and territories had signed bilateral agreements by 10 March 2025. The Justice Laws full text was last modified 6 August 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: School meals convert a child’s daily nutrition and attendance into a statutory federal funding duty rather than a time-limited budget line, so later cohorts keep the meal even when a future cabinet would rather cut discretionary spending. Local-sourcing language ties today’s public procurement to family-farm and Indigenous food systems that the next generation will inherit, while the CRC and SDG recitals make child food access a rights-and-future-generations obligation, not charity.

signals.title: Costa Rica Enacts Law 10896 Reforming Youth Committees under the General Young Persons Act
signals.summary: On 8 June 2026 Costa Rica published Legislative Decree 10896 (file 23.594) in Alcance 71 to La Gaceta No. 104, reforming the second paragraph of Article 24 of Law 8261 (Ley General de la Persona Joven, 2 May 2002) to guarantee that municipal and district youth committees actually exist and function. The Assembly’s Comisión Legislativa Plena Primera and plenary approved the reform on 25 March 2026; President Laura Fernández Delgado executed it on 12 May 2026 with the Ministers of Culture and Youth and of Interior. Each municipality and district council must constitute its comité de la persona joven in October–November of even years, with functions starting 1 January of the following odd year. If force majeure, duly justified to the Consejo de la Persona Joven, blocks that window, an extraordinary call may run through December of the even year and January of the odd year so the committee can still serve the rest of the term. The law takes effect on publication.
signals.why_it_matters: Costa Rica’s youth committees are the local seats through which people under 35 feed municipal agendas; empty or late-formed committees leave later cohorts without a standing voice in local budgets and climate/risk plans. The reform converts a calendar duty into a backstop: if a municipality misses the even-year window, the national youth council can still force constitution rather than leaving a two-year vacancy. Mechanism: statutory amendment of Law 8261 Art. 24 plus an extraordinary-call path supervised by the Consejo de la Persona Joven, so local youth representation is not optional between election cycles.

signals.title: Costa Rica Gazettes Law 10954 Approving a USD 370 Million Climate-Resilient Reconstruction Loan
signals.summary: On 20 May 2026 Costa Rica published Legislative Decree 10954 (file 24.761) approving Financing Agreement 9653-CR with IBRD, plus GCFF trust fund TF0C4693-CR, for the Programa de Reconstrucción y Desarrollo Territorial Resiliente al Clima. The CNE is the executing agency and must form a programme unit reporting to its Executive Directorate. The project objective, copied into the gazetted Spanish translation of Annex 1, is to increase access to disaster- and climate-resilient infrastructure and services in selected regions. Part 1 finances grey/green flood works, slope stabilisation and critical road/bridge reconstruction; Part 2 finances emergency warehouses, multi-purpose shelters, a new CNE headquarters/emergency operations centre, basin-scale early-warning systems, municipal emergency-committee capacity, an inclusive community-recovery policy, and gender-specific design in critical infrastructure; Part 3 covers project management, climate-indicator monitoring and grievance mechanisms. Disbursements for Part 1 go to the Fondo Nacional de Emergencias; Parts 2–3 to CNE accounts. A World Bank letter of 2 March 2026 had reinstated the 2024 financing agreement after it lapsed on 30 January 2026 and extended effectiveness to 30 July 2026; the May gazette is the domestic statute that makes that package Costa Rican law.

signals.title: Dominican Republic Registers NDC 3.0 with a 28–32% GHG Cut and Child-and-Youth Cross-Cutting Measures
signals.source_name: UNFCCC NDC registry / MMARN and CNCCMC
signals.summary: On 9 June 2026 the UNFCCC NDC registry marked Dominican Republic NDC 3.0 (NDC 3.0 RD-2025) active and posted the official Spanish PDF. Versus a 2022-based BAU path the pledge cuts GHG 28% by 2030 (14,732.1 kt CO2eq) and 32% by 2035 (18,349.32 kt CO2eq). Of the 2030 cut, 8.5% is unconditional on national resources and 19.5% is conditional on external finance, technology and capacity; NDC 2.0 (2020) had been 27% by 2030 (7% unconditional / 20% conditional). Mitigation needs an estimated USD 11,468 million across 26 PAMs in energy, IPPU, agriculture, LULUCF and waste; adaptation adds 41 measures and 155 targets in seven sectors at about USD 12,251 million (ministry launch: combined envelope above USD 23,719 million). The text newly names primera infancia, niñez and adolescencia alongside youth, gender, disability, just transition and ACE as cross-cutting elements, cites LCOY-RD and the 2025 CLAC-RD child-rights study, and lists INAIPI, CONANI and the Ministry of Youth among implementation actors. MMARN, CNCCMC and the Ministry of Finance and Economy ran the update with IDB finance. The Presidency announced readiness to deposit on 29 April 2026; MMARN held the public launch on 25 June 2026 during the first Climate Finance Week. A climate-framework statute is still not in Congress.
signals.why_it_matters: As a small-island developing state, the Dominican Republic’s residual cyclone, drought and coastal-erosion risk falls on children who will live with 2035 infrastructure and fiscal space. Registering NDC 3.0 locks a 2026–2035 emissions path, a dated finance envelope, and—unlike NDC 2.0—explicit first-childhood and youth implementation actors, so today’s energy, water and coastal choices are no longer only an adult mitigation account. Mechanism: a Paris Agreement NDC 3.0 on the UNFCCC registry, with ACE and child/youth transversal measures, still without a domestic climate law.

signals.title: Estonia Cabinet Approves Nature Restoration Plan Principles and Targets End-2026 Commission Filing After 1 September Deadline
signals.summary: On 21 May 2026 Estonia's Government Cabinet approved principles for drafting the national nature restoration plan (looduse taastamise kava) under Regulation (EU) 2024/1991. The Climate Ministry page, last updated 10 July 2026, publishes the Cabinet mandate PDF and states the final version is due at the end of 2026. The mandate itself records that Member States must submit a draft to the Commission by 1 September 2026, then explicitly says Estonia will file its draft by the end of 2026 after broad engagement, and asks the energy and climate minister to prepare a protocol decision approving the draft for the Commission by 31 December 2026. Principles include meeting the Regulation at the minimum necessary level, preferring existing programmes, applying new private-land measures outside protected areas on a voluntary basis (except urban ecosystems and river connectivity), preferring state land, and staging measures to the budget. A public involvement seminar on 14 May 2026 opened expert-group measure proposals; a 15 May ministry news item said Estonia aims to submit the plan to the Commission by year-end.

Mechanism: a Cabinet-approved NRP mandate that delays Commission filing to 31 December 2026 and makes most new private-land restoration voluntary shifts restoration costs and ecological deficit onto later cohorts and onto public land, so younger generations inherit both a later start and a narrower privately financed restoration base.

signals.title: Georgia Inserts GHG Emission Authorisation and Annual Verified MRV into the Environmental Protection Law (Law 1525 of 28 April 2026)
signals.summary: Law of Georgia No. 1525-Vმს-XIმპ of 28 April 2026, published on matsne.gov.ge on 1 May 2026, amends the 1996 Law on Environmental Protection. The official English consolidated text inserts Article 51-1 (Authorisation of greenhouse gas emissions) and Article 51-2 (Monitoring, reporting and verification of greenhouse gas emissions). Operators of activities listed by government ordinance must obtain an individual GHG-emissions authorisation from the National Environmental Agency (Civil Aviation Agency for aviation), including a monitoring-and-reporting plan; authorisation is granted for an indefinite period and is transferable. Article 51-2 requires annual GHG reports by 31 March, verified by an accredited verifier, with the granting body publishing verified reports on the environmental information portal within five business days. Matsne flags a transitional provision; at least Article 51-1(14) (portal publication of transfer acts) and the verifier definition become effective from 1 January 2028. Distinct from Ordinance 122 / NDC 3.0 (the international pledge) and from the 2023 Industrial Emissions Law whose integrated-permit articles enter force on 1 September 2026: this is the first gazetted operator-level GHG authorisation and verified annual MRV inside the Environmental Protection Law.
signals.why_it_matters: Without operator-level GHG permits and verified annual reports, NDC 3.0 targets remain a paper pledge while today’s emitters pass the residual carbon stock to later Georgian cohorts. Mechanism: a 28 April 2026 statute, published 1 May 2026, that writes indefinite GHG authorisation, monitoring plans, accredited verification and public MRV into primary environmental law, with specified clauses commencing 1 January 2028.

signals.title: Germany Transposes the EU Right-to-Repair Directive into the Civil Code from 31 July 2026
signals.source_name: Bundesgesetzblatt / Bundesministerium der Justiz und für Verbraucherschutz
signals.summary: The Gesetz zur Umsetzung der Richtlinie (EU) 2024/1799 zur Förderung der Reparatur von Waren sowie zur Verbesserung der Verfügbarkeit von Vorsorgeverfügungen was signed on 16 July 2026 (Steinmeier / Merz / Hubig) and promulgated as BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 212 on 22 July 2026. Article 1 inserts BGB Untertitel 4 “Reparaturverpflichtung des Herstellers” (§§ 479a–479g): for Annex II goods bought by consumers outside seller-liability, manufacturers must repair within a reasonable time, offer spare parts and tools at non-deterrent prices, publish typical repair prices, and must not use hardware or software that impedes independent repair (including used, compatible or 3-D-printed parts) unless justified by IP or product safety. Choosing repair once extends the original defect-claim limitation period by 12 months (§ 475e(5)). EGBGB Article 229 § 72 applies the new sales-contract rules only to contracts concluded on or after 31 July 2026. The Act entered into force the day after promulgation, except Central Precaution Register amendments on 1 October 2026. Distinct from already-ingested EU Circular Economy Act consultations and youth-check events; this is a Member State transposition statute.
signals.why_it_matters: Throwaway electronics and appliances shift material and waste costs onto the next users of the same city. A manufacturer duty to repair, with spare parts at non-deterrent prices and a 12-month guarantee bonus for choosing repair, keeps goods in use so today’s consumption does not lock later cohorts into replacement demand and landfill. Germany’s BGB text is the first large-Member-State gazette implementation of Directive 2024/1799’s 31 July 2026 application date.

signals.title: Vietnam Replaces 2021 Youth Strategy With Decision 1184/QĐ-TTg Adding Green Jobs and Climate Skills

signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Thị Thanh Trà signed Prime Ministerial Decision 1184/QĐ-TTg approving an adjusted Vietnam Youth Development Strategy 2021–2030, effective the same day and replacing Decision 1331/QĐ-TTg of 24 July 2021. signals.title: ACERWC Continental Study Recommends Child-Rights Impact Assessments for African Climate Policies and Projects
signals.source_name: African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7–8 April 2025 the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC), an African Union organ, published and launched its Continental Study on Climate Change and Children’s Rights in Africa during the 45th Ordinary Session. The study treats intergenerational equity as a core concept and, applying Article 4(1) of the African Children’s Charter (the child’s best interests as ‘the primary consideration’), states that policies and projects that may affect children in the climate context should be accompanied by a child-rights impact assessment examining effects and recommending alternatives. It also urges subjecting climate-finance execution and loss-and-damage mechanisms to CRIA, and integrating child-rights, human-rights and environmental impact assessments rather than running parallel processes. The recommendation is interpretive and recommendatory, not a binding AU regulation or a national statute.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the closest continental IIA-cousin methodology yet issued by an AU organ: it tells African Charter states who must assess what (state authorities, before climate policies, NAPs, projects and climate-finance execution), against which legal test (Article 4(1) best interests as the primary consideration, plus intergenerational equity), and with what force (Charter interpretation by the treaty body, not a self-executing CRIA regulation). It fills the Agenda 2063 gap — 2063 has no child-rights IA tool — and is distinct from the already-ingested January 2026 ACERWC African Court observations and the April 2026 47th-session decision to draft NDC/NAP child-rights guidelines.

signals.title: Austria's Binding Jugend-Check Requires Child and Youth Impact Assessment of All Federal Bills
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Since 1 January 2013 Austria's Jugend-Check has been a mandatory dimension of the federal Wirkungsorientierte Folgenabschätzung (WFA). The Federal Chancellery states that a regulation obliges every ministry to assess draft laws' effects on children and young people before adoption, as part of the two-stage WFA published with the consultation draft and government bill. Legal bases are Art. 51(8) B-VG and §§ 17–18 Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2013, implemented by the WFA-Kinder-und-Jugend-Verordnung (BGBl. II Nr. 495/2012), still in force in the RIS consolidation of 1 August 2026. Simplified screening asks whether protection, care, child-cost compensation or medium-term Zukunftssicherung of children and young adults is affected; material cases require a deeper assessment. The 2025 Youth Strategy implementation report (Ministerrat 9 July 2025) keeps Reality Checks alongside the WFA duty but does not replace it.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a binding CRWIA-style IIA cousin: ministries must complete a child-and-youth impact assessment before a federal law or major financially significant project is adopted, and the result travels with the bill. Unlike Germany's administrative Jugend-Check, Austria's duty sits in budget law and a still-current special ordinance, including a forward-looking 'future security' test. The instrument is missing from the GYC corpus despite being one of the oldest statutory youth-impact gates in Europe.

The derogatory provision expressly repeals Articles 7 and 8 of Ley 10/2023: the duty to make visible in budget-programme memoranda how spending advances wellbeing objectives for future generations, and the duty of public bodies to send large works contracts, subsidy plans and strategic projects to the Comisión for an annual impact report to Parliament. Article 6 is rewritten so the former mandatory wellbeing impact report on bills, regulations, territorial plans and sectoral plans — with a public Commission opinion and a duty to consider alternatives after an unfavourable opinion — is replaced by optional civil-society comments in prior consultation. Commission functions shrink to voluntary guidance, on-request advice 'if workload allows', and reports on matters outside Balearic competence. The delayed-entry clause that had kept Titles II–III inoperative until the Commission was constituted and guides approved is deleted, so the hollowed-out statute is immediately in force. Corpus rg found the 2023 enactment (baleares-ley-10-2023) but no 2024/2025 rollback.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a documented IIA rollback: the Balearic Government and Parliament stripped the only Iberian statute that required a wellbeing/future-generations impact assessment before budgets and norms were adopted. Mechanism lost: promoter-prepared impact reports plus Commission opinion inside the legislative and budget dossier, replaced by a non-binding orientation duty and optional consultation comments. The Commission remains on paper as a consultative body with no budget-IIA or annual evaluation mandate. For the 'does it bite?' test, Ley 10/2023 never had to prove it could change a budget because the teeth were removed before the delayed-entry conditions were met.

signals.title: Canada’s Amended Impact Assessment Act Still Requires a Sustainability Test for Present and Future Generations
signals.source_name: Justice Laws Website / Government of Canada
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Canada’s Impact Assessment Act (IAA) remains the closest federal Americas cousin to an intergenerational impact assessment, and it is missing from the GYC corpus. Section 2 defines sustainability as the ability to protect the environment, contribute to social and economic well-being, and preserve health ‘in a manner that benefits present and future generations.’ Section 22(1)(h) requires every impact assessment of a designated project to take into account the extent to which the project contributes to sustainability. Section 63(c), as amended in 2024, then forces the Minister or Governor in Council, before finding significant adverse federal effects justified in the public interest, to consider ‘the extent to which the effects that are likely to be caused by the carrying out of that project contribute to sustainability.’ The Impact Assessment Agency of Canada announced on 21 June 2024 that Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 received Royal Assent on 20 June 2024 and brought the amended IAA into force after the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2023 reference. The 2024 rewrite narrowed federal effects and the public-interest test but kept the statutory sustainability/future-generations definition and the s. 63(c) decision factor. The Justice Laws consolidation fetched on 17 August 2026 is current to a 6 August 2026 page update. This is a project-level environmental impact gate, not a general IIA for bills or budgets.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: the Impact Assessment Agency must assess, and the Minister or Governor in Council must weigh, whether a designated project’s effects contribute to sustainability defined as benefits for present and future generations, before a public-interest approval and before legally binding conditions issue under s. 64. Who: federal decision-makers on designated projects (not every law or budget). Legal force: statute; proponents must comply with decision-statement conditions. It is the strongest enacted Americas EIA-IE test found in this lane, but it is not a Wales/Italy-style IIA that screens ordinary legislation.

signals.title: CEPAL Issues a December 2025 Anticipatory-Governance Guide with Dynamic Evaluation, Not a Statutory IIA Method
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 8 December 2025 CEPAL published Guía básica de gobernanza anticipatoria (LC/MEX/TS.2025/17, 80 pages, Vargas Lama / Rosado / Oddone, Mexico subregional office). A 12 December 2025 CEPAL briefing note presents it as a practical tool for Latin American and Caribbean public officials to exit short-term reactive management. Chapter IV covers multitemporal measurement, dynamic evaluation and strategic adjustment. Recommendations include institutionalising a long-term vision, creating transversal anticipation units, establishing multitemporal legal frameworks, stable resources, public-leadership training, learning networks, state political pacts, standing citizen participation, and making monitoring a learning process. signals.title: Council of Europe Youth Ministers Adopt Reference Framework Requiring Ex-Ante and Ex-Post Human-Rights Impact Assessments
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 8–9 October 2025 in Valletta, Council of Europe youth ministers adopted a Resolution annexing the Reference Framework on a Youth Perspective, distinct from the same-day Final Declaration already in the corpus. The Framework is a three-phase method (preparation; design and implementation; monitoring and evaluation) for integrating youth views across the policy cycle. In the design phase it tells authorities to 'consider conducting' human rights-based expert impact assessments of how policies affect young people before decisions (ex-ante) and after implementation (ex-post). Guiding principles explicitly include intergenerational justice and solidarity: today's decisions must be assessed for consequences on current and future generations. Ministers invited the Joint Council on Youth to develop practical tools (guidelines, checklists, training modules). The instrument is a ministerial standard for 46 member States, not a treaty with automatic legal minimums.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first Council of Europe ministerial standard that writes youth/generational impact assessment into a shared operating method. Mechanism: member-State and CoE policymakers are asked, before adopting policies that concern young people, to run human rights-based ex-ante assessments and later ex-post evaluations involving youth organisations, with intergenerational justice as a named principle. Legal force is soft (consider/undertake) but it is the multilateral checklist that HUDERIA is not: HUDERIA is AI-specific, this Framework is general policymaking.

signals.title: Dutch Senate Instructs Government to Apply the Kinderrechtentoets to All Future Youth-Care Bills
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7 October 2025 the Dutch Senate adopted motion 36.546, I (Perin-Gopie / Volt and others) asking the government to apply the Kinderrechtentoets as standard on all future youth-care bills, to record the outcomes in the explanatory memorandum, and to inform the Senate on implementation before the Christmas recess. signals.title: Flanders Expands Mandatory JoKER Child-and-Youth Impact Reports from Under-25 to Age 30
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 13 March 2026 the Flemish Government, after Council of State advice, finally approved a draft decree amending the Youth Decree of 23 November 2023 and submitted it to the Flemish Parliament (document 754 (2025-2026) No. 1, 19 March 2026). Article 2 replaces the JoKER trigger in Article 7 — a child-and-youth impact report that must accompany every government draft decree that directly affects young people — so the duty covers persons 'up to and including 30' rather than 'younger than 25', aligning JoKER with the decree's definition of youth. JoKER itself has been statutory since 1997 (KER) and 2008 (JoKER): ministers must describe effects on children and young people with and without the proposal, plus alternatives to avoid, limit or remedy serious harm, and the report is inserted in the explanatory memorandum's impact-analysis section. The Department of Culture, Youth and Media's official JoKER page now states the duty as applying to persons through age 30. JoKER remains required only for government draft decrees, not parliamentary members' bills, government decisions, ministerial orders or circulars.
signals.why_it_matters: JoKER is a binding regional IIA cousin: before a Flemish Government draft decree is laid in Parliament, the sponsoring minister must assess effects on children and young people and publish that assessment in the explanatory memorandum. Extending the cohort from under-25 to through age 30 brings late-youth housing, work and education impacts inside a statutory pre-legislative gate rather than leaving 26–30-year-olds outside the child-impact tool. Legal force is decree-level and limited to government bills; the Youth minister and Council of State police missing reports, but JoKER does not bind budgets or administrative decisions.

policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Prime Minister's circular of 2 May 2016 makes a 'clause d'impact jeunesse' mandatory in the ex-ante evaluation of government bills and regulatory texts. signals.title: Ghana Enacts Environmental Protection Act 1124 Making Intergenerational Equity a Guiding Principle for EIA Enforcement
signals.source_name: Environmental Protection Authority of Ghana / Parliament of Ghana
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 6 January 2025 the President of Ghana assented to the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124), gazetted as the 1,124th Act of Parliament. The statute repeals the Environmental Protection Agency Act, 1994 (Act 490), reconstitutes the regulator as the Environmental Protection Authority, and consolidates pesticides, hazardous-waste, e-waste and climate-response functions. Section 3(2)(b)(iii) requires the Authority to ensure compliance with laid-down environmental assessment procedures in the planning and implementation of policies, plans, programmes and projects. Section 29 lets the Authority require an environmental assessment of an undertaking, issue or renew an environmental permit, and block other organs of state from granting environment-affecting licences until the Authority has given written confirmation of EA compliance. Part Six section 161 then directs that, to ensure compliance with the Act, the Authority and other concerned persons shall be guided by five principles, including intergenerational equity. Section 170 defines intergenerational equity as meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs, and defines an undertaking as a policy, plan, programme or project. The Authority later hosted companion Environmental Protection (Environmental Assessment) Regulations, 2025 (L.I. 2504) on its laws page as the replacement for L.I. 1652.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a 2025 African parent statute for environmental assessment that newly names intergenerational equity as a mandatory enforcement guide, not merely a constitutional slogan. Mechanism: before an environmental permit issues under section 29, and before other licensing bodies may approve an environment-affecting activity, the Environmental Protection Authority and concerned persons must apply the section 161(b) intergenerational-equity principle as defined in section 170, covering policies, plans, programmes and projects. Legal force is binding statute in force from 6 January 2025; the 2025 assessment regulations (L.I. 2504) are the procedural vehicle, but the IE test sits in the Act itself.

signals.title: Hungary's Ombudsman Act Requires a Formal Opinion on Draft Laws and Plans Directly Affecting Future Generations
signals.source_name: Office of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights (AJBH)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Act CXI of 2011 on the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights, published in official English translation by the Commissioner's office, creates a standing statutory impact-review duty distinct from Hungary's 2025 climate-act annulment. Section 2(2) provides that the Commissioner shall give an opinion on draft legislation affecting his or her tasks and competences, on long-term development and spatial planning plans and concepts, and on plans and concepts otherwise directly affecting the quality of life of future generations, and may propose amendment or drafting of fundamental-rights legislation. Section 1(2)(b) requires special attention, including ex officio proceedings, to the interests of future generations as defined in Article P of the Fundamental Law. Section 3(1) assigns the Deputy Commissioner responsible for future generations (who may use the title Ombudsman for Future Generations) to monitor those interests, warn of rights infringements affecting future generations, propose ex officio inquiries and Constitutional Court referrals, monitor Parliament's sustainable development strategy, and propose legislation on the rights of future generations. This is an ombudsman opinion-and-challenge power over others' drafts, not a ministry-authored generational impact assessment that must accompany every government bill.
signals.why_it_matters: Hungary's IIA-equivalent is a binding review gate inside the NHRI, not an AIR-style VIG. Mechanism: before draft laws, long-term development plans, spatial plans, or other concepts that directly affect future generations' quality of life proceed, the Commissioner must be able to issue a statutory opinion; the Future Generations Deputy can escalate to investigation or Constitutional Court review. Legal force: Act CXI of 2011, still in force, with the Deputy using the Ombudsman for Future Generations title. This instrument was missing from the corpus as an impact-review statute; the existing operational-ombudsman signal covers continued activity and the climate ruling, not the Section 2(2) opinion duty on drafts and plans.

signals.title: Ireland Department of Finance Publishes Future Forty, a First 40-Year Fiscal Outlook to 2065
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 4 November 2025 Finance Minister Paschal Donohoe published Future Forty: A Fiscal and Economic Outlook to 2065, the Department of Finance's first Australia-IGR-style 40-year no-policy-change assessment of Ireland's public finances. The Strategic Economic Development Unit modelled a Central Scenario plus 2,187 alternatives covering demographics, climate, housing, healthcare, digitalisation, deglobalisation and EU enlargement. In the Central Scenario, age-related spending, slowing productivity and falling corporation-tax receipts drive the annual deficit toward 7.9% of GNI* and national debt to 148% of GNI* by 2065, with a narrowing window to 2037 in which the deficit stays below 3% of GNI*. The full report states that acting now on spending prioritisation would 'prevent an unsustainable debt burden on future generations' and cites Australia's 2023 Intergenerational Report as a comparator.

Mechanism: Department of Finance Strategic Economic Development Unit publishes a recurring long-horizon fiscal test so today's expenditure choices can be judged against the debt left to later cohorts. It is Ireland's first official IGR analogue and is missing from the corpus.

signals.title: Justice Canada Publishes a Federal Child Rights Impact Assessment Tool, Still Voluntary for Cabinet
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 11 July 2023 Justice Canada launched a Child Rights Impact Assessment (CRIA) tool and 2.5-hour e-learning course, still live on the departmental site (page dated 25 July 2023; tool page fetched 17 August 2026). The tool is designed primarily for federal officials developing a law, policy, program or other initiative. It is grounded in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, complements Gender-Based Analysis Plus, and uses a two-stage process: an early screening, then a full CRIA if any direct, indirect, intended or unintended child-rights effects are identified, including mitigation and, where possible, children’s views. Bill S-212 (National Strategy for Children and Youth Act), which passed the Senate on 10 March 2026 and received first reading in the House on 12 March 2026, requires a national strategy with indicators and parliamentary reporting but does not create a CRIA duty. New Brunswick’s 2013 Cabinet CRIA, often cited as North America’s first mandatory CRIA, could not be confirmed on a current official gnb.ca page in 2025–26.

Legal force: administrative guidance only — not a Cabinet or statutory mandate — so it is a cousin CRWIA, not an enacted IIA. signals.title: Mexican Senators Table a Constitutional Duty to Evaluate Long-Term Fiscal Impacts of Public Debt
signals.source_name: SIL / Senado de la República (Comisión Permanente)
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7 May 2025, PRI senators led by Alejandro Moreno Cárdenas filed with the Permanent Commission an initiative to reform Constitution Article 25 and add Article 134 Bis on equidad fiscal intergeneracional. The official SIL PDF (asun_4904191, 11 June 2025) would require the State to consider fiscal equity between present and future generations in national development, and would bind every federal, state and municipal public-debt contract to financial sustainability, transparency and intergenerational responsibility. Proposed 134 Bis would oblige the State to evaluate, justify and limit indebtedness: debt preferably for long-term public investment; no current-expenditure borrowing except national emergency; secondary laws to create ‘mecanismos de evaluación técnica y participación ciudadana para valorar los impactos fiscales a largo plazo’; a federal Fondo de Amortización Intergeneracional; and a national debt register for the states. Transitories give Congress 180 days for secondary legislation and the Executive 12 months to propose the fund. This is distinct from the 30 June 2025 García Medina bills for a Senate Comisión de Futuro already in the corpus. No DOF publication or enacted text was found. Sections 17 and 21 repeal Public Finance Act 1989 s 26KB (wellbeing objectives that had to guide Budget decision-making and be explained in the Fiscal Strategy Report) and s 26NB (Treasury's at-least-four-yearly wellbeing report, first published as Te Tai Waiora in 2022). Finance Minister Nicola Willis's Beehive release on passage said the Act 'removes the need for Treasury to report on wellbeing' so it can focus on core economic and fiscal advice. Treasury's stewardship page was updated 16 June 2026 to record the repeal.

After the repeal, neither duty binds the Budget Policy Statement or Fiscal Strategy Report. signals.title: New Zealand RMA Replacement Bills Drop the Statutory Future-Generations Test from Environmental Assessment
signals.source_name: New Zealand Legislation / Ministry for the Environment
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 9 December 2025 the New Zealand Government introduced the Natural Environment Bill (234-1) and the companion Planning Bill (235-1) to replace the Resource Management Act 1991. The RMA’s purpose clause (section 5), still in force as at 10 February 2026, defines sustainable management as managing resources in a way that enables people and communities to provide for their well-being while sustaining the potential of natural and physical resources (excluding minerals) to meet the reasonably foreseeable needs of future generations. The Natural Environment Bill’s official explanatory note instead states that clause 4’s purpose is only to establish a framework for the use, protection, and enhancement of the natural environment, and lists goals of enabling resource use within environmental limits, safeguarding life-supporting capacity, protecting human health from contaminants, no net loss of indigenous biodiversity, risk-based natural-hazard planning, and provision for Māori interests — with no future-generations or sustainable-management purpose. The Ministry for the Environment’s RMA-reform page records introduction on 9 December 2025 and an aim to pass the Bills in 2026. As of August 2026 the Bills had been reported back from the Environment Select Committee and given a second reading on 4 August 2026; they had not received Royal assent. Remaining future-generations language in the Planning Bill is confined to identified Māori land being retained for present and future generations of owners, not a general environmental-assessment test.
signals.why_it_matters: New Zealand’s live environmental-assessment statute is one of the few common-law EIA regimes with an explicit future-generations purpose test that consent authorities must apply before granting resource consents. The 2025–26 replacement Bills would repeal that test and substitute limit-setting and development-enabling goals that do not name future generations. Mechanism at stake: RMA s5 currently forces every resource-consent and plan decision to ask whether the rate of resource use sustains resources for reasonably foreseeable future generations; if the Bills pass, that statutory IIA-style criterion disappears from environmental impact assessment. Legal force today is still the RMA; the Bills are a live rollback proposal, not yet law.

signals.title: New Zealand Treasury Publishes Budget 2026 Child Poverty Report Required by Public Finance Act s15EA
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On Budget Day 28 May 2026 the Minister of Finance presented the Child Poverty Report 2026 (Te Pōharatanga Tamariki), a statutory companion to Budget 2026. Section 15EA of the Public Finance Act 1989 requires the minister to report to the House on progress against Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 targets and to indicate whether, and to what extent, Budget measures will affect child poverty.
